Very fine is the preparation of the gills of Hexanchus griseus perfused with colored wax to emphasize the respiratory vessels. Thirty liquid (alcohol or formalin) preserved specimens show different apparatuses. Our work deals also on the hystological collections of slides representing microscopic structures like the electric lobes of the brain of Torpedo and other.

22128: The degree of selectivity exhibited by juvenile lemon sharks towards a prey species was determined by presenting individual sharks with differing relative abundances of two prey species and recording the prey choice. The majority of studies on elasmobranch diet have reported the prey items found in the stomach of a number of sharks however, the extent to which an elasmobranch specialises on one prey type has never been demonstrated. Similarly it is unclear whether sharks display periodicity when feeding or are asynchronous and consume prey at all times of the day or night. Individual sharks were exposed to differing relative abundances of two prey species. An electivity index (E*) and a chi squared goodness of fit test were used to elucidate the selectivity of the sharks. Further analysis enabled the sharks’ functional response curve towards the prey items to be determined and any size selection in prey items identified. Stomach contents of the sharks were analysed to identify the times that feeding took place. Results demonstrated that at all abundances of prey the sharks were highly species selective towards yellowfin mojarra (mean E* 0.326) whilst displaying almost complete negative selection for grey snapper (mean E* -0.939). A type II functional response curve (r2= 0.9121) supported evidence that sharks are specialist predators. No size selection of prey items was observed. Stomach content analysis indicated that sharks are asynchronous feeders. The selectivity of sharks arises as a result of the behavioural and morphological characteristics of the prey species.

22129: The basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is the world’s second largest fish and has been exploited by humans for at least two hundred years. There is current concern that past fisheries have reduced populations to low levels and that some stocks still show little signs of recovery. The basking shark is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and was recently included on Appendix II of CITES. To address these concerns, scientific information on the status of specific populations needs to be collected. However, to date there have been few attempts to identify preferred habitats of basking sharks, their distribution and movements, and no reliable estimates of population size have been made. In response to the urgent need for comprehensive information on this species the Esmée Fairbairn Foundation funded a project initiated by the Marine Biological Association (MBA) to collate and combine behavioural, survey and sightings data of basking sharks collected by six UK charities into a single, unique database. The six consortium partners are the MBA, Marine Conservation Society, Marine Environmental Research/UK Wildlife Trusts, Hebridean Whale and Dolphin Trust, International Fund for Animal Welfare, and The Shark Trust. These data will help define their critical habitat in UK waters, resulting in the first practical information for assessing the appropriateness of the present UK marine protected area for endangered basking sharks and whether extension of this zone is required. This information will be vital for identifying population trends and in establishing future conservation and management plans for this species.

22130: Vertebral sections of four captive specimens of sandbar shark, Carcharhinus plumbeus, were analysed. Comparisons were made between different planes of sectioning and different vertebrae. Two of these specimens were neonates, showing only the birth mark in their vertebral centra, and they allowed validating the location of the hatching mark. The largest specimen, a female 200cm TL, lived 5 months in aquaria after being captured, and presented 22 rings in its vertebral centra. The last specimen, a young female 90.5cm TL, was born in captivity, and presented one clear annual mark and an additional mark which was interpreted as a stress mark. The measurement of distances between consecutive marks allowed estimating individual growth rates in the two largest specimens.

22131: Amid concern about the status of skates and rays in Welsh waters the present work set out to provide up-to-date information on the population biology of the thornback ray Raja clavata in North Wales. The von Bertalanffy growth parameters for males were Linf = 100.9cm, k = 0.18yr-1 and t0 = -0.95yrs, while Linf = 117.6cm, k = 0.16yr-1 and t0 = -0.7yrs for females. Male R. clavata reached 50% maturity at a total length of 58.8cm and 3.9yrs, which was smaller and younger than females for whom L50 and A50 were 70.5cm and 5.3yrs, respectively. Although previously over-exploited, the present estimate of total mortality (Z) was 0.48-0.49yr-1 which, in terms of replacement mortality (calculated as 0.7 yr-1), suggests no immediate prospect of recruitment failure. The potential for the recovery of a depleted population is discussed in relation to the Allee effect, along with recommendations for future studies into population genetic structure that could be incorporated into the development of effective conservation and management strategies.
22132: Planktivorous free-ranging elasmobranchs, such as Cetorhinus maximus (basking shark), feed in neritic and pelagic environments circumglobally. Within these environments they can exploit oceanographic features (e.g.) frontal systems, which aggregate zooplankton prey and support primary and secondary productivity. Using movement trajectories reconstructed from pop-up archival tagging, zooplankton abundance data from the Continuous Plankton Recorder Survey and satellite derived sea surface temperature we investigate basking shark habitat utilisation. Real-time coincident monitoring and subsequent mapping of forage availability on comparable temporal and spatial scales to basking sharks is not practicable. However, the CPR Survey provides a unique data source from which to recreate the most probable prey fields encountered by these planktivores. Using a numerical modelling based approach we investigate the prey encountered by these planktivores. When integrated, forage availability and thermal conditions are most likely to determine movements on both coarse and fine scales; as such our approach attempts to understand movement in context with the heterogeneous environment in which these animals live.

22133: This paper describes the spatial distribution and morphometric characteristics of four specimens of the smooth hammerhead shark, Sphyrna zygaena, caught in shallow coastal waters, during a pelagic survey carried out in Angolan waters by R/V 'Dr. Fridtjof Nansen' in July-August 2003. The individuals were caught in two stations with a bottom trawl. Morphometric measurements were taken and the determination of stomach content and presence of parasites were made macroscopically on board the vessel. The preys were identified to the lowest taxa possible. All specimens were immature males with full stomachs. Morphometric measurements were expressed as a percentage of total length for each specimen caught. The stomachs contained mostly digested remains of fish. There is no other published record of S. zygaena from Angolan waters; therefore this record represents an extension of its distributional range. 22134: Larval anurans are found in a variety of aquatic habitats ranging from ephemeral to permanent waters. Species with long larval stages are constrained from inhabiting ephemeral pools because they will die when the pools dry. However, hydroperiod cannot explain why some species with short larval stages tend not to inhabit permanent water sites. Susceptibility to predation may explain this phenomenon. Predation seems to be a major role in shaping larval anuran communities. Permanent water bodies are dominated by fish species while ephemeral habitats contain smaller invertebrate predators. Permanent water breeding species may possess anti-predator mechanisms that allow them to coexist with predators. There are two types of anti- predator mechanisms: (1) Primary anti-predator mechanisms are defined as those mechanisms that protect an organism prior to attack, and (2) Secondary anti-predator mechanisms are defined as those that protect an organism after the initial attack (i.e. unpalatability). I present data on the latter. There are 13 species of anurans in eastern Texas that range from permanent to ephemeral pond breeders. 22135: One goal of the Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative (ARMI) is to quantify changes in amphibian occurrence on DOI lands in the USA. 22136: Several studies have been conducted on the California coast investigating the distribution and abundance patterns of rocky intertidal fishes; however, most of these studies have focused on only one or two sites along a large expanse of coastline. 22137: Delayed maturity, extended longevity, and extreme iteroparity are cornerstones of the life history suite common to most turtle species. 22138: The manifold results of human encroachment have been suggested as the cause of population declines and range contraction of the wood turtle (Glyptemys insculpta) over much of its geographic distribution in eastern North America. 22139: Tail autotomy is widespread in the squamates. The ability of lizards and some snakes to separate their caudal region is an innovative means of escaping predators. 22140: Hylid frogs of the species Phrynohyas venulosa (Laurenti, 1768) occur from the northeastern Mexican state of Tamaulipas to the eastern Argentinian province of Entre Rios. 22141: The goal of this research is to determine if amphibians choose to lay eggs in ponds that have fewer competitors and predators than in adjacent ponds that have neither. 22142: This study was designed to describe the reproductive biology of a sample of wild caught brown treesnakes (Boiga irregularis) and to determine the effect of increased food intake (nutrition) on the development of the testis and sexual segment of the kidney, and on sperm storage in the vas deferens in captive males. 22143: Much research is presently aimed at documenting and understanding the causes of declines of amphibian populations. Data are often collected as time series of abundances in populations. It is generally recognized that most amphibian populations fluctuate naturally, and practical limitations ensure that most population studies are of limited temporal and spatial extent. Natural fluctuations make the results of relatively short-term, small scale studies difficult to interpret. One approach that has been used to circumvent this problem is to combine the results of many such studies and look for general trends. Attempting to determine whether the fluctuations in a large set of population studies differ from those expected in naturally-fluctuating populations requires the specification of a general null hypothesis for the behavior of fluctuating populations. One intuitively appealing hypothesis is that fluctuating populations should increase and decrease on average equally often and in equal amounts; this has been used as the null hypothesis in at least one frequently cited synthetic study. I demonstrate that this null hypothesis is not general, and that depending upon how natural populations are structured and regulated, many other patterns of behavior may be found in short-term, small-scale studies of naturally fluctuating populations. One common pattern of behavior is local populations that decrease more frequently than they increase, which can be caused by metapopulation processes or by the combination of storage effects due to age structure and variation in recruitment. There is therefore no simple universal null hypothesis for the behavior of fluctuating populations. Any attempt to determine whether an observed population time series or set of time series departs from natural fluctuations must ensure that a biologically appropriate null hypothesis is tested. This is likely to complicate attempts at synthesis, as it is likely that different null hypotheses are appropriate for different populations and taxa.

22144: The genus Profundulus, the sole member of the family Profundulidae, currently contains five species endemic to Central America. 22145: Under contract to the Ocean Resources Enhancement and Hatchery Program (OREHP) of the California Department of Fish and Game, nearshore coastal and embayment areas off southern California were sampled to determine the spatial and size distributions, seasonality, and abundance of young white seabass in the shallow (5-10 m) nearshore waters from Santa Barbara south to Silver Strand off San Diego. 22148: Qualitatively, the pattern of embryonic development among turtles, crocodilians, lepidosaurs, and birds is very similar. The general question addressed by this research was whether development is quantitatively similar as well. Comparative studies were conducted using normal tables of development and associated data for incubation temperature, time elapsed between developmental events, and hatchling mass. One issue addressed was the effect of temperature on the rate of development. During the first half of development the rate of development was highly correlated with incubation temperature. During the latter half of development, however, developmental rate was independent of temperature. Overall, temperature accounted for essentially all variation in developmental rate; embryo size (as assessed by hatchling mass) and taxonomic identity explained little to no residual variation. The second issue addressed was whether morphological features appear at the same sequence and at the same relative time during development. Taxonomic differences in the sequence of developmental stages were apparent. For example, limb buds appear before or at the same time as the allantois for turtles, crocodilians, and birds. By contrast, the allantois appears well before limb buds for lizards. The relative time when developmental events occur was a function of temperature across taxa; the higher the incubation temperature the relatively earlier in development specific developmental events occurred. Results suggest that the stage of development as well as temperature should be controlled in experimental studies that assess the effect of incubation temperature on individual phenotypes post-hatching. Results further suggest that comparative data on developmental chronology is a potential source of phylogenetically informative data.

22149: Heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) is a stress response protein inducible through exposure to endocrine disrupting pollutants, such as organochlorine pesticides. 22150: Recent interest in sperm competition has led to a re-evaluation of the "cheap sperm" assumption inherent in many studies of sexual selection. In particular mounting evidence suggests that male sperm availability can be increased by the presence of females. However, there is no information as far as we know on how sperm availability is affected when males are paired with conspecific and heterospecific females. Understanding these effects on sperm production may be especially important in species assemblages consisting of unisexual gynogenetic species that sexually parasitize males of a bisexual species. This study examines the effect on male sperm availability of female presence (conspecific and heterospecific), male body size, and female body size in the Sailfin Molly, Poecilia latipinna. 22152: Roads are the veins of the developed world permeating almost every landscape in the United States. The impacts of this infrastructure are of increasing concern and intrigue to wildlife biologists. Snakes are an ideal organism of investigation having suffered from road mortality that has been documented for over half a century. While it can be assumed that mortality is threatening to the population viability of animals surrounding the road, the extent of road impacts beyond roadkill remains unknown. Due to species-specific ecological tendencies, such as activity patterns and habitat use, it can be ascertained that different species suffer from differing effects of roads. For instance, the road could pose a threat to a fossorial species with avian predators that does not readily enter open spaces such that it avoids crossing, restricting its range to its respective side. Significant levels of avoidance would result in habitat fragmentation, disrupting metapopulation dynamics and leading to genetic isolation. A scientific identification of which species are most vulnerable to which effects is essential to mitigate wildlife impacts of existing roads and effectively design transportation systems in the future. Additionally, responses to passing vehicles (i.e., freeze or flee) are examined to determine differential likelihood of being hit by a vehicle due to prolonged or reduced time spent crossing the road. 22153: Understanding how species coexist in the face of limiting resources is a central focus of evolutionary ecology. 22157: The nasal capsule of frogs is a highly complex, but poorly known morphological assembly. Because the cartilages of the capsule are difficult to identify using traditional methods of dissection and/or clearing-and-staining, they are rarely described. Thus, the nasal morphology of only a few species is known in any detail. The elements of the nasal capsule are important in that they provide support to the olfactory apparatus and the vomeronasal organ, they help close the nares during diving, and they depress to reduce buccal cavity volume during swallowing. Because of their many functions, we might expect that nasal morphology is highly constrained. However, comparisons of the capsules of species for which the morphology is known suggest that their structures are highly variable. Herein, we compare the nasal apparatus of several families of frogs (including bominatorids, pelobatids, pelodytids, pipids, ranids, hylids, and bufonids) using both traditional methods and 3D digital reconstructions (archived in the MorphologyNet digital library, http://www.morphologynet.org). We comment on structures that are conserved throughout frogs, identify structures that are highly variable, and discuss the possible functional implications of differences. We also note the potential phylogenetic utility of the information we assembled.

22158: Ambystomatid salamanders have a generalized body plan, making them ideal models to provide baseline developmental data to which more specialized salamanders can be compared. A thorough examination of the development of several species could lead to a better understanding of the evolution of adult variation and to more detailed knowledge of developmental patterns in these generalized salamanders. Herein, I compare the development of the larval chondrocranium and cranial ossification of several ambystomatid species using linear and geometric morphometric analyses. Additionally, I comment on the potential implications of my results in regard to cranial development and variation in degree of ossification in the group.

22159: The developmental osteology of pelobatid frogs (Anura: Pelobatidae) has been the subject of several studies. Despite this, little is known about the cause of the extreme variation in degree of adult cranial ossification within the group. Pelodytes and Spea are gracile, poorly ossified frogs, whereas Pelobates and Scaphiopus are robust and hyperossified. We used linear and geometric morphometric methods to analyze size-related shape change in the series. 22160: Phylogenetic relationships among New World and eastern Atlantic species in the belonid genera Strongylura and Tylosurus were hypothesized using 3689 bp of nucleotide sequence; including the entire mitochondrial (mtDNA) ATP synthase 6 and 8 genes; partial cytochrome b 12S and 16S ribosomal genes; and introns and exons, 2 and 3 of the nuclear-encoded creatine kinase B gene. 22161: Invertebrate predation in larval fish can increase mortality and lead to a weak year-class and ultimately poor recruitment for some fish species. Although predation by vertebrates, particularly fish, is more common and widely understood, predation by cyclopoid copepods may also have an effect on larval fish recruitment. This predation may have a more significant impact in aquaculture due to the reduced environmental space and lack of alternative food sources. In this laboratory study, the effect of cyclopoid copepod predation on the survival of larval yellow perch (Perca flavescens) was measured. Additionally, the effect of adding another food source (rotifers) to the experimental set-up was determined. Twenty-four 9.5-liter aquaria were used for six treatments with four replicates each. Varying densities of rotifers and copepods were applied across these treatments. Survival of the larval perch was measured daily by counting the number of dead perch. A one-way ANOVA was used on these data. A significant difference was found between treatments suggesting cyclopoid copepods are affecting the survival of larval yellow perch. However, there was not a statistically significant difference between the treatments containing both copepods and rotifers, suggesting that prey switching is not occurring. Copepods were also observed feeding on both dead and living larval perch throughout the experiment. Cyclopoid copepod predation on larval P. flavescens appears to have a significant impact on larval fish survival and may ultimately affect recruitment in this fish species

22162: We investigated variation of incidental captured turtle mortality in response to environmental factors and passive fishing techniques using Long Term Resource Monitoring Program data. Furthermore, we were interested in what percentage of turtles died from passive fishing techniques and what technique(s) caused the most turtle mortality. 22163: Understanding the effects of boundaries is critical for calculating the effective area of habitats within preserves and long-term viability of wildlife populations. I examined the distribution of aeolian-sand-dwelling flat-tailed horned lizards, Phrynosoma mcallii, and Coachella Valley fringe-toed lizards, Uma inornata, adjacent to suburban development. Edge influences differ between these two lizard species, with a more pronounced effect on horned lizards. This difference appears to correlate with activity patterns and susceptibility to avian predators. A lack of arborescent nest sites and hunting perches in sand dune habitats limits the impact of avian predation on lizard populations. However, where protected habitats abut urban areas, planted trees and power poles provide avian predators with enhanced opportunities to prey on lizards. Increased predation results in reduced lizard occupancy, especially for flat-tailed horned lizards, as far as 200 m from preserve edges. Identifying this edge effect allows managers to potentially alter habitat features that avian predators find attractive, and increase effective preserve size and improve lizard population viability.

22164: The Coachella Valley of southern California is one of the fastest developing areas in a region of exploding human population. The valley floor was once dominated by 30,000 ha of aeolian sand dunes providing habitat for a rich community of plants and animals, including many endemics. While our research examines the breadth of floral and faunal components to this community, here we focus on two lizard species, the endemic Coachella Valley fringe-toed lizard, Uma inornata, and the northwestern-most population of the flat-tailed horned lizard, Phrynosoma mcallii. Both of these lizards are arenicolus, restricted or nearly restricted to aeolian sand habitats. Within this habitat, each species appears to select different microhabitats. These differences hint at the complexity and difficulty of accurately determining species distributions in remaining habitat fragments. We compared spatial modeling techniques to predict habitat availability for each species and to describe changes in lizard distribution due to habitat loss. The models include a simple layered GIS coverage model and a more complex statistical model using Mahalanobis Distance. Models incorporate objective microhabitat characterizations based on reflectance values from satellite imagery. We generated initial models using historic distributional data for each lizard and then validated each model with field data collected in 2003. The models were then recreated using just 2003 data to determine potential changes in distributions of these species over the past 20-30 years. Results of spatial modeling efforts focus research on identifying and quantifying factors that restrict species distribution. The results are incorporated into on-going efforts to create a system of preserves within the Coachella Valley to protect remnants of the dynamic community that once dominated this region.

22165: The USGS Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative (ARMI) is charged with providing essential scientific information to support effective management actions in order to arrest or reverse amphibian population declines. Predictive models that illustrate how amphibians use the landscape would be valuable for designing surveys, studying habitat relationships, and developing land management plans to conserve amphibian populations. We are building geospatial models of landscape suitability for amphibians in Yellowstone National Park (YNP) that integrate the elements of both breeding (wetland) and terrestrial habitat requirements. We modeled breeding habitats using a statistical probability approach that incorporated an ancillary model of potential available wetlands, additional predictor variables (e.g., landforms, surficial geology, vegetative cover), and ARMI survey data on actual amphibian wetland use. A subset of reserved ARMI survey data was used for validation of the breeding habitat model results. Terrestrial habitats were modeled based on first principles of environmental biophysics by using mechanistic models of amphibian physiology (developed by Warren Porter, University of Wisconsin- Madison) in conjunction with surface models of weather and vegetation cover density. To estimate the ability of amphibians to regulate body temperature and water loss under different terrestrial conditions, the terrestrial models were calibrated based on distance from wetland habitat as well as biophysical features specific to each of the four amphibian species that inhabit YNP. Initial results showed that the breeding habitat models seemed to capture the distribution of breeding habitats across YNP well. Model refinement is underway to improve breeding habitat predictions. Future efforts will focus on integrating the outputs from the breeding and terrestrial models into landscape suitability maps.

22166: Amphibians occupy a range of habitats throughout the world, but species richness is greatest in regions with moist, warm climates. We investigate relations among climate patterns, location, and amphibian species richness for seven regions in the continental U.S. by using multivariate regression models. Independent model variables are 30-year (1960-99) annual mean climate statistics, location defined as county polygon centroids (x-coordinate and y-coordinate), and mean elevation. The climate data are derived from more than 5,000 first-order meteorological stations and are averaged by or interpolated to counties or minor civil division (MCD) boundaries. The dependent model variables are estimates of anuran (frog and toad) and caudate (salamander) species richness by county or MCD from the USGS Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative (ARMI) National Atlas for Amphibian Distributions. Multivariate regression models of anuran species richness for the seven ARMI regions have adjusted R-squared values ranging from 0.11 to 0.66. Precipitation is a statistically significant, positively related independent variable in anuran models from five regions, and minimum temperature is a statistically significant, positively related independent variable in four regional models. Solar radiation is a statistically significant, inversely related independent variable in three regional models. Models of caudate species richness have adjusted R-squared values ranging from 0.14 to 0.74. Precipitation is a statistically significant, positively related independent variable in five regional caudate models. Minimum temperature is a statistically significant variable in four regional models and is inversely related in three of those regions. Solar radiation is a significant variable in four regional models and is positively related in three of those regions. During the 30-year period, there were trends in many of the climate statistics. The magnitudes of these trends and the regressions models by region are used to map areas in the continental U.S. where amphibian species are potentially under stress from or the beneficiary of recent changes in climatic conditions.

22167: The Bavayia cyclura group is a clade of relatively non-descript arboreal diplodactylid geckos endemic to New Caledonia. Three morphologically distinctive species have hitherto been recognized. We investigated relationships among members of the group using 1478 aligned bp from the ND2 gene and 5 tRNAs from more than 100 ingroup samples as well as morphological data from more than 500 individuals. We identified 19 putative species within the clade as a whole. A large montane form from an isolated locality in southern New Caledonia is the sister group to all remaining taxa. Three other major clades are retrieved: 1) a group of seven taxa from central and northern inland areas; 2) a group of four taxa from the far north of the island as well as both east and west coasts and several isolated massifs; and 3) a group of seven taxa from low to middle elevation localities around the main island and from the Loyalty Islands and the Isle of Pines. All putative species identified on the basis of sequence data correspond to groups that are both morphologically homogeneous and geographically coherent. Our data suggest that the Bavayia cyclura group, like other New Caledonian reptiles, exhibits extreme microendemism. Further, congruent patterns of area relationship across the three major subclades in the group support the hypothesis that common geological events, probably in the late Tertiary, have promoted cladogenesis in each.

22168: Since 1984, teams of ichthyologists have conducted a broadly-based annual sampling effort at a three-day tournament known as the Alabama Deep Sea Fishing Rodeo (ADSFR). Even after 20 years, this program continues to yield many research and community benefits to ichthyology. The ADSFR routinely attracts 3000 anglers who target 30 species of bay, near-shore and offshore gamefishes ranging from elasmobranchs and tarpon to an array of acanthomorphs. Thanks to the generosity of anglers and tournament organizers, large sample sizes for these targeted species have been made available for basic and applied studies. Especially important are incidental catches by anglers, which have yielded more than 200 additional species including gars, eels, anglerfishes, scombroids, carangoids, tetraodontiforms, flatfishes and many others. Specimens of all species sampled have been deposited in permanent natural history collections, chiefly the American Museum of Natural History in New York. We record standard measurements and data for each processed specimen. Most are prepared as partially articulated dry skeletons (using methods explained elsewhere) to allow detailed comparative osteological study. In 1998, we began preserving tissues samples (for DNA sequencing) for selected specimens and taxa, and in 2002 began to photographically document specimens prior to preparation. Because of the ADSFR and generous help from the Dauphin Island Sea Lab (DISL) we have trained nearly 100 research students. Our collecting approach has great potential to facilitate comparative anatomical and systematic studies, but less power to examine trends in abundance or diversity. Nevertheless, two points can be made. First, we continue annually to recover species not previously recorded from the ADSFR. Second, some years produce unusual clusters of abundance of taxa that have not been seen for years. Many publications in systematic ichthyology have benefited from this broadly-based collecting effort and its many intellectual offshoots, and we hope to stimulate interest in developing similar sampling efforts in other regions. 22169: The Rio Grande Silvery Minnow (Hybognathus amarus) is an endangered cyrpinid that is now confined to the middle Rio Grande of New Mexico. Hybognathus amarus spawns semi-buoyant pelagic eggs, consequently much of the annual production of offspring is moved downstream with river currents after spawning. The Rio Grande is now highly fragmented by dams and other diversion structures that impede upstream movement of fish. Long-term monitoring of temporal and spatial genetic variation in H. amarus indicates that the genetic effective size Ne is three orders of magnitude smaller than census size. A potential explanation of low Ne/N is high variance in individual reproductive success that is exacerbated by annual loss of reproductive output by entrainment through diversion dams. Loss of production would exert maximal effect on variance in reproductive success if groups of genetically related eggs were subject to mortality that varies in space and time. The aim of this study was to test the following two null hypotheses: (i) that eggs do not differ in genetic composition among samples collected at a single locality over the reproductive season in 2003; and (ii) that each sample of eggs collected over the reproductive season in 2003 comprises a random subset of breeding adult genes that is representative of the entire population. Genetic screening of eggs using partial sequence from the mtDNA ND4 gene and seven microsatellite markers suggests strong temporal variability among egg samples, implicating high variance in reproductive success as an important factor for lowering genetic diversity in the wild population of H. amarus. Mitochondrial DNA indicates that genetic composition of the eggs is representative of the adult population. The microsatellite data contrasts with this, suggesting that the eggs are not representative of the adult population.

22170: Notropis rubellus species group is a widespread species complex with a disjunct highlands distribution occurring in the unglaciated regions of the Central Highlands and glaciated regions of the Central Lowlands. Until recently N. rubellus was considered a single widespread species exhibiting geographic variation in morphological characters. However, several recent studies have revealed that N. rubellus is a diverse species complex with closely related species endemic to drainages within each highland region. Based primarily on morphological measurements N. suttkusi was described as endemic to tributaries of the Red River draining the Ouachita Highlands. Subsequently, five species were identified within the complex based on geographic variation of allozyme products; N. rubellus (Great Lakes drainages, upper Ohio River drainage above the Green River, northern Atlantic Slope drainages and Cumberland River above Cumberland Falls), N. micropteryx (Green, Cumberland below Cumberland Falls, and Tennessee rivers), N. percobromus (Ouachita and Arkansas rivers, Ozark drainages, upper Mississippi and Wabash river drainages), N. suttkusi and N. sp. (New River). 22172: Cardinalfish occur on every coral reef in all tropical and subtropical waters worldwide and yet, despite this ubiquity, the systematic relationships of the apogonid taxa are poorly understood. The primary objective of this study was to use cladistic methodologies to generate hypotheses of the evolutionary relationships among the genera and subgenera of the family. The results suggest that revision of the generic and sub-generic relationships within the family is necessary, including the possible splitting of Apogon and the raising of a number of subgenera to generic status.

22173: Turtles are characteristically known for their shells, which control the flexibility of their internal volume, retard growth rates, and limit copulating position possibilities. But these shells have allowed turtles to survive extinction in a croc eat all environment since the Triassic. We analyzed the marks left by frustrated predators, such as crocodiles and piranhas, on the shells and limbs of Podocnemis sextuberculata in the Reserva de Desenvolvimento Sustentavel Mamiraua, Amazonas, Brasil. Between February and October 2002 we captured 946 turtles in trammel nets. We noted all indicators of possible predation attempts (broken or missing marginal scutes, scares on the carapace and plastron, full or partial foot amputations). All turtles were measured, marked, and returned to the river. Predation attempts appear to be high, 30.8% of the turtles captured had some mark of a predation attempt. Indicators of predation attempts were recorded for 22% of the females, 44.3% of the males, and 14.6% of the subadults. The percentage of subadults showing predation attempts may have been lower do to predation being more successful on smaller turtles, and also the turtles were younger thus having a fewer number of years in the water to collect battle scars. If this is true then why do females have fewer marks than males since they are larger than males? One factor may be that the average age of females is lower than that of males due to high human and jaguar predation on nesting females, thus lowering the number of chance encounters with predators. Predation indices in areas where crocodiles are not protected are being collected at the present time.

22175: The Mink Frog, Rana septentrionalis, is one of the most nocturnal ranids in North America. It is closely related and behaviorally similar to the Green Frog, Rana clamitans, and the Bullfrog, Rana catesbeiana, but has a much smaller geographical range. In this study, we characterized patterns of calling behavior, and used mark-recapture to estimate male chorus attendance and site fidelity during the breeding season. Nightly calling periods lasted from 2400 until after 0900 h in late June through early August, with peak calling activity between 0100 and 0300 h. Males produce a complex repertoire of single and multi-note calls that are important in attracting females and competing with other males; males respond aggressively to playbacks of advertisement calls. We captured, measured, and individually marked 139 males in 2002 and 85 males in 2003. Each male's initial and subsequent positions were recorded using a Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS), which was accurate to <1 m in 2003. Over half the males (52.5%) were never recaptured in either year. On the other hand, three males were recaptured more than 10 times in both years. Males were recaptured in positions as far apart as 90 m, and as close as 0.6 m. On consecutive nights, however, males were recaptured from positions less than 15 m apart, on average. This suggests that male mink frogs move around in their breeding aggregations during brief periods of reproductive activity. Although aggressive calling, chasing, and fighting occur when males encounter each other, there is no evidence that male mink frogs defend territories with resources, such as egg-laying sites, as in green frogs and bullfrogs.

22176: With at least 20 genera and over 150 species representing an extraordinary range of morphological, behavioral, and ecological variation, the Papuan microhylid frogs are one of the most diverse evolutionary radiations among extant terrestrial vertebrates. Previous workers have attempted to resolve evolutionary relationships for subsets of this group, but a complete consideration of all Papuan microhylids has remained elusive. Phylogenetic analyses using parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian inference all gave largely congruent topologies. We found that even though many groups had good support (nonparametric bootstrapping and decay indices), there are deeper nodes that remain difficult to resolve. Not surprisingly, we found that our molecular data do not support the currently recognized subfamilies (the Asterophryinae and Genyophryninae) and genera of the Papuan microhylids, and here we suggest their revision. Although the monophyly of the Asterophryinae is well supported, the Genyophryninae is polyphyletic in all of our analyses. Our other results support the monophyly of most genera, with some notable exceptions. The genus Austrochaperina, for example, is polyphyletic in all of our analyses and most likely represents at least two new genera. We also discuss ecomorphological guilds in a phylogenetic framework, highlighting guilds and clades that are congruent as well as convergent ecomorph evolution across divergent clades.

22178: One strategy for increasing the water supply in semi-arid rangelands is management of encroaching brush. Removal of deep-rooted woody species, such as mesquite (Prosopis glandulosa) and juniper (Juniperus ashei), is believed to increase groundwater recharge of streams in areas where annual precipitation exceeds 450 mm. However, scientific examination of this claim is scarce, and studies have yielded conflicting results. Effects of brush management on water yields are likely to be subtle and localized in accordance with geology, topography, and other landscape features. Our study focuses on effects of brush removal on headwater streams in the Pedernales River basin of central Texas. The study examines fish and benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages and species-habitat relationships in watersheds with variable vegetation cover. Preliminary results of the fish component of the study are presented. Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA) was used to investigate the influence of environmental variables on fish assemblage structure. 22180: The Fantail Darter, Etheostoma flabellare is highly variable geographically based on morphology and has long been recognized as a species complex. Genetic divergences among populations of E. flabellare were high (0.2%-4.2% for S7 and 0.2% to 14.8% for ND2) and comparable to differences among other Catonotus species, further supporting the recognition of E. flabellare as a species complex. 22181: A significant component of an ectotherm's energy expenditure results from specific dynamic action (SDA), the summed energy expended on meal digestion and assimilation. Therefore, the construction of an ectotherm's energy budget should include an estimation of SDA. Salamanders and toads were each fed cricket meals equivalent in mass to 2.5%, 5%, 7.5%, and 10% of their body mass and maintained at four temperatures (15C, 20C, 25C, and 30C for A. tigrinum and 20C, 25C, 30C, and 35C for B. cognatus). 22182: There are no studies using radio telemetry of juvenile three-toed box turtles on a daily basis. 22183: Bullfrogs are often found in newly created permanent wetlands; are an exotic species that has spread in the western US and Europe; are implicated in amphibian declines in the US; and are listed as one of the 100 worst invasive alien species by the IUCN. Therefore, the bullfrog may be considered an invasive species that could affect populations within and outside its range. Presence of fish also reduced the zooplankton abundance, which led to algal blooms and benefited overwintered bullfrog tadpoles. Overwintered bullfrog tadpoles had negative effects on the amphibian community by reducing mass at metamorphosis of anurans through reduction in their algal food resources. Exposure to nitrate fertilizer appeared to have positive effects on all three amphibian species used in our study; addition of nitrate fertilizer was correlated with increases in algal resources and zooplankton. The insecticide carbaryl also significantly influenced the amphibian community, by having negative effects on survival and growth of spotted salamanders (by reducing their zooplankton food resources) and positive effects on survival of southern leopard frogs (by increasing algal resources through elimination of zooplankton grazers). There were significant interactions among the chemicals, and generally the addition of another stressor appears to make it more likely for the amphibian community to be negatively affected. 22185: The terrestrial nesting behavior of aquatic turtles has been widely studied. 22188: Temperature is critical to the understanding of snake energetics due to the strong thermal dependencies of metabolism. 22189: For many marine fishes, the early life history stages are considered to be the most critical in determining recruitment and survival. Survival during these early life stages is thought to be strongly linked to the ability of fish larvae to locate and capture prey. 22190: Frogs and salamanders are well known predators on insects; however the benefits of pest control attributed to them are usually based on anecdotes. 22191: As part of its bioregional land management plan for the Sierra Nevada, CA, the USDA Forest Service developed an Adaptive Management Strategy including a comprehensive environmental monitoring program. 22193: Many coral-reef fishes are sex-changing and territorial. In this paper, we use computer simulation (C++ within a Linux environment) to investigate the effects swimming rules have on encounter rates (ER) of territory holders with sex-change candidates and intruders. We hypothesize that maximization of ER with both types of individuals is evolutionarily advantageous. Maximization should result in the highest reproductive success because 1) sex changed candidates are prevented from changing sex, and 2) territorial intruders are excluded from resources. The simulation allows parametric investigation of the swimming and territory characteristics on the ER between a male fish, a female fish, and an intruder. All fish use the same rules, i.e. game theoretical approaches are not used in this initial simulation. Simulations consisted of various rates of velocity (5), step size (3), movement angle (18), territory size (5) and territory aspect (4). Each run consisted of 100 simulations of 10000 steps for each combination of the above, i.e. 540000 runs or 5.4 billion steps. The simulation can be used to make a priori hypotheses about swimming behavior that could be readily tested in the field.

22202: Mercury bioaccumulation of amphibians has received little attention despite widespread mercury contamination of surface water ecosystems in the northeastern United States and the documentation of worldwide amphibian declines. Here we report total mercury and methylmercury concentrations of water, sediment, and Green Frog (Rana clamitans) and Bullfrog (Rana catesbeiana) tadpoles from Acadia National Park, Maine and compare our findings with previously collected samples of two-lined salamander larvae (Eurycea bislineata), a lotic amphibian species common in headwater streams. We also evaluate variability of mercury concentrations in water, sediment, and biota among individual wetlands, including amphibian die- off and disease sites, and assess the relationships between tadpole mercury levels, tadpole body size, and, water chemistry attributes. Use of these species as eco-indicators of mercury contamination in lotic and lentic ecosystems in the northeastern United States is also discussed.

22203: The genus Carpiodes of Family Catostomidae, as currently recognized, comprises three species of riverine fishes commonly referred to as carpsuckers. The three species are widely distributed in North America east of the continental divide, but occur sympatrically throughout most of the Mississippi River Basin. Populations in Gulf coastal rivers east and west of the Mississippi River, and along the Atlantic Slope, are more isolated and likely represent distinct species. The species or species complexes are morphologically distinctive and diagnosable by suites of morphometric and external body characters. We sequenced and/or screened (using Single-Stranded Conformational Polymorphism analysis) the mitochodrial cytochrome b gene and introns of one of two paralogous copies of the nuclear growth hormone (GH) gene for samples from throughout the geographic ranges of the three currently recognized Carpiodes species to assess degrees of genetic differentiation. We used geometric morphometric techniques to analyze variation in body shape. We found considerable evidence of genetic and morphometric differentiation of populations of Carpiodes cyprinus and C. velifer east of the Mississippi River Basin. We found evidence of interspecific hybridization within the Mississippi River Basin. Populations long regarded as Carpiodes carpio from the Rio Grande Basin and the Colorado River systems of Texas show close affinities to Mississippi River populations of Carpiodes cyprinus. Despite their morphological differences, the three Carpiodes species complexes failed to form monophyletic groups in molecular phylogenetic analyses. The lack of phylogenetic resolution may be due to interspecific hybridization in the Mississippi River Basin.

22204: Progress has been made in recent years towards resolving phylogenetic relationships of desmognathine salamanders. 22205: Survival rates of free-ranging snakes have been difficult to estimate based on traditional mark- recapture methods because of low population densities and secretive behavior. However, use of radio telemetry with recent advances in demographic modeling, model selection procedures and associated freeware (program MARK) allows for improved estimates of survivorship as well as more flexibility in assessing factors that may affect survival. We used a modified Kaplan-Meier estimator and an information-theoretic approach to model selection in program MARK to assess effects of sex, size, time (season and a block of good years versus bad years) and supplemental feeding on the survivorship of 58 radio-tagged timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) in northwest Arkansas during 1995-2002. The model selection procedure identified three models with essentially equal support. The first was based only on the difference in time periods 1995- 1996 (S = 0.563, SE = 0.133) and 1997-2002 (S = 0.923, SE = 0.025). The second two models alternatively included sex and size in addition to time period. However, due to high variability in survival estimates, strong statements regarding effects of sex and size are not possible with the current data set. A fourth model involving sex, size, the sex by size interaction, supplemental feeding, and time period was also well supported. Significant effects of these additional factors cannot be ruled out, and will be examined in more detail as additional data become available. Combining radiotelemetry data with information-theoretic approaches to model survivorship provides new opportunities for studying life histories of organisms that are not amenable to more standard mark-recapture methods.

22206: The John Heinz National Wildlife Refuge (JHNWR), the only national wildlife refuge in a large metropolitan city, receives pollution from multiple sources, including two landfills on the National Priorities List. We studied the effects of this pollution on the development of snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina) and painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) in the refuge from 2000-2003. We developed a system to rate severity of observed deformities as minor, moderate or lethal. Although they varied in percentage and severity of abnormality, both species exhibited high rates of embryonic deformity. Over the four year study, 89 to 100% of painted turtle clutches examined each year contained at least one deformed embryo, compared to 81 to 100% of all snapping turtle clutches examined. Mean percent deformity of painted turtles over four years ranged from 45 to 63%, while that of snapping turtle clutches ranged from 11 to 19%. The mean percent embryonic deformity of clutches was at least 25% higher every year for painted turtles than for snapping turtles. Minor deformities were dominant in snapping turtle embryos, while lethal deformities were dominant in painted turtle embryos. Adult painted turtles also showed a higher rate of deformity than adult snapping turtles, although the majority of abnormalities were rated as minor in both species. Although the refuge offers many advantages to the resident turtle populations, pollution places them at a developmental disadvantage.

22207: Developing nurseryfish ovaries are bulbous, bean shaped, highly vascularized and average 5453 eggs 1-2 mm in diameter. Ovaries with GSI greater than 1.0 appear mature. A running ripe female had a GSI of 4.48 and 4745 eggs 2.1-2.5 mm in diameter. Histology suggests oocyte maturation begins in June with some ovaries having only early developmental cortical alveoli stage oocytes and others are more advanced with vitellogenic oocytes. Females develop oocytes through the late vitellogenic stage then arrest further maturation perhaps until a receptive male (one not carrying eggs on his supraoccipital hook) is found. Then maturation resumes with yolk coalescence followed by ovulation. This strategy may be functionally intermediate between batch and isochronal spawning, and provides nurseryfish with advantages of both. Egg-carrying males taken in November indicate that the spawning season coincides with dry season (May-November). We describe nurseryfish otoliths and their use in age-and-growth studies for the first time. The sagitta is ovate, moderately thick, lateral surface convex, mesial surface flat; dorsal margin sinuate, posterior margin rounded ventrally, ventral margin rounded and irregular; sulcus divided into ostium and cauda; dorsal depression large, rostrum broad, antirostrum small, separated by wide, shallow excisural notch. Otolith size moderate, averaging 4.6%SL. Annuli on 78 whole sagittae were read. Males ranged from 94-235 mmSL and females from 95-284 mmSL. There was little difference in size distribution of age one fish between the sexes, due to six-month spawning season over which young are continually added to the population. However, age 2 females were significantly larger than age 2 males. The largest fish aged was a 284 mmSL three-year old female, and the oldest age reached was four years by two males. It appears likely that most spawning females are two or more years old, but some larger one-year olds may attain sexual maturity.

22208: The Pacific Cow-nose Ray, Rhinoptera steindachneri, is a common nearshore stingray ranging from the Pacific coast of Baja California Sur to the Galapagos Islands, yet little is known about its basic biology. From 1998-2000, surveys of artisanal fishing camps throughout the Gulf of California (GOC) and in Bahía Almejas identified and characterized elasmobranch fisheries and sampled landings. Fishery-derived R. steindachneri were enumerated, sexed, measured, weighed, and examined for reproductive condition. This species was the sixth most abundant of 44 elasmobranch species observed in northern GOC, comprising 6.92% (n=11,142) of overall landings and 11.45% (n=4,079) of summer landings. In the Bahía Almejas summer batoid fishery, it was the fifth most abundant of twenty-one elasmobranch species (2.13%, n=113). Rhinoptera steindachneri is typically landed with bottomset gillnets in mixed species fisheries for batoids, small coastal sharks, and demersal teleosts. The mean size of females captured in the GOC was 64.4 + 11.8 cm disc width (DW) (mean and SD, n=505) whereas males averaged 64.2 + 14.0 cm DW (n=586). Landed specimens measured from 39 to 98 cm DW, with only females occupying the largest size classes (>89 cm DW). Maximum size records for both males (96 cm DW) and females (104 cm DW) were noted among Bahía Almejas landings. Median DW at 50% maturity was similar between sexes (males=69.9 cm, females=70.0 cm). Fecundity was only one embryo per female in all gravid specimens examined (n=149). The largest embryo was 43 cm, slightly smaller than the largest free-living specimen (39 cm DW). 22209: Luxilus cornutus x Luxilus chrysocephalus is one of the most common cyprinid hybrids in North America. Luxilus cornutus and Luxilus chrysocephalus are known to hybridize extensively in sympatric zones and documented introgression of allopatric populations has proven historical hybridization elsewhere. 22210: Louisiana has the largest area of estuarine habitat in the United States, however little is known about the shark species that occur there. Several studies have documented the presence of bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas, in both the inland waters and coastal estuaries of Louisiana. However, no systematic review or analyses have been produced to define bull shark nursery habitat following the Bass (1978) definition for the state as a whole. In order to synthesize the current information on bull sharks in Louisiana waters, we gathered and analyzed data sets from a variety of previously published and unpublished sources. This included information from state agencies, other universities, and from research conducted at Louisiana State University. Six separate data sets representing six geographic regions were used in this synthesis. Descriptive statistics were calculated for biological and environmental parameters for all data sets. Primary and secondary nursery areas were delineated with convex polygons constructed within the geographic information system (GIS) environment by connecting the inner and outermost sampling locations of each study site and smoothing the lines connecting each point. All six geographic locations were delineated as containing both primary and secondary habitat. This study confirms the occurrence of young bull sharks in several of the low salinity and freshwater systems in Louisiana and provides substantial evidence that such occurrences are not random. The regular occurrence and high abundance of young bull sharks in Louisiana inland waters indicate that low salinity and freshwater environments serve as both primary and secondary nursery habitat and should therefore be considered essential fish habitat for bull sharks.

22211: Theory predicts adaptive responses to parasitic infection resulting in changes of host reproductive strategy. Low resources may inhibit a host's ability to optimize its response to infection. Female Gambusia affinis infected with the parasitic nematode Eustrongylides ignotus were used to examine the combined effects of resource availability and parasitic infection on host reproductive strategy. The experiment was a two factorial design consisting of resource (high-fed once daily and low-fed once every third day) and parasite treatments. Inefficiencies of selective infection resulted in using field-infected fish. 300 females were collected, randomly assigned to feeding treatments, isolated in small aquaria, and exposed to natural light and temperature, for up to 70 days. Aquaria were inspected 2-5 times daily for the presence of neonates. Females found giving birth were moved into breeding traps to minimize possible cannibalism. Neonates were collected daily, preserved, counted, dried and individually weighed. Females were euthanized following the birth of the third brood or after 70 days. All were dissected to remove ovaries and to determine parasitic status; their somas individually dried and weighed. Soluble fats were extracted, to determine body condition. Results indicated no significant difference in average neonate size within or among treatments. Infected females reduced current investment in neonate number (in two of the three broods) and had longer interbrood intervals. Parasitized females maintain body condition at higher levels; however, low resources constrained this investment. Differences in reproductive investment did not result in a net gain of offspring for females within any treatment. These results suggest that offspring size is optimized over number, and that infected females adopt a strategy of reducing current investment, while maintaining body condition, which may increase their chances for future reproductive success.

22213: Phoxinins (Actinopterygii: Cyprinidae) are a very widespread and diverse clade of fishes within North American (NA). Current hypotheses of relationships among NA species are inferred from morphological and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence data. Some of the hypothesized groups are congruent among the data sets, whereas support for other groups is inconsistent. Character classes (e.g., morphological, mtDNA and nuclear DNA (nDNA) sequence data) used in phylogeny reconstruction can reflect independent evolutionary histories within a group of organisms due to inherent differences in the evolutionary forces acting on them. This study adds a third character class (nDNA) to the growing systematics database for NA phoxinins. Non-coding nDNA sequence data from intron 1 of the ribosomal protein gene S7 is used to generate hypotheses of systematic relationships for select NA phoxinin taxa using both maximum parsimony (MP) and Bayesian inference. Results of the MP analysis are compared to the morphological and mtDNA MP results.

22214: Red-eyed treefrog embryos (Agalychnis callidryas) use vibrations transmitted through their gelatinous egg clutches to detect attacking predators, such as egg-eating snakes, and then escape by hatching rapidly and prematurely. We used standard modal testing methods from mechanical engineering to assess the free vibration frequencies of egg clutches at three ages, from just prior to hatching competence through the period of inducible early hatching. We then compared these modal frequencies to the frequencies recorded in important natural disturbances. The natural vibration frequencies of A. callidryas egg clutches are low, with the dominant mode often near 20 Hz, and most of the free vibration energy in the 10-50 Hz range. Although clutches differ in their modal frequencies, and individual clutches vary slightly from day to day, there is no obvious developmental change in natural frequencies. Recordings of vibrations excited in clutches by rainstorms, snake attacks, and embryo hatching show substantial energy in this low frequency range. Raindrops, but apparently not snake bites, also elicit much higher frequency vibrations, mostly in the range of hundreds of Hz and occasionally up to a few kHz. Each clutch has several characteristic higher frequencies, each elicited by a different subset of raindrops. We have also identified rare higher frequency (hundreds of Hz) events in some recordings of hatching. These higher frequency vibrations are well outside the dominant modes of vibration of the whole clutch, and may represent vibrations of clutch subsections, eggs, or parts of eggs. Understanding the relationships between physical disturbances, clutch movements, and vibration patterns will clarify the mechanosensory information available to embryos, and the ways in which they could use this information to assess risk.

22215: Will the use of morphological characters (not to mention other aspects of the phenotype) in phylogenetic analysis survive the sequencing of complete organellar and organismal genomes? Relationships among the major lineages of frogs are in a state of flux, at least as judged from a superficial examination of recent published analyses. Studies of larval morphological characters have yielded results somewhat incongruent with those from analyses of adult morphology and DNA sequences. One possible source of this discordance is taxa with suites of highly apomorphic characters as adults, but many (apparently) plesiomorphic features as larvae. A second source is some relatively depauperate taxa (e.g., Ascaphus and Leiopelma) that are morphologically plesiomorphic, but are found at the ends of relatively long branches of the tree. This talk will integrate data from larval morphology, adult morphology, and DNA sequences, and also examines the levels of incongruence among these data partitions. The results will be discussed in the context of (1) recent papers treating the role of morphology (and more generally, phenotypic characters) in phylogenetic analysis, (2) community efforts to estimate a phylogeny of amphibians, and (3) the general goals of systematics.

22216: Multiple datasets show that marine biodiversity reaches global maxima in the Indo-Malay- Philippines archipelago. Analysis of range data for 2,983 species, over two-thirds of which are fishes, resolves patterns of richness on a finer scale and identifies the peak of marine biodiversity: the central Philippine Islands. This pattern is repeated in diverse higher taxa and habitat classes, leaving geohistorical hypotheses as the most general unifying explanations. Predictions based on area of overlap, area of accumulation, and area of refuge hypotheses are falsified by observed patterns. The hypothesis that the Philippines has served as a center of allopatric speciation cannot be falsified by available data. Special attention to marine conservation efforts in the Philippines is warranted because of the identification of it as the center of the center of marine biodiversity.

22217: Specimens of Graptemys ouachitensis were collected from the Red River in Red River Parish, Louisiana between June 1999 and August 2002. 22218: The Napo basin in the Ecuadorian rainforest has a high degree of endemism attributed to the Pleistocene radiation. However, little is known about its ichthyofaunal composition, diversity, habitat dependence and contribution to the local subsistence. During the dry season of 2001-2002, I collected data from a total of 2989 fishes in three different watershed systems inside the Yasuní National Park. The information was obtained from fishery-dependent and -independent sampling. Systems were sub-divided into lentic and lotic environments, which were subsequently split according to macro- and meso- habitats. Air and water temperature, pH, water level and other abiotic factors were also measured. My response variables included fish species numbers and relative frequencies, length, weight and sex ratio. The non-parametric analysis I used showed that species richness, CPUE, average length and weight of the fishes were all greatest for the Jatuncocha black-water system (p<0.01), followed by the Tambococha and Yasuní (black- and white-water systems, respectively). The Jatuncocha, however, was the heaviest fished system. Both black-water systems also showed significant differences between the lentic and lotic environments; Jatuncocha showed higher values in the lake when compared to the river while the opposite was true for Tambococha. The abiotic factors measured did not explain the variance or patterns in my data. All of these suggest that fish densities and health are a function of the number and/or quality of habitats present over a range of spatial scales in the studied area. Anthropogenic factors such as habitat destruction and the use of non-selective fishing methods (such as dynamite) are suspected to be related to these differences. Oil exploitation and road construction scheduled at the mouth of Tambococha in the near future might severely threat biodiversity in this area; therefore, further research leading to conservation efforts should be conducted in this mega-diverse region of the Amazon.

22219: Despite an informative fossil record, the adaptive reasons for the evolutionary transition between obligatorily aquatic lobe-finned fish and facultatively terrestrial early tetrapods remain contentious. The oldest adequately known amphibians, Acanthostega and Ichthyostega from the final stage of the Upper Devonian, can be clearly distinguished from the most advanced Devonian choanate sarcopterygian fish by the presence of large pectoral and pelvic girdles, limbs generally resembling those of later Paleozoic land vertebrates, and the absence of bones linking the back of the skull with the shoulder girdle. Evidence from the anatomy of Upper Devonian amphibians and from a diversity of footprints from the basal Carboniferous shows the early achievement of the capacity to support their bodies against the force of gravity. Upper Devonian and most Lower Carboniferous amphibians, like their aquatic predecessors, were large, up to a meter or more in length. Thermophysiological modeling demonstrates that animals of this size could have raised their body temperatures substantially by basking in the sun and sustain those temperatures upon re-entry into the water. For ectotherms, the physiological advantage of basking thermoregulation would have enabled adults to raise their metabolic rate significantly and so be more effective predators in the water, as well as benefit from increased rates of digestion, growth, and reproduction. This major selective advantage resulted in the increasing capacity for the ancestors of tetrapods to move into shallow water and, later, to support their bodies against the force of gravity and increase the size and locomotor capacities of the limbs.

22220: We surveyed mitochondrial (cytb) and nuclear gene (S7) variation in Campostoma collected from throughout its range in the United States, as well as a few localities in Mexico, to address hypotheses related to the influences of Plio-Pleistocene glaciation and pre-Pliocene events on the distribution of North American freshwater fishes. Phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) resolved all described species (Campostoma anomalum, C. oligolepis, C. ornatum, C. pauciradii, and C. pullum) and at least three additional lineages (Canadian River/Gulf of Mexico, Ouachita, and New/Roanoke River systems), indicating that the number of described species is almost certainly an underestimate of diversity within the genus. The distribution of mtDNA variation was consistent with the presence of previously hypothesized glacial refugia east and west of the Mississippi River, expansion corridors associated with glacial retreat, and former connections between now isolated river systems. In addition, patterns of mitochondrial variation at several localities were consistent with morphological evidence of secondary contact between species in these regions. However, mtDNA provided limited resolution among some species and the major lineages. To resolve these relationships, we sequenced intron 1 of the nuclear gene S7 from multiple individuals of each species/major mitochondrial lineage. Preliminary results indicate this gene is sufficient for resolving the inter-specific relationships that could not be recovered with mitochondrial genes. Because divergence between some major lineages probably predates the Pliocene, S7 provides a valuable tool for assessing the role of pre-Pliocene events on present distributions of major clades within Campostoma.

22222: Recent authors (Ceas, 1997; Ceas & Page, 1997; Ceas & Burr, 2002) have shown that the Orangethroat Darter, Etheostoma spectabile (Agassiz), is a complex of morphologically variable species. Members of the species complex can be diagnosed using meristic and genetic characteristics, but it is the color patterns of breeding males that are most strikingly different among taxa and allow for easy field identification. Ceas & Page (1997) presented a taxonomic history and a formal diagnosis of the species complex; provided a rediagnosis and redescription of E. s. spectabile; elevated the former subspecies E. fragi and E. uniporum to specific level; and recognized four previously undescribed species (E. bison, E. burri, E. kantuckeense, and E. tecumsehi). Ceas & Burr (2002) described the Headwater Darter, E. lawrencei; suggested that the plural vernacular name "orangethroat darters" be used to refer to all members of the species complex; and provided a discussion of general habitat and natural history for members of the species complex. The study of this species complex is ongoing. Breeding males from some major stream systems in the range of the species complex have yet to be examined, and I predict that the total number of species in the E. spectabile complex will reach at least 18. Distributional data and general diagnoses most of for the 14 recognized taxa, and photographs of some of the species-in- waiting, are presented. This taxonomic and distributional information will contribute to the growing knowledge necessary for the conservation and recovery of the imperiled fishes of the southeastern United States. Phylogeographic analyses will provide critical data for our understanding of the evolutionary history of the stream systems of the central United States.

22223: Traditionally, all of the nearly 100 species of Middle American cichlids were placed in the catch- all Neotropical genus Cichlasoma. The genus was divided into eight sections based primarily on trophic morphology; it has been suggested that each section be raised to generic rank. One of these genera, Nandopsis, is revised based on both molecular and morphological features. As currently recognized this genus is a polyphyletic assemblage of more than a dozen species found throughout Middle America and the Greater Antilles. 22224: Conservation of amphibian populations requires knowledge of species-habitat relationships. Four- toed salamanders Hemidactylium scutatum are listed as Endangered in Indiana, Threatened in Illinois, and Rare or of Special Concern in Maine, Massachusetts, Vermont, Ohio, Wisconsin, Missouri, and Minnesota. Little is known of Four-toed Salamander ecology despite the species' extensive range, in part because no survey method exists for the species. 22226: Wild caught ornamental fishes (piabas) from the Rio Negro basin have sustained livelihood of local people over 50 years, and the fishery may have kept the rainforest of the region mostly intact. The Rio Negro basin has the lowest deforesting rate (<3%) of the Brazilian Amazon (overall average 12%). We have made repeated fish surveys to examine the impact of ornamental fisheries on fish diversity in several floodplain streams (igrapés). We have also collected Piaba fishery statistics from the principal transship point, Barcelos, where 30 - 60 million live fishes are exported annually. The sustainability of the Piaba fishery is evaluated by its artisan collection methods, fishing efforts, biomass ratio, trophic ecological stability, and life history and distribution patterns. Major conservation concerns on diversity of fishes are: (1) collectors remove only populations of target species; over 80% of Piaba catch is a single species (Cardinal Tetra, Paracheirodon axelrodi ), unsustained fishing grounds and diminishing fish sizes have occurred; (2) new target species, such as Green Neon Tetra (P. simulans) have become a major fishery statistics in recent years; (3) more people got into Piaba fishery for seasonal cash revenue and to receive unemployment benefit during the fish protecting period; (4) the biomass of fishes that removed from the floodplain ecosystem is negligible; (5) most piabas are low trophic level species and have short life span; (6)export of freshwater sting rays (Potamotrygon) and arawanas (Osteoglossum) became legal under quota, but their fate as lively pets are dubious; (7) varieties of Betta, Guppy (Poecilia reticulatus), Gourami (Trichogaster spp.) and Tilapia have been introduced to the region; (7) traders pay extremely low price to fish collectors, e.g. $4-5 US per thousand piabas, and illegal commerce of wildlife is still common. Conservation through sustainable fishery is a multi-facet and long-term endeavor, understanding ecological processes and generating direct benefit to fishers are basic steps to ensure the sustainability of the Piaba fishery. If the Piaba fishery collapsed for some reason, we can expect that deforestation, mining, wildlife poaching and massive emigration of the region would happen in the Rio Negro basin.

22227: It has been an enduring belief that increasing aridity combined with Pliocene-Pleistocene glacial cycles resulted in the formation of distinct arid and temperate zone faunas within Australia. I assembled a molecular phylogeny for the Egernia whitii species group, a group of skinks comprising representatives from arid and temperate Australia, in order to test several biogeographic hypotheses regarding the origin of the Australian arid zone fauna. I analyzed the data using Maximum Likelihood and Bayesian techniques and produced a single optimal tree. The phylogeny strongly supports two major clades within the species group, corresponding to temperate-adapted rock-dwelling species and arid-adapted obligate burrowing species. 22228: Facial lesions have been observed in ornate box turtles in our mark-recapture study in eastern Iowa over a 25 year period. Detailed records of these have been maintained for the last 12 years. The incidence of occurrence is lower than that reported for eastern box turtles; the cysts tend to develop in turtles at least 13 years old; and they are much more common in females than males. The cysts sometimes spontaneously resolve but in one instance returned after being expelled in the field. They tend to involve the middle ear but due to the density of unciliated glandular cells, we believe that they arise from salivary gland and because of their size and tightness of the skin, are displaced into the middle ear cavity. Infection believed to be secondary to cyst development sometimes results in reactive bone formation with distortion of the cranium. While it is possible for glanduar cells to undergo complete metaplasia, two lesions in a similar location in a painted turtle had all the characteristics of an epidermal inclusion cyst of non-glandular origin.

22230: Snakes of the genus Atractus are among the less-known neotropical herpetofauna members. 22231: Frogs of the family Centrolenidae are among the most beautiful anurans in South America. 22232: Etheostoma beanii, the Naked Sand Darter, and E. bifascia, the Florida Sand Darter, speciated from a common ancestor approximately 2 to 4 million years ago, and compose a sister species pair. 22233: Several species of live-bearing pitvipers have been observed to exhibit brief maternal attendance behavior with the mother staying near the neonates until their first ecdysis event. Both mother and neonates then disperse. Although it is thought that neonates may follow maternal or conspecific pheromone trails, few field data have documented this event. In September 2003, we radiotracked a postpartum Timber Rattlesnake along with her four neonates. Initial movement behavior of two neonates appeared to be associated with the movement of the mother, but, within one week those two neonates were making movements clearly independent of the mother. Movements by the other two neonates appeared independent from the mother as well. Total movement distance by all five snakes during the first 10 days varied considerably (mother: 22 m; neonates: 3, 21, 49, and 154 m). Continued movements were sporadic with individuals staying several days in single locations. Movements of all individuals, except one neonate, converged to a single wooded rocky hillside for hibernation (320 m from birth site). During their movements to the hibernaculum, one neonate was found with a subadult female and another neonate was found again with its mother.
