22234: Strong evidence supports monophyly of the Zenarchopterinae Fowler 1934 containing all 5 genera of internally-fertilizing halfbeaks, Zenarchopterus (about 19 species), Tondanichthys (1), Hemirhamphodon (6), Dermogenys (12), and Nomorhamphus (16). Monophyly of the group as a subfamily was proposed by Anderson & Collette (1991), Collette (1995), Meisner & Collette (1997), and Meisner (2001) based on 5 synapomorphies: 1) some anal-fin rays modified in males; 2) nasal fossa reduced in size; 3) an elongate nasal barbel projecting conspicuously out of the nasal fossa; 4) reduced number of vertebrae (38-51); and, presumably 5) internal fertilization. Characters of spermatozoal ultrastructure such as the bilateral arrangement of mitochondria support monophyly of the clade (Jamieson & Grier 1993). Several characters from the osteology and myology of the pharyngeal jaw apparatus support monophyly such as a trough-like pharyngocranial articulation facet; 5th ceratobranchial keel small; shape of 5th ceratobranchial muscular process; insertion of posterior levatores, etc. (Tibbetts 1992). Molecular data, both mitochondrial (cytochrome b and 16S) and nuclear (Tmo-4C4), also support monophyly (Lovejoy 2000). The preponderance of molecular and pharyngeal jaw characters indicate that the Zenarchopterinae is more closely related to the clade of needlefishes plus sauries (Belonidae + Scomberesocidae) than to halfbeaks. Thus this clade should be recognized as a separate beloniform family, the Zenarchopteridae, rather than as a subfamily of the Hemiramphidae.

22235: The main events that shaped the differentiation of the Cerrado herpetofauna involve the establishment of a climatic gradient, associated with the formation of three floristic provinces in early Tertiary, a major marine transgression during the Miocene, the uplifting of the Brazilian Shield and the arrival of North and Central American immigrants at the closing of the Tertiary, and Quaternary climatic fluctuations. 22236: New World species of Cyprinodon are represented by several morphologically diverse groups inhabiting desert aquatic habitats. 22237: We studied the life-history patterns of the Yazoo Shiner, Notropis rafinesquei, a species endemic to upper Coastal Plain streams in the upper Yazoo River, Mississippi. Mature females from Hotopha Creek were smaller than mature females from Cypress Creek in 1993, but size did not differ between streams in 1994. Females in Hotopha Creek appear to mature at a smaller size than those from Cypress Creek. Ova diameter increased with size (SL) for individuals from Cypress Creek regardless of sample date. In contrast, ova diameter was not related to SL in Hotopha Creek but decreased throughout the reproductive season. Further, SL of mature females increased throughout the reproductive season in Hotopha Creek in 1993, but not in 1994 nor either year in Cypress Creek. The strong variation in life history traits between years and creeks is likely a response to highly variable conditions found in these two highly unstable, channelized streams.

22238: We tested the Bigger is Better hypothesis (hatchling body size is positively correlated with traits that are assumed to be related to fitness) by monitoring body growth and survivorship of 708 hatchling painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) released over 9 years (1977-1985) on the University of Michigans E. 22239: Sexual dimorphism in the South American apteronotids (Gymnotiformes) has been previously documented, particularly as it relates to the shape of the head, length of the snout and presence of enlarged teeth. However, little work has been done on the underlying skeletal variation of this dimorphism. Here we document sexual dimorphism in Apteronotus bonapartii, a species described from the Ucayali of Peru; the name A. bonapartii is often misused and this will be discussed. Principal Components Analysis revealed that when males and females reach a certain size, the depth and length of their body and shape of their snout begin to differentiate. Although no clear groups were found, the largest males with the longest snouts tend to cluster in the lower part of the PCA diagram. With the cleared and stained specimens we investigated the anatomical differences in the cranial skeleton. In males, some elements of the skull roof (e.g., frontal) and suspensorium (e.g., mesopterygoid) are elongated, relative to females. In males, the lateral ethmoid is more obliquely positioned than in females. However, most elements of the skull are similar between males and females. In the lower jaw, however, there is dimorphism not only in the length of the elements, but also their morphology. In females the dentary and angulo-articular are deep and give the anterior portion of the lower jaw a roughly triangular shape, whereas in males the dorsal margin of the lower jaw is smoothly arched. 22240: Mating system evolution and sexual selection can be fully understood only by using polymorphic genetic markers to confidently assign parentage in natural populations. Such technology is particularly needed in animals that are difficult to observe when mating and fertilize eggs internally, such as ambystomatid salamanders. We used an enrichment technique to isolate and sequence microsatellite DNA from two species of ambystomatid salamanders, Ambystoma talpoideum and A. opacum. We designed and optimized primer pairs for six and seven polymorphic loci for the two species, respectively. Additionally, we report successful cross- amplification of previously reported microsatellite primers developed for congeneric species at six loci in A. opacum and two loci in A. talpoideum. We used a subset of these A. opacum loci to investigate the extent and frequency of multiple paternity in unmanipulated populations. Unlike other ambystomatids, A. opacum offers a good system for such a study because females attend their egg clutches during the embryonic period, allowing confident assignment of maternal genotype. During the fall nesting season of 2002, egg clutches and their attendant mothers were located at two Carolina bays on the Savannah River Site in Aiken County, South Carolina. Clutches were returned to the laboratory and allowed to develop to the point of hatching before being submersed in well water. We genotyped 32 hatchlings from each of 15 clutches at four microsatellite loci. Multiple paternity occurred at a high frequency; most clutches were fathered by at least two different males. However, statistical analyses showed that few clutches, if any, were fathered by more than two males. This result contrasts the mating system of A. maculatum, in which several sires are often represented in a single clutch. Our study shows that female polyandry is common in marbled salamanders and invites further investigation of genetic mating systems in ambystomatids.

22243: Ecological constraints are known to influence bone growth strategies, and thus life history strategies, in a wide variety of amphibians and reptiles, however few such studies have been done on tortoises. Gopherus agassizzi are long-lived tortoises, living in a habitat where their survival is extremely dependent on temperature and resource availability and quality. I obtained carcasses ranging in size and age from three different geographic areas: Arizona, East Mojave (CA, NV) and West Mojave Desert (CA). These populations were chosen because they represent a wide range of inter- and intrapopulational growth strategies in desert tortoises living in extreme arid environments. I processed, sectioned (20 µm) and stained various skeletal elements to investigate individual growth histories, variation with age and possible population trends. Preliminary results showed that bone microstructure and growth ring formation differed considerably within and between individuals from all populations. In general, the smallest juveniles exhibited fast growing embryonic bone. As body size increased, bone tissue varied from parallel-fibered bone (intermediate growth rate) to fibrolamellar bone (fast growth rate) with many transitions between these two bone tissues. The occurrence and localization of vascularization and secondary bone formation also varied considerably. Bone remodeling and remodeling rates differed within populations, as did the expression and distinction of growth rings. Hatching lines were visible in some juveniles and subadults, a phenomenon not yet documented in chelonians. Moreover, certain individuals showed segmented, sac-like structures in the medullary cavity area, the function of which is unknown. The range of desert tortoise bone microstructure was surprising because such variation is not common within single reptile species. This is the first study attempting to answer questions about tortoise biology across a broad geographic scope and time range and has the added advantage of not having to harm, kill or disturb living animals of this threatened species.

22244: Brown treesnakes (Boiga irregularis) display nocturnal behavior patterns in wild and captive situations, but the effects of abiotic and biotic factors on their use of microhabitats are not well understood. 22245: The Nile Monitor (Varanus niloticus), a large, intelligent, carnivorous lizard native to central and southern Africa, was established in Cape Coral, Florida circa 1990. These generalist predators reach over 2 m in length and are excellent runners, swimmers, tree-climbers, and burrowers. Monitor lizards continue to horrify Cape Coral residents by climbing on their houses, eating their pets, and scaring their children. They currently occupy at least 50 km2 of residential areas, canal banks, and surrounding pine flatwoods, mangroves, barrier islands, and other natural habitats in and around Cape Coral. More importantly, they have been found in the adjacent Charlotte Harbor State Buffer Preserve, and without intervention, could easily reach two major National Wildlife Refuges and a number of other conservation areas. They have the potential to devastate the populations of native invertebrates, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals that such preserves were established to protect. With funding from the Charlotte Harbor National Estuary Program and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, I assembled a partnership between federal, state, and local agencies and the private sector and initiated an eradication program. 22246: With approximately five percent of California's riparian habitat remaining, groups like the Nature Conservancy and local government agencies are working together to restore these habitats. 22247: There is a paucity of ecotoxicological research focusing on reptiles and amphibians, despite the fact that this taxonomic group may provide some unique insights into the dynamics of toxicants in ecosystems. In particular, turtles are documented to be able to live and even thrive under harsh environmental conditions and tolerate significant disturbance events that many organisms are unable to withstand. In addition, the potential for long life spans permits multiple observations and an extended period of uptake and bioaccumulation of toxicants that serves to integrate sporadic contamination events. Although organisms might be subsisting in contaminated areas, often the timing and concentrations of the contamination event might be unknown, as well as the relative effects on the organisms within the ecosystem. To assist in developing a methodology for answering these types of questions, 500 hatchling red-eared sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans) were gavaged with nickel citrate at concentrations of 25ppm, 100ppm, 400ppm and a metal-free control on a bi-monthly basis. All turtles are contained in experimental mesocosms with three replicate mesocosms per treatment level. To date, control and 400ppm individuals were analyzed using a Synchrotron x-ray fluorescence (SXRF) microprobe at the National Synchrotron Light Source (Brookhaven National Lab, Upton, NY). Turtles receiving the 400ppm dose displayed higher nickel levels in marginal scutes compared to turtles in the control group. The estimation of relative concentrations among dosed organisms will allow the design of methods for spatial analysis of contamination events within a given time period for a specific turtle. By estimating the amount of toxicants ingested within a temporal context, there is potential for estimating effects of contamination events on other organisms within the ecosystem and thus estimating ecosystem effects.

22248: Coralsnakes represent an extraordinary radiation of brightly colored venomous snakes including about 90 species. 22249: In Ohio the Variegate Darter, Etheostoma variatum, is a riffle inhabitant of large to medium sized streams (7th-3rd order) that drain to the Ohio River (about 2/3 the drainage area of the state). Some of the largest populations were found in the glaciated portions of the three major drainages which have exceptional riffle habitat: Great Miami, Scioto and Muskingum. Outstanding populations of more than 3/sq. meter were found in the Little Miami River, Big Walnut Creek, Big Darby Creek, Deer Creek, Paint Creek, Salt Creek, Walhonding, Kokosing and Mohican Rivers. Fluctuations in variegate population size have been recorded for a number of these streams over the last 60 years. However, severe declines in population size were noticed beginning in 1996 for some streams that previously maintained strong populations. In the Great Miami River drainage the Variegate Darter has virtually disappeared, having been lost from five streams where it formerly occurred. In the Little Miami drainage it has been lost from three streams plus the upper half of the mainstem. In the Scioto drainage the variegate has been lost from four streams in the upper (glaciated) half of the drainage area. In the Muskingum drainage only two streams have lost populations. In direct tributaries of the Ohio River, variegate populations have for the most part held their own with the exception of Raccoon Creek, Hocking River and the Mahoning River where the variegate darter has been lost. 22250: The tribe Stelliferini is endemic to tropical Americas and is unique among Sciaenidae by having a two-chambered gas bladder and two pairs of large otoliths (lapillus and sagitta). Among the six genera, Stellifer and Ophioscion are morphologically most similar; Corvula and Odontoscion, and Elattarchus and Bairdiella are two pairs. The tribe is probably related to an Indo-Pacific tribe Johnini. The genus Stellifer can be further differentiated from the rest by having a pair of variablely developed appendages on the posterior margin of the anterior gas chamber. Stellifer, star drums, includes 27 species (13 East Pacific, 14 West Atlantic). External morphology of the genus are quite similar, they can be identified with artificial keys and distribution ranges. Three new species of Stellifer from shallow coastal waters of Caribbean and Northeast Brazil have been recognized as Stellifer sp. A, B and C for years. Recent collections from Belize to Colombia showed that S. sp. C is distinct from S. colonesis with a wider range of distribution. S. sp. A was first collected from Guyana coast to Amazon delta; digging through museum specimens has extended its range to Southeast Brazil. S. sp. B is known from few specimens off Venezuela coast. Among the Stellifer species, S. naso and S. venezuelansis are similar to Ophoscion by their distinct inferior mouths, well serrated preopercular margins and larger eyes, except that they also have a pair of large kidney-shaped diverticula on the gas bladder. None of the East Pacific Stellifer has this feature. There are at least 7 East Pacific species of Ophioscion, but only one valid species form West Atlantic and may be two more undescribed species from Northeast Brazil. Lack of detailed phylogenetic studies of the genera and the tribe, external morphology and macro-anatomical characters are still the basis of their classification.

22251: Bryconops caudomaculatus was described by Gunther with the type locality listed as "South America". 22252: A recent hypothesis of phylogenetic relationships of the Moxostoma--group suckers based on molecular phylogenetic evidence (cytochrome-b) was proposed by Harris et al. (2002). The results differed from Smiths (1992) cladistic hypothesis based on morphology, early life history, and biochemical data. The only statistically significant difference discovered between the two analyses was that cytochrome-b sequences recovered the genus Scartomyzon as polyphyletic. Cytochrome-b was unable to resolve many basal nodes among the Catostominae with high bootstrap confidence. The cytochrome-b based classification resurrected the tribes Erimyzonini and Thoburniini and considered Scartomyzon a junior synonym of Moxostoma. Due to my interests in systematics, phylogenetic relationships, and biogeographic patterns of western species traditionally allied with the genus Scartomyzon, an additional cytochrome-b analysis was conducted. Similar to the study of Harris et al. (2002), the present analysis failed to resolve many basal nodes among the Catostominae and also recovered Scartomyzon as polyphyletic. However, there were inconsistencies in the placement of certain taxa and constraining trees to conform to the hypothesis of Harris et al. (2002) resulted in significantly longer trees (173 steps longer, p<0.0001). The major differences between the molecular analyses involved the phylogenetic positions of S. ariommus, S. lachneri, S. sp. cf. austrinus (Rio Juchipila, Mex), S. rupiscartes, and S. congestus (Devils River, TX). 22253: As part of an attempt to reconstruct the original distribution and relative abundance of Lake Sturgeon in tributaries to Lake Michigan, we have surveyed old newspapers and other documents for accounts of sturgeon captured by sport and commercial fishers. Newspapers in some cities provided an abundance of anecdotal information about sturgeon captured locally, which generally was consistent with historical patterns in the overharvest and decline of sturgeon populations elsewhere and with modern data on the biology of the species. In some locations, newspapers included accounts of sturgeon captured in distant drainages, but a lack of accounts of sturgeon captured locally suggested that they were absent from the local tributaries. 22254: Prolonged exposure to microgravity conditions during space flight has been linked to various physiological changes in humans, including reduced bone density and muscle mass and aberrations in vestibular function. In order to better understand the processes underlying these phenomena, and to develop appropriate countermeasures for future long-term space occupation, cell and cell monoculture responses have been extensively studied with the use of a ground-based analogue for microgravity provided by the rotating cell culture system, or RCCS (Synthecon™) . However, such studies do not address the possible deleterious effects of microgravity on more complex interactions occurring within and among developing tissues during ontogeny. To evaluate the effects of simulated microgravity on ontogenetic processes, Rivulus marmoratus embryos were maintained from shortly after fertilization through to hatching in either a static container, or an RCCS environment. Survival of embryos to hatching was 100% in both experimental and control groups. Control post-hatchlings exhibited normal morphology, swimming and feeding behavior. In contrast, experimental fish exhibited: extensive axial skeleton curvature; frequently a pronounced dorso-cranial depression; a failure to visually track or capture live prey; and rapid mortality, all dying within 7 days of hatching. A histological examination revealed that, in addition to skeletal and behavioral deficits, experimental fish exhibited extensive abnormalities in brain and eye structure. The presence of these abnormalities suggests that exposure to microgravity conditions during human development, without appropriate countermeasures, may have considerable deleterious consequences. These early results also indicate that Rivulus marmoratus may be an excellent vertebrate model for future microgravity research linked to human endeavors in space. 22255: The three species of river sturgeon, genus Scaphirhynchus, are endemic to the large turbid rivers of the United States. Pallid Sturgeon (S. albus) and Alabama Sturgeon (S. suttkusi) are considered endangered throughout their range and many populations of Shovelnose Sturgeon (S. platorynchus) are in decline. Because critical information on the early life history of these species is lacking, we described the sequence and timing of embryologic development of Shovelnose Sturgeon (n = 850) reared at a constant 20±0.5°C. Artificially inseminated, fertilized eggs were held in a recirculating system and embryos were subsampled hourly for the first 48 hours of development and every three hours subsequent to that. These embryos were viewed and imaged under a stereo microscope at 35x magnification. Developmental patterns were consistent with other Acipenserid species, displaying holoblastic cleavage. The first cleavage furrow appeared after two hours post-fertilization and cleavage was complete after seven hours. Blastulation concluded at sixteen hours when the dorsal blastopore lip formed. The slitlike blastopore appeared at 29 hours signifying the completion of gastrulation. At 33 hours, the rudiments of the excretory system emerged, followed by closing of the neural tube at 36 hours and formation of the s-shaped heart at 60 hours. Mass hatch occurred at 102 hours. After hatch, larvae swam into the water column and drifted in the flow for approximately two days after which the larvae became positively rheotaxic. Because shovelnose sturgeon show developmental patterns similar to those of other sturgeon, we can use this species as a model for the closely related pallid and Alabama sturgeon.

22256: The Commercial Shark Fishery Observer Program has placed observers on commercial shark fishing vessels since 1994 to collect biological information on the sharks caught in the fishery. Knowledge of at-vessel mortality (sharks caught that arrive at the vessel dead) is important for management of the various species taken. We compared the at-vessel mortality rates of nine commonly captured large and small coastal sharks, Carcharhinus plumbeus (N=14,890), C. limbatus (N=2896), C. acronotus (N=1560), C. obscurus (N=1221), C. leucas (N=447), Rhizoprionodon terraenovae (N=10,726), Galeocerdo cuvier (N=4955), Sphyrna lewini (N=733), and S. mokarran (N=282), with reference to soak time, water depth, water temperature, and the shark's fork length. 22257: The Rocky Mountain Region of the USGS Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative is conducting monitoring of the status of amphibians on a transect that extends along the Continental Divide from Canada to Colorado and comprises four National Parks and several National Wildlife Refuges. Monitoring uses visual encounter surveys to determine site occupancy, with multiple visits to a subset of sites to estimate detection probabilities for each species. Detection probabilities varied among species and for some species were influenced by cover of aquatic vegetation. There was a gradient in site occupancy, with most species scarce in the south and relatively common in the north. For example, Bufo boreas is close to extinction in Rocky Mountain NP, was found at fewer than 5% of sites in Yellowstone and Grand Teton NP, but occurs in approximately 10% of sites in Glacier NP. Rana luteiventris was found at about 30% of sites in Glacier, but only about 20% in Yellowstone and Grand Teton. Pseudacris maculata was detected at about 35% of sites in Yellowstone and Grand Teton, but <20% of sites in Rocky Mountain. Ambystoma macrodactylum occurs at >50% of sites in Glacier, while A. tigrinum was present at < 10% of sites in other parks. There are numerous differences among parks, such as latitude, climate, numbers of visitors, and human population density in the surrounding landscape, but chytrid fungus is suspected to have been a major factor in declines in Colorado.

22258: Variation in vertebral counts and other meristic characters have been used for identification in ichthyology, and may also potentially be used as characters in phylogenetic analysis. Vertebral morphology has been less commonly used. I describe notable variation in vertebral morphology and related meristics in the characin subfamily Serrasalminae (pacus and piranhas). These characteristics are explored for their utility as characters for indicating relationships within the Serrasalminae. 22259: Due to high rates of wetland habitat destruction and subsequent re-creation efforts, it is crucial to understand the biological processes of these systems. I am investigating species divergence in a tribe of sunfishes that primarily utilizes blackwater wetland habitats. Enneacanthini sunfishes occur throughout the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coastal plains, but often display distinct local distributions. Specifically, I am using a combination of dietary, morphological and functional approaches to determine if foraging ecology influences the local distributions of the group as well as test the hypothesis that selection for exploitation of alternative resources was the primary cause of divergence. Phylogenetic evolutionary momentum would predict a high degree of trophic influence on the assemblage structure of these fishes. A meta-analysis of dietary data for this group indicates significant separation of Enneacanthus species based on prey assemblages, as well as prey size and microhabitat associations. Quantitative evaluation of trophic skeletal morphology also indicates significant differences among sunfish species. I used performance feeding experiments to determine functional feeding capabilities and efficiencies of these fishes on three prey types representing differing prey microhabitats, and a multi-approach factor analysis to evaluate the ability of trophic morphology and function to explain Enneacanthini feeding ecologies. Canonical correlations were used to determine the relationships of morphology to both diets and feeding efficiencies as potential factors in Enneacanthus speciation. The documented uniqueness of intact wetland communities coupled with their inherent isolated nature, suggest an important role of assemblage-level interactions in determining wetland community structure and composition. An increased mechanistic understanding of these processes will allow for the development of more effective management and conservation practices for these resources and their biological communities.

22260: Predation imposes important selective pressures on prey resulting in a great diversity of defense mechanisms, one of the most intriguing being repellent defense, like venoms and toxins. The acquisition of toxicity can come from either intrinsic synthesis, in which the organism’s own genetic or metabolic machinery produces the toxic compounds, or uptake, sequestration and/or storing of toxic compounds produced by other organisms. Toxicity and bright coloration has evolved multiple times in Neotropical poison frogs (Dendrobatidae), a group with both toxic and non-toxic species (Santos et al., 2003, PNAS 100:12792-12797). Some researchers have suggested that poison frog toxins come from a diet of ants and other small arthropods, which are rich in toxic alkaloid chemicals; the frogs sequester the alkaloids in their skin for defense. A critical prediction from the diet-toxicity hypothesis is that the more ant-specialized species of poison frogs will be more toxic. To test this predication in an evolutionary framework using the Santos et al. molecular phylogeny, we assessed toxicity using thin layer chromatography, and diet- specialization by analyzing stomach contents. Using these data and a compilation of data from the literature, we tested the diet-toxicity hypothesis for a total of 15 species, using independent contrasts and generalized least squares models. We found a significant correlation between level of toxicity and degree of ant-specialization for each of the evolutionarily independent origins of toxicity in poison frogs. This reveals a recurring association of toxicity and diet-specialization in the evolution of poison frogs, which suggests a sequestration mechanism in the ancestor of poison frogs and parallel evolutionary trends in defense mechanism driven by predation pressure.

22261: Notropis heterodon is a threatened species in Illinois, and little is known about its reproductive or dietary habits. During the summer of 2002 and 2003 I sampled Leopold Lake in Grayslake, Illinois, and found that the reproductive period extended from mid to late May through early August. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) had two peaks, one at the end of May and the other at the beginning of June during both years, indicating the species may produce multiple clutches. 22262: There are concerns that some populations of anadromous alewife, Alosa pseudoharengus, commonly referred to as River Herring, have substantially declined in Connecticut. 22265: Compared to some temperate and tropical areas, relatively little is known about the historical biogeography of arid regions of North and Middle America. Snakes of the genus Trimorphodon (lyresnakes) are xeric-adapted species that inhabit deserts and subhumid regions of the southwestern U.S., Mexico, and Central America. Most workers recognize at least two species within the genus: the Mexican Lyresnake, T. tau, found over much of mainland Mexico north of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and the more widely distributed and polytypic Western Lyresnake, T. biscutatus, ranging from the southwestern United States southward along the pacific lowland versant of Mexico to northwestern Costa Rica. Given their broad geographic ranges, lyresnakes provide the opportunity to test a number of biogeographic hypotheses that have been proposed for North and Middle American aridlands. I investigated populations of both T. biscutatus and T. tau using mitochondrial DNA sequence data to infer geologic and paleoclimatic events that may have played a role in the diversification of this group. Results suggest that vicariance associated with the periodic separation and reconnection of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts, and formation of the Baja California Peninsula, Transverse Volcanic Axis, and Guatemalan highlands contributed to differentiation within Trimorphodon. Additionally, the steep ecological gradient from Sonoran desert to tropical deciduous forest has strongly influenced species borders. Patterns of differentiation in other co-distributed organisms are largely congruent and suggest shared history. This work contributes to a better understanding of how historical forces have shaped genetic, species, and community diversity in the aridlands of North and Middle America.

22266: Gopher tortoises inhabit well-drained, upland, sandy soils, areas highly desirable for development. Because sacrificing tortoises is illegal in some areas of its range, as well as undesirable (due to public outcry), relocation to off-site habitats has become a common practice. Although frequently used, relocations of gopher tortoises have rarely maintained a viable population. One of the major criticisms of most tortoise relocation studies is that they were not designed as ecological experiments but rather as actual mitigation measures. In addition, most relocation studies have monitored tortoises for very short periods of time (usually less than one year and often less than three months), a period clearly inadequate given the long lifespan of tortoises. Our objective is to experimentally determine whether length of time in a holding pen (a so-called "soft" release) affects the probability of relocation success. In this study, 24 tortoises were relocated from nearby development sites to a restored longleaf pine habitat within their historic range in the DeSoto National Forest in southern Mississippi. Tortoises were equipped with radio transmitters and placed into replicated intermediate-term (2-3 months) and long-term (12 month) enclosures. Digital cameras were placed at burrows occupied by females to monitor social encounters. More than 4000 photos were generated and categorized into male-male, male- female, and female-female interactions and further categorized into territorial encounters, mating attempts, and unknown interactions. The interactions are currently being quantified, and levels of interactions will be compared to determine differences among enclosures as well as individuals. Results from interactions will also be used to assign a social ranking for each tortoise and establish a representative social hierarchy within the enclosures, which may explain post-release behaviors and movements. Understanding particular behavioral interactions at certain levels could play an important role in predicting the success of gopher tortoise relocations.

22267: In the last few years, the evolutionary history of the lizard family Gymnophthalmidae has gone from virtually unknown to relatively well studied. 22268: A critical variable in both ecological and conservation field studies is determining how many individuals of a species are present within a defined sampling area. Labor intensive techniques such as capture-mark- recapture and removal sampling may provide estimates of abundance, but there are many logistical constraints to their widespread application. Many studies on terrestrial and aquatic salamanders use counts as an index of abundance, assuming that detection remains constant while sampling. If this constancy is violated, determination of detection probabilities is critical to the accurate estimation of abundance. Royle (Biometrica, 2004) recently developed a statistical approach that allows abundance and detection to be estimated simultaneously from counts. We adapted this model to estimate these parameters for salamanders sampled over a six year period in area-constrained plots in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Estimates of salamander abundance varied among years, but annual changes in abundance did not vary uniformly among species. Except for two species, abundance estimates were not correlated with site covariates (elevation, soil and water pH, conductivity, air and water temperature). The uncertainty in the estimates was so large as to make correlations ineffectual in predicting which covariates might influence abundance. Detection probabilities also varied among species and sometimes among years for the six species examined. We found such a high degree of variation in our counts and in estimates of detection among species, sites, and years as to cast doubt upon the appropriateness of using count data to monitor population trends using a small number of area-constrained survey plots. Still, the model provided reasonable estimates of abundance that could make it useful in estimating population size from count surveys.

22270: Historical and contemporary factors affect the distributions of amphibians and reptiles found on tepuis of the Lost World. 22271: AmphibiaWeb was established to assemble and share relevant data on the biology and conservation of amphibian species. 22272: We mapped 114 restriction sites in the mitochondrial (mt) DNA genome of Speckled Dace (Rhinichthys osculus), a small cyprinid fish broadly distributed in western North America. 22274: The characid Astyanax mexicanus consists of an eyed epigean (surface) form and at least 29 different populations of eyeless hypogean (cave) forms. 22275: Body size is a critical component in understanding the life history of an organism because of its interplay with physiology, ecology, and behavior. 22277: Polystomatids are known from all continents and most of the larger islands inhabited by their hosts. The family Polystomatidae is represented by 19 genera. 22278: Over the past decade, while several studies have shown the tremendous amount of morphological and behavioral variation that exists within and among species of anuran larvae subjected to varying predator regimes, none have revealed the link between morphology and burst swimming speed. 22281: Theoretical evolutionary ecology generates testable predictions concerning the effects of species interactions on ecological, behavioral, and morphological traits. Both regions are significantly larger than those previously studied in other Plethodon communities (4X and 10X larger). 22284: When territorial quality varies, theory predicts that animals may vary in the degree to which they defend territories. Defects were observed in 13.5% - 98% of each collection (mean = 1.4 - 5.9 defects/tadpole). Tooth rows contained 80% of all observed defects, whereas jaw sheaths and marginal papillae contained 13% and 7%, respectively. Absent teeth with and without disrupted adjacent tissue were the most common defects overall at 59.8% and 17.7%, respectively. Tooth rows A-2 and P-2 had the most tooth row defects (24.2% and 22%). Lack of pigment was the most common jaw sheath defect (57.5%), while missing portions were the most common defect in the marginal papillae (60%). The ventral marginal papillae had 48.5% of the marginal papillae defects, whereas the upper jaw sheaths had 73% of the jaw sheath defects. 22286: In predictable environments a single, optimal offspring size that maximises parental fitness should evolve. Variation in maternal investment is expected to evolve if there is unpredictability in the offspring environment and these multiple offspring size optima can exist due to temporal or spatial differences in the quality of the offspring environment. A critical variable determining offspring success in the temporary aquatic environments that frogs use for reproduction is pond persistence. In ponds where water level fluctuates unpredictably, larvae can become vulnerable to desiccation and exposed to higher densities of aquatic competitors and predators at times of low water level. Within an assemblage of frog species in southwestern Australia some species have low intra- and interclutch variation in yolk volume and some have very high variation in yolk volume within and between clutches. There is a negative relationship between the magnitude of variation in egg provisioning and the predictability of water levels in ponds that these species use for reproduction. Crinia georgiana breeds in very unpredictable ponds and has high variation in yolk volume within and between clutches. Larvae from large eggs metamorphose in less time and at a larger size than larvae from smaller eggs, and can reach metamorphosis without feeding. Less investment per egg, allowing the production of more eggs is beneficial in producing more offspring in a persistent pond, however, producing fewer, larger eggs, ensuring survival, is beneficial in a drying pond.

22287: The objective of this study was to assess amphibian habitat-use in the highly modified Aspen Parkland of the Beaver Hills, Alberta, Canada. The Wood Frog (Rana sylvatica) and Boreal Chorus Frog (Pseudacris maculata) were the most widespread species, occurring at > 75% of ponds. The relative abundances of these two species were lowest in crop and pasture ponds. Western Toad (Bufo boreas) abundance was greatest at natural and pasture ponds, and Tiger Salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum) abundance was greatest within crop ponds themselves. Canadian Toad (Bufo hemiophrys) was extremely rare and found only in Elk Island National Park. Several landscape and local habitat features were significantly correlated with relative abundances of Wood Frog, Chorus Frog, and Tiger Salamander. 22289: The Desert Tortoise, Gopherus agassizii, is native to the North American desert southwest and is recognized as having a Sonoran population and a threatened Mojave population. We used 981 base pairs of mitochondrial DNA sequence data to estimate genetic variation between and within the Mojave and Sonoran populations. Our results are consistent with previous studies that have shown that Mojave and Sonoran populations have substantial fixed nucleotide differences between them, indicating that gene flow has not occurred between the two deserts for approximately 6 million years. Tortoises at sites in the western Mojave, where habitat is fairly continuous, exhibit a population genetic structure characteristic of isolation by distance. Although study sites in southern Arizona appear more isolated by landscape heterogeneity, we also found little genetic differentiation among the majority of study sites, indicating that gene flow also occurred historically among these Sonoran population study sites. Our results suggest that geographic features are not necessarily a good predictor of what constitutes an evolutionarily significant unit for the desert tortoise. 22290: The Plethodon glutinosus Complex is a geographically widespread salamander group inhabiting forests throughout the eastern United States and is locally abundant throughout the coastal plain. As such it is exposed to a variety of climatic conditions and makes the perfect candidate group for examining large-scale variation in thermal tolerance limits and heat shock protein expression. We examined thirteen populations of the P. glutinosus complex representing three physiographic regions for variation in hsp70 levels along environmental gradients. Hsp70 levels varied significantly among populations and physiographic regions but not among heat shocked or control treatment groups. In addition, there was an unexpected inverse relationship between the stress response and climate: piedmont populations contained significantly higher levels of hsp70 than either coastal plain or montane populations. The patterns observed in the stress response of the P. glutinosus complex reflect what is described as a constitutive based heat shock strategy. This strategy acknowledges that hsp70 induction incurs a fitness cost and that organisms from both relatively stable and highly disturbed habitats should trade-off inducible thermotolerance for high levels of constitutive protein. This strategy predicts that organisms from habitats with intermediate levels of disturbance should have the highest levels of inducible protein. However, because this confers a potentially high energetic cost, selection should ultimately push the population towards one side of the model or the other.

22291: The Red-backed Salamander, Plethodon cinereus, is abundant and widespread throughout woodland habitats in eastern North America from North Carolina to Canada. Most populations throughout the range of the species exhibit a color polymorphism for the presence or absence of a dorsal stripe. The proportion of striped (red-backed) and unstriped (lead-backed) individuals varies from location to location, but seems temporally stable within a given location. In 1968 Williams Highton and Cooper documented what they called a breakdown in the polymorphism on Long Island, NY. They noted that the populations on the west end and north shore of the island were almost entirely striped and populations on the eastern and southern parts of the island were almost entirely unstriped. They proposed that this pattern could be attributed to isolation of the Long Island population accompanied by strong selection for lead-backed color morph in the dry pine barren habitats, which were predominant on the island throughout the Pleistocene, followed by re-establishment of red-backed individuals during the post-Pleistocene expansion of mesic, deciduous forest across the west and north of the island. Our surveys of color morph frequencies at >70 locations throughout LI, confirmed the basic pattern of geographic segregation of striped populations in the west and unstriped populations in the east, with a relatively narrow band of mixed populations in the center of the island. Phylogeographic evidence from mtDNA sequence data from throughout Long Island and the mainland is consistent with recent recolonization of the island. This implies that the segregation of color morphs cannot be attributed to long-term isolation of the unstriped population, but more likely evolved under strong selective pressure since the last glacial retreat. 22293: One the primary objectives of the newly-formed Pacific Shark Research Center (PSRC) at Moss Landing Marine Laboratories (MLML) was the creation of a comprehensive life history data matrix covering the entire body of literature on all chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras) of the eastern North Pacific, from the eastern Bering Sea to the southern tip of Baja California. 22295: The use of skeletochronology in many reptile groups has become a commonplace method of incremental growth analysis over the last twenty years. With the exception of sea turtles, this method has been largely overlooked as a feasible alternative to scute annuli counts or carapace/plastron lengths in turtles and tortoises. Incremental growth layers in many reptiles and amphibians have been correlated to annual growth cycles. In bone thin sections, a light, wide band represents a season of rapid growth, and a thin, dark band represents a season of slow growth or stasis, making up a single year's growth. The technique was then applied to the fossil remains of two North American tortoise species collected in the Nebraska Badlands. Stylemys nebrascensis and Gopherus laticuneus were collected in the summer of 2002 and prepared for sectioning. Humeri from 22 fossil specimens were included in this survey, all showing positive results. Information derived from incremental growth assessment includes approximate age of the individual and approximate age at sexual maturity. This data can be used to determine the population dynamics of a group of individuals. Mean and average ages and age at sexual maturity of a population can all be deduced from skeletochronology studies. Other aging techniques (i.e., scute annuli counts) have proven to be misleading, showing either too many or too few annuli.

22296: Among visually oriented animals, color signals play an important role in social interactions and have important fitness consequences. We hypothesized that FBC is a signal to males that either attracts or deters courtship and mating. We tested this hypothesis using hormone-implantation and color-manipulation experiments. Randomly paired lizards were introduced to a laboratory arena where we quantified their behaviors using videotape. Hormone implanted males attempted to copulate with females regardless of female coloration and male behavior did not differ before and after the development of FBC. Moreover, males exhibited no preference for FBC in color-manipulation experiments. 22297: We tested the hypothesis that stable isotope techniques can be used as dietary indicators with three controlled diet experiments using lab colonies of pigmy rattlesnakes (Sistrurus miliarius), corn snakes (Elaphe guttatta), and horned frogs (Ceratophrys cranwelli). We randomly assigned each animal to one of two isotopically distinct diets. At the start of the experiment, we collected a scale/skin tissue sample from each animal and fed each animal its first experimental meal. Again, we fed the animals every 10 days and collected tissue samples every 15 days. For each colony, tissue δ13C and δ15N values diverged from their initial values, steadily approached each set of diet isotope ratios, tracked the diet switch at day 60, and again approached each set of diet isotope ratios. 22308: Because of their morphological constraints and relatively high trophic levels, the foraging ecology of snakes has been an important area of study. However, much of the literature on food habits of particular species is incomplete. Prey records are often grouped with no regard to the large ontogenetic changes in body size of snakes or differences that might occur relative to seasonal differences in prey abundance. We examined the prey of the Western Ribbon Snake, Thamnophis proximus, in a large floodplain hardwood forest in northeastern Texas, where prey availability is very stochastic. Snakes were collected under coverboards placed near ephemeral pools and streams where prey was often aggregated. Snakes were sexed, measured and weighed; and prey items were palped out of the stomach, identified and weighed. Small snakes tended to eat tadpoles (mostly Rana sp.) and salamander larva (Ambystoma texanum and Notophthalmus viridescens) with some elongated species of fish such as darters. Larger snakes ate small sunfish and pirate perch but frogs comprised the majority of the diet of adult snakes. Medium size snakes caught newly metamorphic Rana with tails in early summer but for the remainder of the year most snakes had empty stomachs or had eaten larger frogs. 22309: One of the most interesting traits to vary among groups of squamate reptiles is the presence or absence of multiple clutches, i.e., repeated production of eggs or live young produced by the same female within the same reproductive season. Although multiple clutches are widespread among lizards, multiple clutches remain very rare among snakes in the wild. However, some snakes are known to have the potential of producing multiple clutches in captivity, allowing a better understanding of inter- versus intra-individual variation in reproductive traits. Our specific goals were to (1) determine variation among females in their ability to produce multiple clutches, (2) determine the repeatability of reproductive traits among different clutches, and (3) determine if trade-offs between such traits as clutch size and offspring size were variable within the same female over time. We found that the presence of multiple clutches in this species was highly variable, with the number of clutches produced varying from 1-11, even though snakes were in the same body condition during the study. Conversely, a multivariate repeated-measures ANOVA showed no significant variation in either clutch size or egg size for the first five clutches, suggesting that reproductive traits are highly consistent within individuals.

22310: We sampled the distribution of Northern Dusky Salamander (Desmognathus fuscus) nests at 24 randomly selected 15 m stream reaches throughout a third-order watershed in eastern Maryland to investigate the distribution of nest in relationship to physical habitat variables at three scale: (1) watershed, (2) meso or reach scale, and (3) micro or nest site scale. 22311: The Weedy Sea Dragon, Phyllopteryx taeniolatus, endemic to kelp forests off southern Australia has been red listed by the IUCN. 22312: Between 5 August and 5 September 2002, we conducted a preliminary inventory of fish species within Odzala National Park located in the Cuvette-Ouest Province of the Republic of Congo. 22313: The fish assemblage of the rocky reef kelp forest habitat of Santa Catalina Island, California was compared inside and outside of a marine reserve. 22314: The paleoclimatological events associated with Pleistocene glacial advance and retreat have been shown to influence the process of genetic differentiation in North American vertebrate poikiolotherms. 22315: We compared the structure of herpetofaunal communities across a spectrum of canopy tree- removal treatments in an ongoing study in the Cumberland Plateau of northern Alabama. 22316: Marine butterflyfishes (Chaetodontidae) and angelfishes (Pomacanthidae) are conspicuously beautiful and abundant animals found on coral reefs worldwide. Additionally, at least three current subgenera within Chaetodon do not exhibit monophyly. Using this phylogeny and new models of jaw function, we analyzed the evolution of jaw mechanisms in select lineages throughout both families. In angelfishes, the unusual shape of several jaw bones contributes to a novel mechanism of jaw protrusion and allows a strong bite with the jaws protruded.

22317: This study was conducted on Tombigbee National Forest and Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge in east central Mississippi from spring 2000 to fall 2003. 22318: Characters such as foraging behaviour can determine a species’ relative specialization. 22319: Populations of Yellow Perch, Perca flavescens (Percidae: Teleostei), in the Great Lakes have fluctuated substantially in recent years with unstable recruitment patterns, leading to management concerns for this popular sport and commercial fish. 22320: As amphibian populations continue to decline, it is important to consider the many factors that may be the driving forces. 22331: Of the nine currently recognized species of logperch, subgenus Percina, two are federally endangered (P. rex, P. jenkinsi) and one is critically imperiled (P. burtoni). These species are resolved as basal members of the subgenus in contrast with the more widespread terminal species (e.g., P. caprodes, P. macrolepida, P. carbonaria). Percina jenkinsi is restricted to 18 contiguous river kilometers of the Conasauga River, and occurs at low densities. Percina rex is restricted to the Roanoke and Chowan river drainages and has a distribution fragmented by impoundments, but is often locally abundant. Percina burtoni occupies a large geographic area in the Tennessee River drainage, but has a highly fragmented distribution and occurs at low densities. Genetic variation in each of these taxa was examined using sequence data from the mitochondrial cyt b and ND2 genes. Levels and patterns of genetic variation found within these taxa did not reflect current conservation priorities. High levels of variation within P. rex and little evidence of geographic structuring suggest a very recent decline in gene flow across its range. In contrast, P. burtoni exhibited significant genetic differences across almost all populations, and substantial differentiation between Duck River/Whiteoak Creek populations and those in the rest of the Tennessee River system. Almost no haplotypes were shared between populations in the Tennessee River system, suggesting limited dispersal. Two discrete clades of P. jenkinsi were recovered, and differed by approximately 1% sequence divergence. This suggests a more complex evolutionary history than currently understood. Critical examination of the mechanisms driving divergence within such a restricted species is crucial for better management. Comparative examination of patterns of genetic variation provide new insights into the historical abundance and dispersal ability of these fishes, and suggest reassessment of conservation priority is needed.

22332: We measured relative gut length, Zihler's index, and relative gut mass in four species of prickleback fishes and determined the effects of ontogeny, diet, and phylogeny on these gut dimensions. Gut dimensions were compared in three categories of the four species: (1) small, wild-caught juveniles representing the carnivorous condition before two species shift to herbivory; (2) larger, wild-caught juveniles representing the natural diet condition of the two carnivores and the two species that have shifted to herbivory; and (3) larger, lab-fed juveniles produced by feeding a high-protein animal diet to small juveniles until they have reached the size of the larger, wild-caught juveniles. Comparisons of gut dimensions in categories (1) vs. (2) tested for an ontogenetic effect, in (2) vs. (3) for a dietary effect, and within categories (1) and (2) for a phylogenetic effect. 22333: The ornamental (home aquarium) fish trade has boomed over the past 50 years, often providing much-needed income to local communities. However, claims that the ornamental fishery is sustainable (Chao, 1999) have not been supported by systematic ecological sampling. The purpose of this study was to determine whether heavy ornamental fishing around Iquitos, Peru on the Nanay River was impacting the abundance, species diversity and overall sustainability of the trade in Peru. 22334: The family Fundulidae includes the North American killifishes with thirty-six extant species in North America, Bermuda, and the northern Yucatan Peninsula. 22335: Playa wetlands represent the main habitat for amphibians in the Southern High Plains. 22336: Partners in Amphibian and Reptile Conservation (PARC) is a multi-sector partnership dedicated to the conservation of herpetofauna and their habitats. 22337: North American cyprinids exhibit a range of trophic specializations. Some species feed largely on diatoms, others on detritus, while still others are carnivores feeding on insects or other aquatic invertebrates. Specialized morphologies are associated with each of these trophic specializations. For example, although exceptions to this generalization exist, herbivorous cyprinids have elongate guts and black peritonea. Little is known of the evolution of trophic specialization and associated trophic morphologies. We examined diet and trophic morphology in the genus Pimephales and its putative sister group Opsopeodus. This clade contains five species distributed widely in eastern North America. We obtained descriptions of diet from the literature and described trophic morphologies from museum specimens. A phylogenetic hypothesis for this group was constructed based on mitochondrial cytchrome b and nuclear S7 DNA sequences. Our presentation will discuss the evolution of trophic shifts and associated trophic morphologies in Pimephales and Opsopoeodus in a historical context, by mapping these traits onto a phylogenetic tree based on the aforementioned molecular data.

22338: A first step towards conserving aquatic biodiversity requires knowledge of the spatial distribution of organisms across a landscape and how these organisms respond to environmental gradients. Aquatic systems in the Great Plains are temporally variable habitats that typically select for fishes with generalist life history strategies. Thus, it may be difficult to associate species occurrences or abundance with environmental gradients at intermediate spatial scales. Spatial gradients in temperature and precipitation should associate with fish assemblage structure at large scales, whereas at smaller spatial scales, longitudinal changes in fish assemblage structure should exist in streams from headwaters to large rivers. The goal of this research was to evaluate spatial patterns of fish assemblages in the Great Plains, and how they are structured along environmental gradients across multiple scales. We used a geographic information system and multivariate techniques to quantify the concordance between fish assemblage structure and environmental gradients. Our results not only revealed changes in assemblage structure across both large and small spatial scales, but that several species were associated with geologic features of the landscape at intermediate spatial scales. 22339: While many aspects of tortoise biology are well studied and successful captive-breeding programs exist for several imperiled species, spatial variation in the growth of wild juvenile tortoises is poorly understood. We assessed the efficacy of remotely sensed imagery at coarse spatial scales for predicting spatial patterns in growth and improving restoration ecology programs. Between 2001 and 2003, we marked and recaptured nearly 300 juvenile Galápagos tortoises on Santa Cruz Island. Data recorded for each tortoise included latitude and longitude via GPS, mass, and curved carapace length. Except for an extremely dry period in 2003, the growth of tortoises followed an expected pattern of decreasing growth rate with increased size. The rate of growth did not vary between seasons, despite a distinctly seasonal environment. Individual tortoises also did not exhibit a tendency to grow faster or slower than their conspecifics when compared between seasons An analysis of residuals from regression models of growth failed to reveal a spatial clustering of either fast or slow growing individuals; however, the ratios of positive to negative residuals did vary between study areas. Using remote sensing software and imagery at various spatial scales (ground resolution 4m-28.5m), we developed models predicting areas of rapid and slow growth in relation to the rest of the population. For most models, accuracy was no better than 70% though higher resolution imagery greatly improved the resolution of rapid and slow growth areas. While in case of Galápagos, better data on tortoise movement is needed to improve the models; the accessibility of coarse scale remote imagery and the relatively low cost of software and processing can greatly enhance ecological restoration programs for many species.

22340: Ameiva chrysoleama is a widespread teiid lizard on the island of Hispaniola. 22341: My purpose was to identify circumstances that would cause male pickerel frogs (Rana palustris) to call underwater. An informal survey of Pennsylvania ponds demonstrated that although males usually vocalize into the air from stationary calling sites, calling can occur exclusively underwater in some populations. Males have a complex vocal repertoire consisting of an advertisement call and two additional calls (snicker and growl) that are emitted during aggressive interactions. All call types are emitted into the air or underwater. I conducted several experimental manipulations with resident males that, initially, were calling above water. Three of these involved playbacks in which I presented males with either one conspecific advertisement call, or two minutes of continuous advertisement calling from Pseudacris crucifer or Bufo americanus. When I broadcast a conspecific advertisement call, eight of 14 males emitted underwater some combination of the three call types before calling above water again. In contrast, males did not call underwater in response to P. crucifer calls (N=5) and only two of 15 called underwater in reponse to B. americanus calls even though most males emitted snickers during the test period. In a final experiment, I poked 16 males in the rear with either a pencil or the tip of a fishing rod. All but one male predictably moved underwater in response to this disturbance. Eleven of these recommenced vocalizing within 10 to 95 seconds and called underwater for up to four minutes before calling above the water's surface again. These data demonstrate that pickerel frogs potentially communicate through both air and water, and that when threatened, it may be better to call underwater than to not call at all.

22343: The Grand Cayman blue iguana, Cyclura lewisi, is critically endangered and in need of intensive management. 22345: Amphibian population declines have been documented around the world, but on the Colorado Plateau, very little is known of population dynamics of amphibian species. 22346: The superfamily Echeneoidea includes the Echeneidae (remoras), Rachycentridae (cobia) and Coryphaenidae (dolphin). 22347: This study investigated the daily thermal patterns of six free-ranging black racers (Coluber constrictor) in Middle Tennessee. 22348: Viperid snakes strike, envenomate, and release mammalian prey to prevent their being harmed by the prey; snakes must then track prey in the process of strike-induced chemosensory searching. 22349: The federal listing of the Mojave Desert Tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) as a threatened species elucidated the need for the development of effective conservation strategies. 22351: Reductions in effective population size brought about by harvest are one potential source of loss of genetic variation. 22352: Distinctive morphological traits are often presumed to be adaptive. Such hypotheses pertaining to current utility can be resolved in a comparative framework. If a character is adaptive, we should expect a performance advantage relative to the phylogenetically antecedent condition. Furthermore, if we are to explain the potential historical origin of adaptive traits, then we must demonstrate that an ecological regime exists within which the presumed adaptive character would be selectively favored. I compared the mass ratio of Dasypeltis to 18 other species of snakes as well as a qualitative assessment of the number of meals per year required by Dasypeltis. 22353: Bavayia cf. crassicollis is a relatively large-bodied, arboreal species of forest gecko that is endemic to the New Caledonian region. 22354: I measured the activities of proteases, carbohydrases, and a lipase in Phytichthys chirus to determine whether this fish exhibits digestive enzyme activities supporting its current position in a clade of largely herbivorous pricklebacks (Stichaeidae) or in an adjacent clade of carnivorous species. 22355: Many amphibians exhibit defensive behaviors that have evolved through the co-evolution of predator and prey. These behaviors sometimes entail the ability to recognize and respond to potential predators via olfaction. The purpose of this study was to determine if Spotted Salamander larvae (Ambystoma maculatum) detect and respond to vertebrate (large-mouth bass) and/or invertebrate (crayfish) predators via visual and/or chemical stimuli. Analyses showed that salamanders exhibited more activity when exposed to crayfish chemicals than in the control condition, but activity levels during exposure to bass cues did not differ significantly from the control. 22356: We tested whether experience with predatory and nonpredatory stimuli influences habitat choice by rainbow darters, Etheostoma caeruleum . First, we exposed darters in two different habitats (woody debris and rocks) to chemical stimuli from predators (sculpins) and nonpredators (stonerollers, blank control). When subsequently offered a choice between the two habitat types, darters previously exposed to predatory stimuli preferred the rock habitat regardless of the habitat occupied in the training trials. Rocks are the most common shelter available to rainbow darters in their natural stream habitat, and so attraction to this habitat could be an antipredator response. Habitat choice was not different from random for darters previously exposed to the nonpredatory stimuli. In a second experiment, we found that exposure to chemical stimuli from injured conspecifics did not influence subsequent habitat choice. However, habitat choice was influenced by prior exposure to chemical stimuli from non-injured conspecifics. Darters preferred the rock habitat if they had previously experienced conspecific cues in that habitat, indicating that social facilitation can also influence use of habitat.

22357: Reproduction is energetically expensive in most animals, and red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) are no exception. Previous studies have suggested that females require two years after producing one clutch to meet the energetic requirements of yolking their next clutch. Females oviposit in early summer, brooding their eggs until hatching. I conducted a three-year field study on red-backed salamanders at Mountain Lake Biological Station. I established 400 artificial cover objects (ACOs) and uniquely tagged all individuals (n = 3487) that I found under these ACOs, sampling boards approximately once weekly during the field seasons of 1998 through 2000. By candling females, I counted eggs before oviposition; I also counted eggs in clutches laid under the ACOs. I also determined the reproductive status (gravid or nongravid) of some females (n = 94) for three or four consecutive years. I found that 71% (n = 56) of these females were gravid in consecutive years. This is higher than the 50% predicted by our current understanding of red- backed salamander physiology, which holds that females oviposit biennially. By recording the fate of clutches laid under ACOs, and determining the reproductive status of those females for the following year, I found that females that lose their clutch during brooding can oviposit the following year, while females that do not lose their clutch and thus brood their clutch to hatching are unlikely to yolk eggs for the following year. I suggest that the energetic cost of brooding, not the energetic cost of yolking eggs per se, limits reproductive output. If females could escape the cost of brooding, they could potentially double their fitness. Future research could examine reproductive decisions that a female must make based on the costs/benefits of brooding a current clutch versus the potential for ovipositing the following year or in two years.

22358: The adaptive radiation of Greater Antillean Anolis lizards is best known for the independent evolution of distinct microhabitat specialists (ecomorphs) on different islands. However, most species are the result of intra-island speciation within rather than between ecomorph classes. Cuba, for example, is home to a clade of 14 trunk-ground specialists. My research combines morphological, ecological, and molecular data to examine these intra-island radiations. My goals are to (1) identify evolutionary lineages and factors that contribute to their divergence, (2) determine how species specialized for the same microhabitat are able to coexist on an island, and (3) test hypotheses that may account for differences in the species richness of intra-island radiations. First, I conducted detailed studies of intraspecific geographic variation in ten widespread species. These studies uncovered strong genetic breaks that were often concordant with previously recognized morphological variation. This result suggests that geographic processes are important to anole diversification and that the already high species richness of Anolis has been underestimated. I examined the second question through detailed morphometric studies, which revealed that members of some ecomorph radiations have further specialized to occupy different forest types or climates. This pattern has likely facilitated the coexistence of multiple allopatric species belonging to the same ecomorph category on each island. Finally, I tested three general hypotheses (age, gene flow, and environmental heterogeneity) that may account for the higher diversity observed in trunk-ground versus trunk-crown ecomorph radiations. This test compared comprehensive intra- and interspecific phylogenies for independently evolved trunk-ground and trunk-crown radiations on each Greater Antillean island. Overall, my results reveal new dimensions of the anole radiation and suggest specific mechanisms that have contributed to the remarkable diversity of this group.

22359: The Gonorynchidae (Ostariophysi: Gonorynchiformes) consists of one extant genus, Gonorynchus, and an assemblage of fossil forms whose interrelationships are largely unresolved. Ramallichthys orientalis Gayet (1982) described from Cretaceous limestone beds of Ramallah, Israel is pivotal to a better understanding of gonorynchid interrelationships, but is known from poorly preserved material. Presented here is a reassessment of the morphology of Ramallichthys orientalis based on new and better-prepared material. The information generated from this study, especially from the skull and anterior vertebral region, has lead to a redescription of the genus, and one step further to a better understanding of the phylogeny of Gonorynchidae as a whole.

22360: Populations of boreal toads (Bufo boreas) and northern leopard frogs (Rana pipiens) have declined severely and populations have been extirpated in the southern Rocky Mountain region in the last 20 years. We conducted a health survey of endemic amphibians in and adjacent to Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP) in an effort to document current disease problems within the Park and identify disease issues outside the Park with the potential to affect populations inside the Park. Amphibians (A. tigrinum, B. boreas, B. woodhousei, Pseudacris maculata and R. sylvatica) from 8 sites within RMNP and 7 sites <150 Km of Park boundaries were collected and examined. 229 amphibian eggs, larvae and post-metamorphs were subjected to necropsy, virus, bacterial and fungus cultures, radiography and histology. Swabs from an additional 14 captured and released adult toads also were cultured. Severe infections by Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis were detected in post-metamorphic amphibians in 3 of 5 species (B. boreas, P. maculata, and R. sylvatica) from 5 of 8 sites within RMNP and in 1 of 3 species (P. maculata) from 3 sites outside the Park. Of the post-metamorphic animals (B. boreas, P. maculata, and R. sylvatica) tested, chytrid was found in 50%, 46% and 58%, respectively. Bacterial and fungal cultures were attempted on 74 and 68 amphibians, respectively. Virus cultures were completed on 176 amphibian egg masses, larvae and post-metamorphs; no evidence of Ranavirus was found in cultures or histological examinations. Chytridiomycosis was the only lethal pathogenic infectious disease detected in 3 endemic amphibian species within or adjacent to the Park. The high rates of chytrid infection in chorus and wood frogs suggest population declines either have, or will occur.

22361: The Rainbow Trout, Oncorhynchus mykiss, is known to spawn once per year as do other synchronously spawning fishes, such as mullet. In order to understand the changes taking place in the rainbow trout ovary that are associated with spawning, we histologically compared trout ovaries before and after hormone-induced spawning. In prespawn trout ovaries, there were two classes of oocytes: 1) preovulatory oocytes and 2) primary growth oocytes that had not entered into vitellogenesis. After spawning, only the primary growth oocytes remained. However, other structure was quite apparent: there was an active germinal epithelium producing single oogonia with associated prefollicle cells or cell nests of oogonia and prefollicle cells, all destined to become follicles composed of a single oocyte and surrounding layer of follicle (granulosa) cells. The germinal epithelium, like all epithelia, was subtended by a basement membrane as were the cell nests that protruded into the stroma. Quite obviously, the oocytes that would ovulate the following year were composed of the primary growth oocytes remaining in the ovary after spawning and those that would recruit from the germinal epithelium. In addition, there were huge post ovulatory follicles in the ovary after spawning. After 16 days, they had degenerated in appearance.

22362: The anuran genus Eleutherodactylus occurs in Central and South America, as well as the West Indies, and comprises more than 600 recognized species. The diversity of Eleutherodactylus makes it difficult to study the genus as a whole; as a consequence, several authors have divided the genus in phenetic species groups. This division is based in similarity and is not necessarily congruent with monophyletic groups within the genus. Nevertheless, species groups can be considered as hypotheses of natural (monophyletic) groups. Herein, I focus on the E. orcesi Group, which contains six species distributed in the paramo and montane forests (3000-4150 m) of Colombia and Ecuador. The main objectives in the present study are to: (1) describe the osteological variation within the E. orcesi Group, (2) diagnose the group based on osteological characters, and (3) search for homologies that might support the monophyly of the group. Additionally, I describe two new species that are hypothesized to belong to the E. orcesi Group. Osteological descriptions for the eight species were made from cleared-and-double-stained specimens. To minimize possible effects of heterochrony and sexual dimorphism, only adult females were examined. To determine the validity of potential synapomorphies of the E. orcesi Group, I examined cleared-and-stained specimens of 135 species of Eleutherodactylus and used published information for another 26 species. The skulls of all the species of the Eleutherodactylus orcesi Group have a large portion of the frontoparietal fontanelle exposed anteromedially. I hypothesize that the presence of an exposed frontoparietal fontanelle is homologous in the E. orcesi Group and supports the monophyly of the group. Finally, I discuss intraspecific variation in several osteological characters of the cranium and postcranium of species of the E. orcesi Group.

22363: An estimated 34,056 fish died in the Klamath River, California in September 2002. The proximate cause of death was heavy infections of two fish pathogens, Ich and columnaris. The fish kill in the lower Klamath River in 2002 was a result of a combination of factors that began with an early peak in the return of a large run of fall Chinook salmon. Low river discharges apparently did not provide suitable attraction flows for migrating adult salmon, resulting in large numbers of fish congregating in the warm waters of the lower River. The high density of fish, low discharges, warm water temperatures, and possible extended residence time of salmon created optimal conditions for parasite proliferation and precipitated an epizootic of Ich and columnaris. This was the largest known pre-spawning adult salmonid die-off recorded for the Klamath River and possibly the Pacific coast.

22364: The maintenance of the unisexual, sexually parasitic Amazon Molly (Poecilia formosa) is an evolutionary paradox. We examined the conflict in species versus mate quality recognition cues as a possible mechanism for the maintenance of Amazon mollies. Amazon mollies require sperm from closely related species (i.e. sailfin mollies, P. latipinna) to start embryogenesis but inheritance is strictly maternal. Previous work demonstrated strong evidence for reproductive character displacement with male sailfin mollies in sympatry showing a significantly greater strength of preference for sailfin molly females than those in allopatry. When choosing mates, male sailfin mollies from populations sympatric with Amazon mollies may rely on traits indicating species identity (genetic compatibility) rather than those indicating mate quality (increased fitness benefits), while males from allopatric populations may rely more on traits indicating mate quality. As male sailfins prefer larger (more fecund) conspecific females, we paired males with a larger Amazon molly (high quality) and a smaller female Sailfin Molly (low quality). We tested males from several allopatric populations and several populations sympatric with Amazon mollies. In each trial we scored the number of gonopodial thrusts that males directed to conspecific and heterospecific females. We found that males in most sympatric and allopatric populations lost their conspecific preference. In addition, there was a significant difference in preference between allopatric and sympatric populations. These results indicate a conflict between species and mate-quality cues, which may explain the persistence of Amazon mollies. Amazon mollies may also be exploiting visual cues that males use for species recognition of females. To examine this, we created models that isolate individual female traits differing between the species.
