22365: I sought to discover behavioral mechanisms that permit northern water snakes, Nerodia sipedon sipedon, to forage for fish in cold water along the shores of Beaver Island in northern Lake Michigan. Five snakes were fitted with temperature-sensitive radio transmitters and monitored daily, mostly between sunrise and sunset, during the summer of 2001 and the spring of 2002. Body temperatures (Tb) of the snakes and the environmental temperatures available to them were recorded at 15-minute intervals, with more frequent observation directed toward individuals in the lake. Snakes first entered Lake Michigan in late May, when courtship activity had apparently declined, operative temperature regularly exceeded 30ºC, mean water temperature exceeded 14.5ºC, and fishes apparently began to arrive at the study site. The snakes remained diurnal throughout the activity season and foraged mostly between 1000 h and 2000 h, with more snakes observed in the lake at 1500 h than during any other hour. The numbers of snakes observed in the lake daily (spring only) and hourly (both spring and summer) were significantly correlated with environmental temperatures. The duration of foraging excursions was significantly correlated with the amount of time since the most recent excursion but not with Tb. Snakes appeared to prolong foraging in cold water by making occasional visits to the shoreline, where they elevated Tb in warmer water. These visits occurred when Tb dropped to approximately 16ºC. Snakes did not significantly elevate Tb before or after entire foraging periods. The snakes at this site thus appear to have used two strategies that enabled them to forage in cold Lake Michigan: they waited until the water had reached a sufficiently warm seasonal threshold, and they shuttled between cold and warm water during foraging excursions.

22366: Morphological characters support three diverse clades of Neotropical catfishes each nowadays given family rank: Pimelodidae, Pseudopimelodidae, and Heptapteridae. There are no unambiguous morphological synapomorphies uniting these three into a higher "pimelodoid" group. However, recent molecular studies recover them as the monophyletic constituents of an exclusively "pimelodoid" clade, with heptapterids sister to pseudopimelodids plus pimelodids. Within Pimelodidae molecular and morphological data are largely congruent in resolving three major clades: a "phractocephaline" group (Steindachneridion, Phractocephalus, Leiarius and Perrunichthys), a "calophysine" clade (Calophysus and allies, Cheirocerus, Exallodontus, Duopalatinus and Pimelodus), and a clade largely corresponding to Sorubiminae. Uniquely, the molecular data place the enigmatic genus Hypophthalmus as sister to sorubimines. To provide estimates of cladogenetic dates among "phractocephalines", two methods of rate calibration were employed: vicariance (Maracaibo Basin formation, ca. 8-10 Ma) and a dated fossil (Steindachneridion, ca. 25 Ma). This approach produced conflicting results. The vicariance-based calibration underestimated the age of the lineage leading to Steindachneridion by approximately 10 Ma. The fossil-based rate suggested that cladogenesis of vicariant species pairs containing Maracaibo endemics predate its formation by several million years. Artifacts capable of producing erroneous node ages were not identified. Though less parsimonious, a reconstructed history inferring pre-Maracaibo diversification and subsequent reciprocal extirpation of trans- barrier "phractocephalines" is preferred given the corroborated late Oligocene to early Miocene age of the fossil. Does this result reveal reciprocal extirpation as an explanation of some modern distributions of Maracaibo endemics and their sister taxa? Could this indicate cryptic vicariant diversification on a little-known pre-Maracaibo landscape?

22367: The rate of oxygen consumption is commonly used to measure whole organism metabolic rates. Few studies have measured whether animals that appear relaxed and at rest are truly at rest, or whether the stress of being in a novel environment elevates metabolic rate. We investigated whether conditioning of the gecko Naultinus manukanus to experimental procedures influenced the resting metabolic rate and probability of attaining a constant rate of oxygen consumption over five consecutive trials. Resting metabolic rate was measured in 22 post-absorptive N. manukanus until a steady state was attained, or for 80 minutes if no steady state was obtained. Measurements were taken on five consecutive days at 24 C. Metabolic rate varied with mass with a metabolic scaling exponent of 0.76 and did not differ between the sexes. Metabolic rate and the probability of not reaching a steady state were significantly higher at the first trial compared with subsequent trials. Geckos were most likely to behave in particular trials as they had in the immediately previous trial. For example, geckos with a lower than average metabolic rate at one trial were more likely to have a lower than average metabolic rate at subsequent trials. 22368: The positive effect of species richness on ecosystem function has been demonstrated for plant, microbial, and aquatic invertebrate communities, making the biodiversity ecosystem function hypothesis (BEFH) somewhat of an emerging ecological paradigm. However, tests of the BEFH have not been conducted in vertebrate communities. In this study, I offer the first evidence that vertebrates also support the BEFH. I used fish as a model vertebrate taxon to test the BEFH because much is known about the effects of many fish species on ecosystem function, there is much functional and trophic diversity among fish species, and stream mesocosms make controlled diversity experiments with fish possible. To test the BEFH, I randomly composed fish communities ranging from 1 to 6 species in large, outdoor stream mesocosms. With timed behavioral observations and gut content analysis, I concluded that many of the fishes were indeed in distinct functional and trophic groups. I measured periphyton biomass and benthic primary productivity (as the measure of ecosystem function) at 2 week intervals in this 6 week experiment. Periphyton biomass and primary productivity increased with fish richness, which resembled published results from diversity experiments in plant and microbial communities. The effect of fish richness on periphyton strengthened with time with the greatest effect occurring on week 6. The observed effect of fish richness on periphyton was well above the effect predicted by the summation of each species singly contributed effect (additive model), suggesting that the observed results are likely due to complementation among co-occurring taxa.

22369: Based on an expanded dataset, we report on progress made on phylogenetic analysis of the Coral Goby genus Gobiodon. 22370: Disturbance, as a result of hurricane impact, is a regular threat to Caribbean ecosystems. 22371: A plethora of analytic techniques have been used to determine sexual dimorphism in vertebrate morphological measurement data with no emergent consensus on which technique is superior. A further confounding problem for frog data is the existence of considerable inherent measurement error. To examine dimorphism, we demonstrate that frog measurement data meet assumptions for statistical general linear models. Results from these models address the question of dimorphism in an unambiguous hypothesis-driven manner. Therefore, we advocate the use of the general linear models rather than those of exploratory multivariate techniques such as principal components, correlation, or correspondence analysis. In order to distinguish the biological from statistical significance of our hypotheses, we propose a new protocol that incorporates the following factors: measurement error and effect size. Measurement error is evaluated with a novel measurement error index. Definitions for small, medium, and large effect sizes specifically for frog measurement data are presented for the first time. Examples are presented with measurement data for species of the frog genus Leptodactylus. The new protocol is recommended not only to evaluate sexual dimorphism for frog data but for any animal measurement data for which the measurement error index and observed or a priori effect sizes can be calculated.

22373: The Superfamily Doradoidei includes many species that use both swimbladder and pectoral spine stridulation mechanisms to produce sound, such as the tropical driftwood catfish, Trachelyopterus galeatus. These sounds are used for communicating in a variety of contexts: stridulation is typically used when a fish is disturbed whereas swimbladder drumming is usually associated with intraspecific aggression and courtship. These two sonic mechanisms greatly broaden the degree of complexity of acoustic signals, allowing for a more flexible communication system. Furthermore, males and females may differ in the degree to which they use these mechanisms, and may exhibit morphological, physiological, and biochemical differences contributing to functional differences in relevant muscles. In this study, we tested the hypothesis that differences in muscle biochemistry are related to functional properties in muscle adaptations. We measured activities of two enzymes indicative of the aerobic capacity of muscle: citrate synthase (CS) and 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (HOAD); and one enzyme important in the glycolytic pathway, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Enzyme activities were assayed in five muscles that contribute to locomotion and sound production in T. galeatus: the elastic spring apparatus (ESA), pectoral fin abductor (AB) and adductor (ADD), axial (AX), and fin ray adductor (FIN). The ESA had significantly higher CS and HOAD activities, and the ADD had significantly higher LDH activity in both males and females than the other muscles. Only CS activity in the AB differed significantly between the sexes, and was higher in females. This suggests, first, that the ESA has a high aerobic capacity, and can support long periods of swimbladder drumming. 22374: The Gag (Mycteroperca microlepis), a hermaphroditic grouper, has experienced a dramatic shift in sex ratio over the past 25 years due to high fishing mortality rates. The highly female-skewed sex ratio (25 to 40 females per male) generates some concern about the overall fitness of the population. Management efforts may need to be directed towards maintenance of sex ratio as well as stock size, with evaluations of recruitment based on sex ratio or male stock size in addition to the traditional female-based stock assessment. Alternative management strategies, including marine reserves, need to be considered and compared with traditional take limits. Gag segregate by size across depth strata, with larger fish found in deeper water. They also segregate by sex, with males remaining on aggregation sites year round while females disperse; thus, a spatial reserve would not be able to protect all life cycle components. We used an age-structured, stochastic recruitment model to compare management strategies for the long-term sustainability of this species. We included a simple asymptotic function to describe possible relationships between sex ratio and fertilization rates. Our response variables included population size, sex ratio, female biomass, and gamete production. The most rapid population response and highest biomass was obtained by protecting female gag on their feeding grounds or decreasing overall fishing mortality by 50%. Protected areas on spawning grounds, which were modeled as protection for adult females for 25% of the year and males year round, showed strong population recovery and improved sex ratio. Sex ratio skew affected results for some management strategies, but the level of impact was strategy-dependent. Further study is needed on the behavior of spawning fish and the relationship between fertilization success and sex ratio, and whether fishing pressure has caused disruption of the social structure itself on spawning aggregations, thereby adversely affecting reproduction.

22375: A recent study suggested that reproductive nest association of nonindigenous Rough Shiners (Notropis baileyi) to Bluehead Chub (Nocomis leptocephalus) nests may be contributing to decreases in abundances of native nest associates in the Chattahoochee River system, Alabama/Georgia. 22376: Toe-clipping is a common marking technique for anurans. However, this can be harmful to species such as hylids because of their dependence on their toes for survival. Consequently, noninvasive techniques for uniquely identifying individuals are needed. Adult gray treefrogs (Hyla versicolor) have dark dorsal patterns that improve their camouflage abilities during periods of color change. The objective of this study was to determine if dorsal pattern could be used for individual identification in field studies. I observed the consistency of these patterns on 13 adult H. versicolor (3 females, 10 males) as they went through different color changes. I used a variety of different colored backgrounds to encourage color change. As the frogs changed color the patterns also changed color, but never altered position or shape on the back. During the dark and light extremes the pattern became harder to see as the dark borderlines became faint; however, the pattern returned to its original condition as the background was adjusted. After establishing that the patterns were individually constant through color change, I studied the pattern consistency in 21 adult H. versicolor (5 females, 16 males). I took initial pictures of the pattern and toe-clipped each specimen. Upon recapture, I compared the individual's pattern with the initial photograph. Ground colors changed but dorsal patterns stayed constant in all cases. To test if this method could be easily used as a method of identification 31 people were asked to identify 10 frogs by matching two pictures taken at different times. Twenty-eight people correctly identified all 10 frogs and the average was 97%. Thus, dorsal patterns can be used as a form of identification for Hyla versicolor in studies of small populations.

22377: Circulating androgens are implicated in the expression of many male-typical traits, including reproductive and aggressive behaviors. Both sex and species differences in aggression correlate with the presence/absence of a trait used in signaling aggression, abdominal blue patches, in several species in southwest U.S. We have previously shown that sex and species differences in blue patches arise from differences in organizational actions of androgens. Here, we examined a possible endocrine correlate of differences in aggression, brain androgen receptors. We determined the distribution of the androgen receptor (AR) in the brains of breeding-season adults, using the polyclonal AR antibody PG21. In males of a typical sexually-dimorphic species (S. undulatus, males blue and high aggression), AR-immunoreactive (AR-ir) nuclei were observed in the external nucleus of the amygdala; the arcuate, ventromedial and periventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus; and the basal forebrain. Dense concentrations of AR- ir fibers were found in the medial cortex, periventricular hypothalamus, and lateral forebrain bundle. Fiber staining was also present in the preoptic hypothalamus, habenula, and deep layers of the optic tectum. In males of a derived monomorphic species (S. virgatus, white abdominal skin and low male-male aggression), AR-ir nuclei also exhibited a similar distribution. In females of both species, AR-immunoreactive fibers were relatively sparse, but showed a similar distribution to that in males. 22378: Acipenseridae includes 25 living species in four genera (Scaphirhynchus, Pseudoscaphirhynchus, Huso, Acipenser) and is the largest extant group of non-teleostean actinopterygians. This family is interesting from anatomical, phylogenetic, and conservation standpoints (most species are threatened or endangered). There are two major goals for this presentation. First, we will present the results of our studies of the skeletal anatomy of A. brevirostrum. We assembled an extensive growth series (<15 mm to >1000 mm TL) of this species, which serves as the basis for our developmental, descriptive, and comparative anatomical studies of sturgeons. This portion of our study has yielded new anatomical interpretations of sturgeon morphology. For example, dorsal and lateral scutes develop in an anterior to posterior direction, whereas ventral scutes develop bidirectionally from a posterior position within the series. Dorsal scutes develop within an elongate dorsal fin fold, whereas lateral scutes develop as ossifications of the lateral line sensory canal; ventral scutes develop independently of other structures. Our series includes many adult specimens, allowing us to comment on late stage (post maturational) ontogeny and individual skeletal variation. For instance, we discovered an articular bone in the lower jaw of an exceptionally large individual (899 mm SL); this element had been reported as absent in sturgeons. The second major goal of our study is to explore the phylogenetic systematics of the family Acipenseridae. We will present preliminary morphological evidence supporting the non- monophyly of Acipenser as it is currently constructed. For example, we discovered shared (and putatively derived) similarities between Pseudoscaphirhynchus and A. stellatus, including: presence of large spines on the skull roofing bones; shape of the border rostral bones; size and shape of the jugal; and details of the rostral sensory canal. 22379: Food habits of the Giant Water Bug, Lethocerus deyrolli, and the two species snakes, Elaphe quadrivirgata and Rhabdophis tigrinus, were studied in rice fields of Japan. 22380: Thermoregulation was investigated in the exotic nocturnal gecko Hemidactylus turcicus. 22381: Evolutionary relationships of Nearctic hylids have remained elusive despite numerous attempts to clarify them. We define Nearctic as including Canada, the US, and the Mexican Plateau. Using sequence data from 2.4 kb of 12S and 16S mtDNA and 700 bp of the nuclear gene rhodopsin, we examined the phylogenetic relationships of these frogs. We tested the hypothesis that Nearctic Hyla, Pseudacris, and Acris form a monophyletic group using parametric bootstrapping. In fact, Nearctic Hyla are monophyletic, but representative samples from Mexico and Central America are more closely related to these Hyla than are Pseudacris and Acris, suggesting two colonization events of the northern Nearctic region. Within the Nearctic Hyla, there are three well-supported groups: (1) the versicolor clade includes avivoca, chrysoscelis, and versicolor, (2) a western eximia clade contains arenicolor, euphorbiacea, eximia, plicata, and walkeri, (3) the cinerea group contains cinerea, gratiosa, and squirella. Hyla andersonii froms a fourth lineage by itself and H. femoralis is the sister lineage to all other Nearctic Hyla. The H. arborea group, represented by H. japonica in our study, was also derived from Nearctic Hyla. This finding suggests intercontinental dispersal from the eastern Nearctic into Eurasia. The eximia group also dispersed from the Nearctic, moving from the Mexican plateau south into southern Mexico and Guatemala. Finally, we showed that Pseudacris and Acris are sister to one another and are each monophyletic.

22382: Lionfish (Scorpaenidae: Pterois volitans) are crepuscular reef predators that stalk and orient toward their prey with little apparent fin movement. They also possess bilaterally symmetrical, extrinsic gas bladder muscles that originate on the posterior neurocranium and insert on the posterior gas bladder. These muscles appear not to produce sound in contrast to most fishes with similar muscles. Bleich et al. (in prep.) hypothesized that these muscles function to induce changes in gas bladder length or position, thus changing the center of buoyancy and allowing for observed pitching behaviors. I tested this hypothesis by examining gas bladder movement within P. volitans using a high-speed digital cineradiographic system. Two lead markers were inserted in the dorsal musculature and one subcutaneously on the opercular bone to serve as reference points for digitizing. Lionfish were then induced to pitch head-up or head-down in response to food. Five pitching sequences and five swimming sequences (controls) were filmed for three fish each. From these sequences gas bladder length (cm) and the angle between the main axis of the gas bladder and the dorsal markers were calculated. Gas bladder length did not change during swimming or pitching and gas bladder angle did not change during swimming. However, as the fish pitched head-up, the gas bladder angle increased. This suggests that lionfish use their gas bladder muscles to move their center of buoyancy in relation to their center of mass by shifting the gas bladder within the body cavity. This shift would then allow for observed pitch changes and thus be a novel function for extrinsic gas bladder muscles in fishes.

22383: Our growing dependence on pesticides brings to the forefront concerns about the effects of pesticides on ecological communities. For amphibians, most pesticide research has focused on single species in isolation of their natural ecology. However, amphibians live in complex communities where pesticides can have potentially far-reaching direct and indirect effects. In this study, we examined how an anuran tadpole community responds to the factorial combination of three different pesticide treatments crossed with three different predator treatments. We used outdoor pond mesocosms containing communities composed of three anuran species, zooplankton, periphypton, and phytoplankton. To these communities, we added either no predators, red-spotted newts or predaceous beetle larvae. We also applied either no pesticides, the insecticide malathion, or the herbicide Roundup. After three weeks, we found that predators and pesticides had dramatic direct and indirect effects on anuran communities. In the absence of pesticides, both predators greatly reduced the survival and biomass of tadpoles. Adding Roundup reduced tadpole survival and biomass by 50% in the no-predator treatments. The combined impact of predators and roundup on amphibians appeared to be additive. Despite being an herbicide, Roundup did not significantly affect periphyton biomass. Thus, it appears that Roundup has a major direct effect on the tadpoles but few indirect effects on the other players. In contrast, malathion by itself had no effect on tadpoles. When combined with newts, malathion continued to have no effect. However, with beetles, tadpole survival and biomass were five times greater because malathion killed 80% of the beetles. Thus, while high concentrations of malathion can certainly kill larval amphibians, ecologically relevant concentrations can have a tremendous positive impact on larval amphibians. Our study highlights the importance of moving from single-species laboratory experiments to more complex outdoor community experiments to understand the direct and indirect impacts of pesticides on amphibians.

22384: The Pallid Sturgeon (Scaphirhynchus albus) was not described until 1905 when it was commonly caught by commercial fishers. This species began to decline in the early 1900s presumably because of overharvest and habitat degradation. The U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service listed S. albus as an endangered species in 1990. In this paper, we describe the first collections of larval S. albus from the wild using a modified slingshot balloon trawl (the Missouri trawl) designed to capture small fishes in deep, turbulent rivers. We postulate that Scaphirhynchus spp. spawned at the heads of islands upstream from where we collected larvae but we can not be certain. 22385: Accumulated evidence from parentage analyses of natural populations shows that genetic mating systems may differ substantially from observed mating systems. In our study population of collared lizards, most males that are 2 yrs and older defend territories that overlap female home ranges, whereas reproductively mature first year (yearling) males use subordinate, non-territorial tactics. Because territorial males court females more frequently and females often reject the courtship advances of yearlings, we hypothesized that territorial males should sire more hatchlings than non-territorial yearlings. To test this hypothesis, we used genotypes of four microsatellite and two mitochondrial loci to assign the parentage of 128 hatchlings in a central Oklahoma population of lizards for which we know the social tactics of individual males. Parentage analysis assigned 85% and 15% of hatchlings to territorial and nonterritorial males respectively; with territorial males obtaining significantly higher reproductive success than nonterritorial males. A potential confounding factor in behavioral estimates of mating success is overlap among male territories and female home ranges with potential for multiple paternity of clutches. We examined our study population for multiple paternity of clutches to better understand the impact on behavioral estimates of mating success. Multiple paternity was frequent in this population at 89% percent of the females. Most multiple paternity clutches were sired by two males, usually two territorial males (63%). No clutches were sired solely by yearling males. Using genetic markers to assign paternity, our results agree with earlier results using estimates of mating success based on the relative frequency of courtship by territorial and non-territorial males.

22386: Body temperature has a profound effect on ectotherm fitness. Many ecotherms use behavior to control body temperature within a narrow set-point range. Biologists have long assumed that the set-point range should be centered on the body temperature that maxizes fitness. However, because thermal fitness curves are asymmetric, a temperature above the optimum will depress fitness more than a temperature below the optimum. Thus the optimal set-point should actually be centered below the temperature at which fitness is maximal. We develop a formal model of behavioral thermoregulation and explore how asymmetry of the fitness curve influences the optimal deviation of set-point temperature. We then test the model with data on the thermal dependence of sprint speed in lizards: species with highly asymmetric performance curves have thermal preferences set well below the temperature at which speed is maximal, consistent with our model predictions.

22387: Individuals that have a low maximal performance capacity may be forced to compensate by using a greater percentage of their maximal capacity compared to those individuals that have higher maximal performance capacities. We investigated the potential for locomotor performance compensation in collared lizards (Crotaphytus collaris) by measuring maximal sprint speed in the laboratory, as well as field-realized sprint speed for the same individuals in three different contexts: foraging, escaping a predator, and responding to a rival intruder. Adult males and adult females did not differ in absolute maximal speed or in field-utilized speed, but juveniles had lower absolute maximal and field-utilized speeds than both adult sexes. Of the three contexts, females used closer to maximal speed while escaping predators than in the other contexts. Adult males, on the other hand, used closer to maximal speed while responding to an unknown intruder tethered within their territory. Sprint speeds during foraging attempts were far below maximal capacity for all lizards. Juveniles appeared to compensate for having lower absolute maximal capacity by using a greater percentage of their maximal capacity while foraging and escaping predators than adults of either sex did. 22388: Atlantic Sturgeon (Acipenser oxyrhinchus) have been harvested for food from the earliest days of European settlement of America and before. NMFS received a petition in 1997 to list this subspecies (A. o. oxyrinchus) under the ESA. 22389: Numerous techniques are available to study reptile and amphibian communities. Researchers must often choose among sampling methods to obtain the most useful data. Since 1999, several trapping techniques have been used at Weyerhaeuser’s Cool Springs Environmental Education Center. Located near New Bern, this 1700 acre site includes diverse habitats ranging from cypress-tupelo swamp to longleaf pine ridge. 22390: Bottomland floodplains are regarded as ecosystems high in species diversity and biological productivity. The management techniques and the erection of dams can negatively affect species composition and the diversity of flora and fauna by altering the habitat and natural flood pulse. Due to their physiology and abundance, reptiles and amphibians are excellent representatives of the impact of anthropogenic activities imposed of vertebrates in riparian bottomlands. The study was conducted at the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, Old Sabine Bottom Wildlife Management Area, Smith County, in northeast Texas. Amphibians and reptiles were surveyed within and surrounding ephemeral pools in three habitat treatments: undisturbed forest, deer food plots, and adjacent to active oil pumps. Cover items (wood and tin), minnow traps, and visual searches were used to collect individuals. Each animal collected was weighed, measured, and marked before release. Ambient and soil temperatures were recorded at the time of each capture. When water was present, dissolved oxygen, pH and depth of each pool were measured weekly. Habitat characteristics for each treatment were compared using Principal Components Analysis and Discriminate Function Analysis. Species richness was the highest for the for the food plots with 18 species, followed by the forest and oil plots with 16 and 12 species respectively. 22391: The bright colors and diurnal habits of day geckos (Phelsuma) set them apart from other species of geckos. Day geckos are especially abundant on the islands of the Indian Ocean, where up to four species can be found sympatrically. Little is known, however, about the structure of these day gecko communities. In communities of other diurnal lizard species, sympatric species often partition their structural habitat (i.e., perch height and diameter). Furthermore, morphological differences between and within species often reflect adaptations to these different structural habitats. I set out to test the hypothesis that day gecko communities are similarly structured. In particular, I predicted that day geckos would exhibit structural habitat partitioning among sympatric species, and would show ecomorphological correlations reflecting these differences. I conducted field studies in the Mascarene Islands, including Mauritius, Réunion, and surrounding islands, comparing morphology and structural habitat use of seven species of day geckos occurring in communities of varying composition. I found that similar to other diurnal lizard groups, sympatric species of day geckos partition the available structural habitat, with individual species shifting their perch heights and diameters in response to congeners. I also found ecomorphological variation in one species, Phelsuma ornata, which occurs on Mauritius and several surrounding smaller islands. This species shows substantial morphological variation between island localities, many of which have probably only been separated for several thousand years. I combine geographic and ecological information to investigate the causes of this morphological variation.

22392: Palatable species (mimics) may resemble toxic or venomous species (models) with which they co-occur and thus gain protection from predators. This phenomenon, termed Batesian mimicry, occurs in numerous plant and animal taxa. A critical prediction of Batesian mimicry is that its benefits should break down in areas where the model is absent, because predators that do not co- occur with the model will not be under selection to recognize it, or any other species that resemble it, as dangerous. Previous research supports this prediction. Contrary to expectation, however, the distributions of many mimics extend well beyond that of their models. For instance, the range of our study species, L. t. elapsoides, extends well outside that of coral snakes despite the apparent maladaptive nature of the mimetic phenotype in those areas that lack coral snakes. Gene flow, historical and/or contemporary, could possibly maintain this maladaptive phenotype despite selection against it. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a phylogeographic analysis of L. t. elapsoides to determine the level of contemporary gene flow and uncover the demographic history of this organism. There is significant genetic structure throughout the range of this organism. Results of a number of tests seem to indicate that historical gene flow has been the primary factor in spreading the mimetic phenotype outside the range of the model.

22394: The Diamondback Terrapin inhabits brackish waters on the Atlantic and Gulf Coast, ranging from Massachusetts to western Texas. I have used six nuclear microsatellite DNA loci and mitochondrial D-loop sequences to investigate population genetic structure among seven estuaries between South Carolina and New York. Although number of alleles and heterozygosities were high, I found little population genetic structure. Genetic differentiation increased only slightly with geographic distance indicating much higher rates of gene flow than mark-recapture studies would predict. In addition, I have isolated a mitochondrial microsatellite locus and have used it to genotype over 150 individuals from the seven estuaries. I have found that rates of heteroplasmy and allele frequencies differ among these populations. This may indicate different population histories which were not discernable using nuclear loci. I am currently determining transfer of this mitochondrial microsatellite across generations as part of a paternity study of over 50 terrapin clutches.

22395: The Diamondback Terrapin is the only species of turtle in North America that exclusively inhabits brackish waters. Depending on the latitude of this wide-ranging species (Cape Cod, MA to southern Texas), terrapins lay between 1-3 clutches per year and between 5-17 eggs per clutch. During the mating season, March-April, terrapins aggregate in large groups. Mating attempts by males can be observed throughout the summer. These behaviors suggest that female terrapins are likely to mate with multiple mates per season. During the 2003 nesting season at Long Island, NY, tissue samples were collected from mothers and all hatchlings from 50 clutches, including 7 double clutches. I am using six polymorphic microsatellite markers to assess paternity. Preliminary results indicate that multiple paternity is rare in this species.

22396: Headwaters of Appalachian streams provide important fish habitats, but are degraded by multiple land uses, such as forestry, coal mining, and highway construction. Stream sedimentation resulting from such anthropogenic land disturbances can alter community composition, and decreases survival, population size, and reproductive success of fishes. Evaluating sediment prevention methods, and understanding the affects of land disturbances on fishes requires monitoring (often long-term) and measurement of sedimentation. Most sediment-monitoring approaches, however, are not applicable to repeat-sampling designs and long-term studies, and are costly and labor intensive. To monitor sedimentation, we designed an inexpensive sampler with a 10.16-cm PVC union and removable sediment trap that collects multiple sediment samples over long time periods. We examined the efficacy of our samplers in riffle habitat upstream and downstream of highway construction on a small first-order Appalachian stream. Sediment samples were collected at six-week intervals, dried, and separated into 5 size classes with nested sieves (US Standard Sieve No. 4, 8, 14, and 20). Six models represented alternative hypotheses concerning sedimentation at sites upstream and downstream of road construction. We used information theoretic methods to select models for statistical inference. Data for each sediment size class supported a trend model, where mean values of sediment weight decreased at the downstream site, with mean values unequal among periods at the upstream site. The sediment sampler design allowed for long-term placement of traps without continual disturbance of the streambed, and was successful at evaluating sedimentation between paired sites. Our sampler design is directly applicable to long-term evaluations of sediment prevention methods. Also, given the link between physical effects of stream sedimentation and biotic impacts, long- term data collected from our sediment samplers could be used as covariates in studies linking sediment accumulation and changes in fish communities.

22397: The main goal of this study was to comprehensively assess the importance of body size in modulating thermoregulatory strategy. Although body size was inversely related to heat exchange rate, all size classes of Varanus giganteus exhibited highly effective thermoregulatory abilities. Varanus giganteus of all sizes demonstrated high thermal effectiveness (E) and thermal accuracy in a thermally harsh environment. Behavioral plasticity enabled V. giganteus to maintain thermal efficiency through ontogenetic changes in thermal strategies. Size-related costs and benefits varied through time and season such that no single size was inherently more beneficial than another. Varanus giganteus are diurnal with daily activity pattern determined by availability of suitable microhabitats. Summer activity pattern was bimodal. During winter, 2/3 of study animals became inactive for several weeks or months, while the remainder exhibited a daily unimodal activity pattern. Active V. giganteus, regardless of season, maintained consistent high body temperatures through most of the day with little variation. Christian-Weavers plots of Te sun, Te shade (operative temperatures for full sun and shade respectively), and Tset (preferred temperature range) were valuable for predicting activity time and may be extended to inquiries of thermal ecology of extinct ectotherms. A synthesis of thermoregulatory strategy was constructed by updating existing predictions with Hertz et al. (1993) indices. Extrapolation of observations to larger ectotherms indicates that mass-induced inertial homeothermy could have facilitated the evolution of endothermy.

22398: Colubrid snake venoms contain a greater number of proteins homologous with front-fanged snake venoms than has been previously recognized. As part of our work characterizing the venom of the Brown Treesnake (Boiga irregularis), a 26 kD protein, designated irregulin, was purified from this venom and its amino acid sequence was determined using both N-terminal protein sequencing and cDNA cloning. Sequence analysis demonstrated a high degree of sequence identity with other recently identified proteins from viperid, elapid, colubrid and Heloderma venoms, as well as with the mammalian cysteine-rich secretory protein (CRISP) family. Western blot analysis indicated that homologs of these proteins are present in numerous species of all families of venomous reptiles, suggesting that they are ancient and basal venom components. Venom proteins from this new protein family exhibit a variety of biological activities including the blockage of Ca2+ release in muscle tissue and interference with temperature regulation, but many recently identified proteins have no currently known function. This family of proteins appears to be very broadly distributed among venomous reptiles, and it likely will be very useful for exploring the evolution of these animals and their venoms. The potential biological role of irregulin in envenomation and the phylogenetic distribution of these toxins as currently known will be discussed.

22399: Snakes play an important trophic role as secondary consumers in virtually every habitat in the southwestern United States. However, there are few studies that examine the abundance of snakes or the causes of snake abundance across different habitats. The Sevilleta Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) site is an excellent place for examining factors that affect snake abundance, especially those that deal with biotic transitions. The Sevilleta has different habitats in close proximity, many collaborative studies, up to 28 species of snake, and minimally traveled roads that cross different habitats and thus allow comparisons in a biotic transition zone. The Sevilleta LTER is located on a National Wildlife Refuge in central New Mexico among the Chihuahuan Desert, Great Plains Grassland, Colorado Plateau Shrub-Steppe, and Conifer Woodland. Driving roads at night is an effective and efficient means of assessing the presence of snakes in an area. This approach allows a researcher to survey a large area of suitable habitat quickly, and has been used to answer several ecological questions including differences in abundance of snakes between years and between habitats. We used this technique of searching from a vehicle at night to examine snake abundance at the Sevilleta. We drove a transect through Chihuahuan Desert Shrubland (CDS) and Rocky Mountain Conifer Savanna (RMCS) habitats in the northwestern region of the Sevilleta. We found snakes to be significantly more abundant in the CDS habitat. Furthermore, we discuss why snakes might be more abundant in one habitat versus another.

22400: Red-footed tortoises (Geochelone carbonaria) are threatened throughout their range. In the Bolivian Chaco, red-footed tortoises are important to the Izoceo and Aroyeo indigenous groups, who seek to protect these tortoises. We will apply landscape ecology approaches to assess habitat use by tortoises, and determine differences in habitat use between sexes, size classes, and seasons; identify food plants, study seed dispersal, and determine how tortoises interact with the landscape to access resources. The proposed research will help managers understand specific habitat needs of tortoises, such as proximity to refugia, accessibility to potential mates, availability of nesting sites, patchiness of critical food resources, seed dispersal, and the potential affects of habitat structure on interspecific interactions such as predation. Only with this kind of information can we understand the mechanisms allowing tortoises to persist in the environment, and how habitat quality influences tortoise population size. Understanding habitat use and movements by tortoises in an undisturbed setting such as Kaa-Iya National Park will be applicable to efforts to restore tortoise populations in disturbed areas. Capacity building of local parabiologists and community-based conservation approaches are important conservation aspects central to our research plan.

22401: Phrynosoma, horned lizards, are unique lizards easily recognized by their wide, flat body shape and expanded skulls adorned with parietal and squamosal horns. This genus represents an ideal group for studying character evolution because substantial diversity in morphology and ecology is present, yet it remains a tractable group with 13 extant species. Using morphological and molecular data, Hodges and Zamudio presented two most parsimonious phylogenies, which I use in studies of character evolution. I will first present analyses of reproductive mode and life history traits. Viviparity, altitude, and latitude exhibit strong phylogenetic signal within Phrynosoma. Viviparous species occur at higher minimum and midpoint altitude, which partially supports the cold-climate hypothesis for the evolution of live bearing in squamates. Then, I will show how to use phylogeny and mathematical techniques to reconstruct ancestral traits using the evolution of horns in Phrynosoma as an example. I apply these methods to 3-D reconstructions of morphological data generated from a high-resolution x-ray, computed tomography scanner. Changes occurring along a phylogeny will be shown via metamorphosis (morphing). Morphing is a dynamic process that allows us to visualize transformational changes from one form to another in real time. All CT data from this project are available through the NSF-supported, public digital library, www.digimorph.org

22402: Acanthuroids and tetraodontiforms were long hypothesized to share a sister group relationship. This changed, however, when Rosen proposed that tetraodontiforms are more closely related to caproids and zeiforms. As a result, subsequent analyses of acanthuroid relationships were conducted without the inclusion of tetraodontiform representatives. Recent data from the RAG1 gene suggest that tetraodontiforms may indeed share a close relationship with the acanthuroid fishes after all, prompting a re-examination of acanthuroid relationships that includes tetraodontiform fishes. Portions of the nuclear genes RAG1 and Tmo-4c4 were sequenced and analyzed using parsimony for members of both Acanthuroidei and Tetraodontiformes as well as several outgroup representatives. Results of this new analysis will be discussed.

22403: The roles of embryonic diapause and embryonic aestivation as potential mechanisms for synchronization of embryonic development and hatchling emergence with unpredictable optimal environmental conditions were investigated. Semi-natural incubation experiments were conducted in the Los Tuxtlas region of southern Veracruz, Mexico to document variation in ontogenies during fluctuating environments and to identify optimal developmental conditions for Kinosternon leucostomum, the White-lipped Mud Turtle. One hundred and forty-three eggs were collected from 12 October 2002 to 24 April 2003. On 7 Feb 2003 soil moisture decreased and soil temperature increased after a southern high-pressure system brought high dry winds marking the end of the rainy season. Thirty days after this event 40 of 42 embryos, oviposited from 16 Dec. 2002 to 5 Feb. 2003, synchronously broke embryonic diapause and began rapid development. Embryos oviposited from 3 to 16 Mar 2003 differed from early embryos by halting embryonic diapause asynchronously, ranging from 4 Mar to 29 Apr 2003. There was a significant negative relationship between length of embryonic diapause and the date of oviposition (r2= 0.438, F1, 76 = 57.92, P<0.000), yet there was not a significant relationship between number of days in morphogenesis and date of oviposition (r2= 0.0432, F1, 76 = 3.38, P<0.0697). Seasonal differences in embryonic survivorship along with seasonal differences in hatchling sizes will be discussed. Furthermore, I will elaborate on the hypothesis that the ability to manipulate the timing of morphogenesis may enable small-bodied Neotropical endemic turtles, which lay few relatively large eggs, to increase their clutch frequency by having an extended egg-laying season starting in the beginning of the cold rainy season and ending 6-8 months later.

22404: Large springs in northern Mexico and Southwestern United States have endemic spring fishes that have congenors as stream fishes. In Texas, Gambusia nobilis, G. heterochir, G. gagei, and G. geiseri are spring fishes, and G. affinis, G. speciosa, and G. clarkhubbsi are stream species. A series of minnow traps and/or seines were set at the spring head and downstream at 11 spring systems. At each spring system the spring species dominate at the spring head and the stream species dominate downstream. A series of 7 environmental parameters were measured at the same time interval at each trap station. Temperature variation (stenothermal vs. eurythermal) correlates well with relative fish abundance at each spring system, as does pH and ammonia in part. The other parameters do not. Long before the cessation (2 spring systems) of spring flow, spring endemics decline in abundance or are extirpated when flows are reduced. Similar data have been obtained on spring vs. stream cyprinids and percids.

22405: Hellbenders often exhibit injuries (missing toes, limbs, flesh wounds) on their bodies. Several explanations for these injuries have been suggested, including canoe traffic along streams and rivers. Studies of Japanese giant salamanders, Andrias japonicus, close relatives of hellbenders, have shown that these salamanders exhibit socially intricate and violent interactions during the breeding season, resulting in badly injured individuals, and sometimes death. Similar intraspecific aggression may occur in hellbenders. I studied a population of hellbenders in West Virginia during 1998-2000 and North Carolina during 2003-2004 using mark-recapture techniques. In both populations, larger individuals tended to exhibit more injuries than smaller ones, but data collected thus far suggest differences between populations in injury frequency among different size classes and genders. The discovery of an apparent nest site surrounded by multiple males and a single female in North Carolina will also be discussed.

22406: Movement is a large missing piece in the area of reef fish population dynamics, and this lack of knowledge is becoming difficult to ignore. As the complex interactions of processes that shape fish communities became apparent, a more comprehensive approach to understand these mechanisms replaced former single-factor debates. However, movement has been largely neglected in past discussions, and has fallen behind in terms of understanding. One way to bridge the knowledge gap is to start with an empirical approach using model organisms at a manageable scale. I plan a two-year study using artificial reefs to examine fish immigration to destination reefs after experimentally decreasing available shelter on the reef of origin. I hypothesize that coral dwelling fish will migrate to low-density destination reefs when fish to shelter ratios on the reef of origin are high. Additionally, the following variables are hypothesized to have an affect on this migration success: distance to destination reef, fish size, predator presence, and the movement capabilities of each species. In order to unequivocally show movement, common coral reef fish in the Caribbean that have settled on artificial origin reefs will be tagged. A second set of destination reefs will be deployed, the sheltering holes on the reef of origin will be plugged, and the movement of the tagged fish will be observed. Basic ecological understanding is the foundation for a large range of studies including the advancement of movement models, and substantiating the spillover of adult fishes from no-take areas to fishing grounds. Furthermore, the experimental design of reducing sheltering holes parallels natural and anthropogenic changes that are affecting the coral reef ecosystem, and can provide insight into the effects of habitat alteration on coral reef fishes.

22407: The Species at Risk Program is a new partnership that potentially can provide substantial funding for amphibian and reptile conservation. Its aim is to develop conservation plans and actions that will protect rare species occurring predominantly on U.S. military lands before they become threatened or endangered. The project is sponsored by the U.S. Department of Defense (which is funding it through its Legacy Program), U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and NatureServe, a non- governmental organization that serves as an umbrella to state natural heritage programs. In late 2003, these groups selected four species (one for each military branch) to demonstrate the project, with the hope that the resulting prototype plans will provide stimulus for future funding for many additional species. The four species include two plants and two animals that are endemic to the states of California, Colorado, Florida, and North Carolina. Fortunately, these include one of our herpetological friends -- the Florida Bog Frog, Rana okaloosae. In this presentation, I will (1) familiarize the herpetological community with the Species at Risk Program, and (2) address the bog frog, its biology, threats to its habitat, and proposed conservation measures.

22408: Some red-backed salamanders Plethodon cinereus appear to form long-term socially monogamous pair bonds. We examined how these social relationships develop from the first meeting of male-female individuals until two weeks after living together in a territory. Both male and female territorial residents are aggressive towards unfamiliar heterosexual individuals when they first meet them, but this aggression decreases during the time of cohabitation. When the "partner" is removed and a new heterosexual individual enters the territory, both male and female residents again escalate aggressive displays. Our results suggest that increasing familiarity between a male and a female leads to decreased aggression and, thus, may provide the basis for future socially monogamous relationships.

22409: Brittanichthys species are incertae sedis in the family Characidae, but exhibit some similarities to fishes of the characid subfamily Glandulocaudinae. They are excluded from Clade A characids, a group including the glandulocaudines, by lack of derived gross morphological features defining that group. However, Brittanichthys axelrodi has three glandulocaudine synapormorphies: the presence of insemination, presence of a testis that is comprised of an anterior spermatogenic region and a posterior sperm storage area, and presence of elongate sperm nuclei. Light microscopy reveals that the testes of male B. axelrodi are uniquely tripartite, divided into an anterior spermatogenic region, a middle storage area, and a posterior region made up of a coiled tube lined with a simple cuboidal epithelium. Female Brittanichthys are inseminated, although the method of sperm transfer by the male is unknown since no distinct intromittent structure is evident. Transmission electron microscopy shows the heads of sperm cells to be spatula-shaped. The elongate nuclei (approximately 6 µm in length) are flattened in transverse section. Mitochondria flank the nucleus posteriorly and continue beyond the nucleus. The flagellum is located within a cytoplasmic collar attached along the nuclear and mitochondrial portions of the cell before exiting from the collar. The A-tubules of the peripheral microtubule doublets are electron-dense along the entire length of the flagellum. Both with light and electron microscopy, pairs of spermatozoa appeared to be attached to one another at their anterior tips. Perhaps the most obvious feature of male B. axelrodi is the uppermost inferior caudal-fin ray, which is thickened, projects to one side only, and is curved sigmoidally. The problem of the cladistic relationships of Brittanichthys remains to be clarified.

22410: Arid and semi-arid ecosystems in Australia support lizard communities of exceptional species richness (20-50 sympatric species). The pioneering studies of Pianka as well as more recent studies by other workers have largely focused on understanding the ecological structure of these communities. Historical perspectives of this phenomenon have on the other hand lagged behind owing to a lack of phylogenetic information. All five lizard families presently found in Australia underwent dramatic radiations suggesting that environmental factors were powerful enough to drive the diversification of unrelated lineages. Key questions pertaining to the evolution of this diversity are therefore: When did these radiations occur? What was the tempo of speciation? And what caused these radiations? I addressed these questions using the lizard family Pygopodidae as a model clade. Pygopodids are a group of at least 38 extant species endemic to Australia and New Guinea. Results of this study indicate that: (1) the majority of speciation events giving rise to contemporary species took place in the last 23 million years (my); (2) speciation rates peaked early in the group's history before leveling out over the past 10 my; (3) speciation was primarily the result of climate-induced vicariance due to increasing aridification of the Australian continent; and (4) several species are sympatric with their sister species. The relevance of these findings to previous studies of Australian vertebrate diversity will be discussed.

22411: From videotapes of 11 male Anolis carolinensis during the breeding and post-breeding seasons, we analyzed 3,065 displays from the non-directed, advertisement context as males maintained a perch (monitoring activity) and as they moved between perches (traveling activity). Breeding males, as well as after the breeding season, used three different display types (labeled A, B, and C) and varied the pattern of signaling by kind of activity as follows: i) ratio of display types (C:A + B = 4:1 for monitor; 1:1 for travel); ii) duty cycle (n = 750 displays, mean = 46/h for monitor; n = 1558 displays, mean = 209/h for travel); iii) ratio of display volleys (a burst of closely sequenced displays) to single displays (volleys:singles = 1.7:1 for monitor; 0.5:1 for travel); and iv) volley length (displays/volley = 3.3 for monitor; 2.5 for travel). The use of three display types and the different pattern of signaling between monitor versus travel activities mirror the same signaling features that characterize interacting males when at long versus short inter-male separation distances. This suggests that advertising males may be anticipating a greater risk of inter-male contact when traveling between perches than when monitoring from a secured perch. Furthermore, the pattern of non-directed displaying carries few features seen during courtship. Therefore, we conclude that in the female-defense polygyny practiced by male A. carolinensis, advertisement signaling by territorial males appears to be directed primarily toward a potential male audience.

22412: Widespread fragmentation of terrestrial habitat has increased the need to understand core habitat requirements of organisms that undergo seasonal migrations such as pond breeding amphibians. Current research indicates that most pond-breeding amphibians spend much of their lives in terrestrial habitat at some distance from breeding sites. However, past studies have focused primarily on activities during the breeding season to define amphibian habitat requirements. These studies do not include movements and activities that occur away from aquatic breeding habitat that may be important aspects of a species' life history. We monitored movement of treefrogs through terrestrial habitat adjacent to breeding ponds using mark-recapture techniques in artificial arboreal refugia. Additionally, a subset of individuals captured in PVC pipe refugia were implanted with radiotransmitters and followed to overwintering sites. We found that movement and the use of arboreal rufugia varies temporally, as well as in response to environmental conditions such as temperature, humidity, and rainfall. Furthermore, average migration distances differed between males, females, and juveniles. Most radiotracked individuals were ultimately located in overwintering sites at or below ground level following periods of nearby arboreal retreat use. Our results indicate that treefrogs may travel distances greater than 200 m away from breeding sites between breeding seasons to reach overwintering sites. Appropriate arboreal foraging and terrestrial overwintering microhabitat are important variables to consider when defining non-breeding season habitat use of gray treefrogs. We suggest that accurate estimates of core habitat requirements for amphibians include non-breeding season movement distances and location of overwintering sites in addition to an understanding of habitat utilized by amphibians during the breeding season to fully protect amphibian populations.

22413: Many animals defend territories to increase their chances of obtaining resources. Despite much work on interspecific variation in territoriality, virtually nothing is known about the role of habitat structure in this behavior. Nevertheless, habitat structure, or the three- dimensional configuration of the preferred microhabitat of a species, may strongly influence the costs and benefits of defending territories. We predict that the costs for males to defend a territory with low visibility are high (or the benefits are low), as they may not be able to effectively survey the territory for intruders and defend against them. In contrast, the costs of defending a high visibility territory should be relatively low (or the benefits high). Therefore, species in open habitats should be the most territorial, i.e. perform the greatest frequency of aggressive behaviors, and species in cluttered habitats should be less territorial. We performed preliminary analyses among species occurring in different habitats to elucidate the effects of habitat structure on territoriality. To this end, we conducted field observations and microhabitat measurements of Anolis cristatellus, A. gundlachi, and A. krugi in Puerto Rico. Anolis cristatellus and A. gundlachi are adapted to living a few meters from the ground on the trunks of trees, a relatively open habitat; while A. krugi is a species that lives in the cluttered habitat of bushes and tall grass. Results suggest that species adapted to high visibility habitats (A. cristatellus and A. gundlachi) perform aggressive behaviors more frequently than those adapted to low visibility habitats (A. krugi), and that territorial behaviors in one species (A. cristatellus) may not change significantly when introduced to a novel habitat type.

22414: As part of the Department of Interior’s congressionally mandated Amphibian Research and Monitoring Initiative (ARMI), we began a study at St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge, FL, to compare current amphibian species richness and count data with a similar study conducted by the US Fish and Wildlife Service 25 years earlier. We used the same array design and sampled the same locations as the USFWS study. We opened traps for 6 consecutive days a month from Oct 2002 to Sep 2003. During 12 months of sampling, we captured 1403 amphibians representing 20 species (15 anurans and 5 caudates). Eastern spadefoots (Scaphiopus holbrookii), eastern narrow- mouthed toads (Gastrophryne carolinensis), southern toads (Bufo terrestris), and southern leopard frogs (Rana sphenocephala) comprised 90% of all captures. However, using different methods (e.g., automated acoustic sampling, aquatic trapping, dip netting) we detected eight of these species on the refuge. Additionally, we captured bronze frogs (Rana clamitans) and the nonindigenous Greenhouse Frog (Eleutherodactylus planirostris), which were not captured in the 1970’s. striped newts (Notophthalmus perstriatus) were considered “locally abundant” by the USFWS biologists, but this species was conspicuously absent during our study. 22415: Shell degradation in Gopher Tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) is physically similar to shell dyskeratosis in desert tortoises (Gopherus agassizii), a disease that causes erosion of shell scutes and may increase adult mortality. We hypothesize that keratin-degrading bacteria found in soils contribute to shell degradation in gopher tortoises. To test this, we first examined the association between the abundance of bacteria on gopher tortoise shells and shell degradation. Bacteria were sampled from 8 gopher tortoises without symptoms of shell degradation and 7 tortoises with such symptoms. Bacterial colonies grown on a generalized medium were 46 times more abundant on symptomatic than asymptomatic tortoises. Bacteria grown on a medium of beta keratin were approximately 36 times more abundant on tortoises displaying symptoms of degradation than on tortoises not displaying such symptoms, an observation consistent with the hypothesis that such bacteria contribute to shell degradation. We next examined the association between shell degradation and soil texture at four sites distributed across the northern geographic portion of the range of the gopher tortoise. Percentages of sand, silt, and clay were determined for random locations and burrow aprons for each site. Photographs of the carapace and plastron of captured tortoises were used to determine the percentage of shell degradation, a figure that was adjusted for differences in body size among individuals. Using these adjusted values, we found a negative correlation between mean sand content of soil and shell degradation. From this we suggest that keratinolytic bacteria colonize tortoise shells indiscriminately from the outside environment. Because of this, increased amounts of degradation on tortoises in western portions of the range could be an indicator of habitat quality and may increase adult mortality.

22416: Few fish habitat compensation projects are rigorously assessed against a reference. We examined the efficacy of four types of added habitat structures and the overall effectiveness of an artificial stream in the Northwest Territories, Canada. We quantified changes in fish abundance and growth at each structure, and for the enhanced stream as a whole, using a before-after-control- impact approach; we also used nearby natural streams as references against which production of Arctic Grayling (Thymallus arcticus) in the artificial stream could be quantified. The artificial stream restored watershed connectivity, allowing fish migration, and provided spawning and nursery habitat. Structures attracted significantly higher densities of young-of-the-year (YOY) grayling than nearby unenhanced sections, yet growth of grayling was not reduced at structures, suggesting that they provided energetically favorable microhabitats. Relative to reference streams and pre-structure conditions, however, the addition of structures did not increase overall density, biomass, or growth rates of YOY grayling in the artificial stream. Indeed, mass of individual YOY grayling in the artificial stream was only 57% of that in natural streams at the end of summer growing season. These differences in growth, together with estimates of grayling density, meant that net production in the artificial stream averaged 37% of that seen natural streams. Weather conditions and a lake-outlet effect strongly affected the production of grayling in the region, but bioenergetics modeling indicated that slightly cooler water temperatures in the artificial stream had limited influence on growth. Instead, low amounts of autochthonous and allochthonous organic matter and generally poor physical habitat appeared to limit the productivity of benthic invertebrates and therefore of fish in the artificial stream. We suggest that habitat compensation programs not be limited to physical aspects, but also consider the organic matter that is available to the benthic fauna and fish.

22417: Eastern box turtles are omnivorous terrestrial reptiles found throughout much of the Eastern United States. Turtles are known, through anecdotal data, to eat many types of wild fleshy fruits. However, the extent in which they are dispersing seeds is relatively unknown. Our objectives were 1) to determine the ecological function of box turtles as seed dispersers by capturing wild turtles and collecting fecal samples to quantify the number of seeds passing through the digestive tract of the turtles, and 2) to determine temporal relationships of seed dispersal events. We collected a total of 38 fecal samples between April and September 2003. Of the 38 samples collected 37% contained seeds. The numbers of seeds found in the samples varied from 2 to 1024 seeds, and were from at least 4 different plant species. During specific periods of time turtles are actively dispersing seeds that are available to them. We conclude that turtles function as seed dispersers and temporal shifts are present in dispersal events in South Central Illinois.

22418: Most studies of stream salamanders have relied on population indices based on counts rather than estimates based on techniques such as capture-recapture and removal. Measurement of detection probabilities (p, the proportion of total animals present that are detected during a survey) and their associated sampling error are essential for assessing unbiased estimates of population sizes and trends. In this paper, we compare capture-recapture (using visible implant elastomer over 6 weekly capture sessions) and removal (three removal passes on each of 2 days) methods for estimating populations of adult northern dusky (Desmognathus fuscus) and seal (D. monticola) salamanders along 50 x 1 m transects at four streams in Shenandoah National Park in Virginia, U.S.A. We analyzed capture-recapture data using program CAPTURE (model Mo which assumes a constant capture probability) and a Bayesian estimate of population size (more valid for small sample sizes), and analyzed removal data using program CAPTURE (model Mb which assumes a behavioral response to capture). Detection probabilities from removal data were higher for both species than those from capture-recapture, though errors were higher. Detection probabilities based on the removal data did not differ between the two species, but differed among streams for D. fuscus. From 2001-2003, we conducted two to three removal passes consecutively during the day along transects at eight streams in Shenandoah National Park. Transects were 15 m long x 2 m wide, spanning 1 m along the stream bank and 1 m in the stream channel. Population estimates often could not be calculated for salamander species because of low sample sizes. Even for abundant species like the northern two-lined salamander (Eurycea bislineata), detection probabilities sometimes could not be calculated because salamander counts in subsequent passes were higher or equal to those in earlier passes. Detection probabilities were fairly high for E. bislineata (0.54 ± 0.216, n = 6) and did not differ between adults and larvae or among streams. Based on these results, we recommend the removal method over capture-recapture estimation, and that at least three passes be used with removal sampling.

22419: The Wandering Salamander, Aneides vagrans, is a species of lungless salamander found in northwestern California and on Vancouver Island, British Columbia. It is believed that Aneides vagrans was introduced to Vancouver Island from Humboldt County, California as a result of the leather tanning industry during the nineteenth century. I investigated the phylogeography of the species throughout its range. In addition to reconstructing historical relationships between populations, I used this data set to evaluate the accuracy of nested clade analysis using Monte Carlo simulations of DNA sequences. The confidence of the phylogeographic conclusions were assessed using simulated haplotypes based on the branch lengths and parameters of the maximum likelihood tree. Based on a combination of nested clade analysis and phylogenetic analyses, I conclude that the phylogeographic pattern in California is consistent with past fragmentation, with mitochondrial haplotypes restricted to relatively small geographic areas. On Vancouver Island, there is no geographic pattern and the haplotype diversity is consistent with a single source population, or populations in close proximity in Humboldt County California. However, no exact matches of haploytpes were found between California and Vancouver Island, which may be due to extinction or incomplete sampling. The simulations confirmed the efficacy of nested clade analysis in some cases, but suggest that caution should be used in some cases for inference of historical events.

22420: Amphibian populations have been in decline worldwide, therefore it is necessary to collect ecological and life history data upon which sound conservation and management strategies can be based. From April 2002 until December 2003 we monitored salamander growth, clutch size, and seasonal abundance in two adjacent ravines. We conducted Visual Encounter Surveys in both the creeks and the forest ridge between them. Oviposition commenced in April, and hatchlings could be found by late May. Clutch sizes ranged from 1 egg to 105 eggs. Seasonal abundance varied among age cohorts, with adults being most common from April through June and larvae being more abundant in late summer and fall.

22421: The Blanding’s Turtle, Emydoidea blandingii, is a semi-aquatic turtle that inhabits shallow, freshwater habitats principally within the Great Lakes region, with scattered peripheral populations in the northeastern United States and Canada. Populations are declining throughout much of the range and the species is listed as threatened in New York. We evaluated the potential threat to habitat caused by disruption of the natural hydroperiod of the St. Lawrence River by the Moses Saunders Dam. We characterized turtle populations and vegetation associations in twelve freshwater marshes stemming from the upper St. Lawrence River and Lake Ontario. Habitat suitability models were developed and contrasted among different water regulation scenarios. The variables water depth and the presence of open water were significant in predicting Blanding’s turtle presence. Both of these factors are direct impacts of water regulation. More detailed information on habitat selection was gathered by using radio-telemetry to track eighteen Blanding’s turtles in four of these wetlands for 1.5 years. Together, these results will allow us to better understand the potential effects of water regulation on the Blanding’s Turtle in Northern New York State and can be used to make specific recommendations regarding conservation.

22422: The woman who discovered the first living Coelacanth, Dr. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, has been recognized many times over for her remarkable discovery, including having the fish named after her. Little, however, is known about the rest of her life and her many accomplishments aside from the coelacanth discovery. A self-taught naturalist, Dr. Courtenay-Latimer nearly single- handedly built the early collections of the East London Museum in South Africa, after being hired as a curator of a museum that, at the time, had essentially no collections. Her lengthy career, first as a curator and later as the director of the museum, included specimen collecting, exhibit production and administration, among other things. Locally recognized for her knowledge of birds, she established nature reserves to encourage the protection of native wildlife and to ensure future enjoyment of the natural surroundings by the public. She was also artistically creative, having painted scientifically detailed watercolors of native fungi starting at a young age and, later in life, creating sculptures, one example of which, albeit an unfinished one, bears a striking likeness to her long-time friend and colleague, Dr. J. L. B. Smith. At age 96 Dr. Courtenay- Latimer lives alone, is mentally sharp, witty, and has a sparkle in her eye, and remains close to family members (all younger than she). The author had the pleasure of meeting and interviewing her during a visit to South Africa and will share some of her experiences.

22423: For many organisms, varying selective pressures exist throughout ontogeny. This is often observed as different mortality rates along some gradient of age or size. Different mortality rates may be observed because of different predator-prey relationships or, when predator-prey relationships are similar, because changes in morphology and/or performance through ontogeny mediate differences in predator vulnerability. Additionally, in ectotherms, ontogenetic variation in morphology and performance should be ecologically significant because parental care is essentially absent. Thus, juvenile lizards may be expected to respond similar to adults to their environment. We chose to test the hypothesis that juvenile lizards scale proportionately in morphology and performance to adults by following individuals through ontogeny to sexual maturity. We used lab reared Sceloporus undulatus and Sceloporus woodi from field captured gravid females in an attempt to control for both environmental and genetic factors affecting juvenile morphology and performance. Additionally, lab reared juveniles would presumably reflect a wider range of phenotypes as no post-natal selection has occurred. The results of this study will be discussed in terms of intraspecific variation in morphology and performance and a comparison of two closely related species with different habitat requirements.

22424: The extent of evolutionary divergence of phenotypes between habitats is due to the balance of differential natural selection and gene flow. Lava lizards (Microlophus albemarlensis) on the small island of Plaza Sur in the Galápagos archipelago inhabit contrasting habitats: dense vegetation on the western end of the island thins rapidly in a transitional area, before becoming absent on the eastern half. Associated with these habitats are phenotypic differences in traits linked to predator avoidance (increased wariness, sprint speed and endurance in lizards from the sparsely vegetated habitat). This population provides an opportunity to test the hypothesis that gene flow constrains phenotypic differentiation. In agreement with previous studies, we found phenotypic differences among lizards from the different habitats. However, there was no evidence of any differences among habitats in allele frequencies at six out of seven microsatellite loci examined, nor was there any indication of congruence between patterns of genetic variability and the change in vegetation regime. We infer that gene flow between the habitats on Plaza Sur must be sufficiently high to overcome genetic drift within habitats but that it does not preclude phenotypic differentiation. Our results contribute to the growing body of evidence that ecological mechanisms, with or without concurrent neutral evolution, are a potent source of phenotypic diversification within and among species.
