22426: Beyond the somewhat casual characterization of salamanders as generalist carnivores, the food habits of many salamander species are not very well known. Such is the case for the Black Mountain dusky salamander, Desmognathus welteri, which occupies stream-side, semi-aquatic habitats in the Cumberland Mountains and Cumberland Plateau. For this study, samples of D. welteri from southeastern Kentucky, preserved for other studies, were used to examine its diet. We dissected specimens, emptied the stomachs, and identified stomach contents to the most specific taxon allowed by the state of digestion. Most insects were identifiable to order, in spite of a level of digestion which made consistent size measurement impossible. Thus, in this study, we concentrate on dietary diversity and ignore any prey size relationships. A food item occurrence was defined as the appearance of one taxon in one stomach. Salamanders with a SVL of 55 mm or larger were considered adults; smaller individuals were considered immature, although some may have shown some signs of maturing. We examined stomach contents of 36 male, 27 female and 39 immature salamanders. Only 7 (6%) of 113 individuals had nothing in their stomachs. Almost all food items, 140 (87.5%) of 160, were insects; only 1 of 160 was not an arthropod (it was a small dusky salamander). Overall, Coleoptera comprised slightly more occurrences than Hymenoptera; together they comprised 55% of the food item occurrences. Adding the occurrences of Diptera to those of these two insect orders accounted for 65% of occurrences. The rank of these three orders was the same for males, females and immatures.

22427: The Northern Dusky Salamander (Desmognathus fuscus) is a common streamside inhabitant in the forests of the northeastern United States. In Ohio, females typically deposit their egg clutches under rocks or debris in July and guard them until September when they hatch and the gilled larvae move into the stream. Oviposition frequency for dusky salamanders, including D. fuscus, has generally been described as either an annual or a biennial cycle. It is possible that some populations exhibit each of these patterns; another possibility is that different females in the same population exhibit each of these patterns. We evaluated changes in the size of ova of female D. fuscus from a Hocking County, Ohio population captured either in the early autumn, after the nesting season, or in late spring, just before a season. Females were "marked" photographically using unique color patterns for identification of individuals upon recapture. Since ova with deposited yolk are detectable through the abdominal wall, we were able to measure the size of the eggs. Egg sizes were recorded for all females collected at these times. Median egg size peaks in June just prior to oviposition, and is at a minimum in October, just after brooding is complete. From one autumn-spring-autumn cycle, median egg size was 1.0, 2.2 and 1.2mm, respectively (n=57, 56 and 45 females). Analysis of three years of recapture data support the hypothesis of annual oviposition for a majority of the females. However, some females clearly are not breeding in some years, perhaps as many as 20% of mature females. Smaller females appear less likely than larger females to lay eggs in successive nesting seasons, perhaps because they deposit yolk more slowly. Other factors may affect strict annual reproduction.

22429: The fossorial habits of the enigmatic amphisbaenian reptiles make obtaining tissues for molecular phylogenetic studies difficult. We achieved sufficient taxonomic sampling for phylogenetic analysis by extracting DNA from bones of museum specimens using a modified protocol, which augmented fresh tissue samples obtained for some species. Phylogenetic analysis of two nuclear genes suggests substantial morphological convergence within the group. The limbless Rhineuridae are placed as the most basal lineage, whereas the limbed Bipedidae occupy a more derived position, suggesting that limbs were lost at least twice within the group. Convergence in skull shape and scalation is also prevalent according to this topology. The molecule-based topology exhibits areas of congruence and incongruence with a recent morphology-based analysis. The topologies are congruent in supporting the following hypotheses: i) Amphisbaenia is monophyletic; ii) Amphisbaenidae is the sister-group to Trogonophidae; and iii) Blanus is not an amphisbaenid as previously thought, but a relatively basal lineage within Amphisbaenia. The topologies are incongruent in the following ways: i) the limbless Rhineuridae is most basal in the molecular topology whereas the limbed Bipedidae is most basal in the morphological topology; and ii) "shovel-headed" and "keel-headed" amphisbaenians are monophyletic in the morphological topology, but polyphyletic in the molecular topology. This incongruence seems to be attributable to widespread homoplasy in limb and skull evolution, mosaic evolution in the skull vs. postcranial skeleton, and incomplete fossil records for some lineages.

22430: Grotto Sculpin are troglomorphic populations of the Banded Sculpin (Cottus carolinae) endemic to caves within Perry County, Missouri. A high degree of genetic heterogeneity (FST=0.668, P<0.001) was detected among seven sample sites within Perry County. 22431: Over 98% of the scaleless black stomiid species (270 in 25 genera) have mental barbels, ranging from simple to elaborate, that figure prominently, sometimes exclusively, in species level diagnosis. 22432: We measured the intensities of amylase and trypsin gene expression in four species of carnivorous and herbivorous prickleback fishes (family Stichaeidae) and determined the effects of ontogeny, diet, and phylogeny on these intensities. Of the four species, Cebidichthys violaceus and Xiphister mucosus shift to a more herbivorous diet as they grow (>45 mm SL), whereas X. atropurpureus and Anoplarchus purpurescens remain carnivores throughout life. A. purpurescens belongs to a carnivorous clade, and the three other species belong to an adjacent, mostly herbivorous clade. Gene expression was determined using in situ hybridization with cRNA probes and the intensities of expression quantified using image analysis. Intensity was compared in three feeding categories of the four species: (1) small, wild-caught juveniles representing the carnivorous condition before two of the species shift to herbivory; (2) larger, wild-caught juveniles representing the natural diet condition of the two carnivorous species and the two that have shifted to herbivory; and (3) larger, lab-raised juveniles produced by feeding a high-protein animal diet to small juveniles until they reached the size of the larger wild-caught juveniles. Comparison of intensities in categories (1) vs. (2) allowed us to test for an ontogenetic effect, in (2) vs. (3) for a dietary effect, and within categories (1) and (2) for a phylogenetic effect. Our results showed a significant ontogenetic effect but no dietary effect for both enzymes in the four species. A significant phylogenetic effect was seen with the sister taxa being indistinguishable in gene expression for both enzymes, despite their different natural diets, but seen between clades for the amylase gene only. Overall, the expression of both the amylase and trypsin genes appears to be transcriptionally regulated, but that of trypsin more phenotypically plastic and that of amylase more phylogenetically constrained.

22433: Twenty-seven microsatellite loci were identified for the Bog Turtle (Glyptemys muhlenbergii) and surveyed in approximately 480 turtles collected throughout the range. 22434: The subfamily Colubrinae currently comprises 600 species assigned to 87 genera with a cosmopolitan distribution, and widely distributed and diverse in the Neotropics. The monophyly of this subfamily is supported by hemipenial features: the hemipenis is non-symmetric with a simple sulcus spermaticus (when bilobed, the sulcus runs along the right lobe). Their monophyly is also corroborated by molecular analyses. The phylogenetic relationships among New World colubrines and between New and Old World genera are poorly understood, and until presently there have been no attempt to produce a broad phylogenetic analysis of the group. The hemipenis has been used extensively in the classification of snakes and show a large number of characters with potential phylogenetic value. An analysis of the hemipenial morphology of 108 species of Colubrinae from both New and Old World genera allowed the diagnosis of groups which share similar uniquely derived morphologic patterns. In an attempt to understand the hemipenial patterns, a preliminary phylogenetic analysis using molecular data has been performed. The genbank sequences used were those of the mitochondrial genes cytb (n=30) and 12s (n=40), as well the nuclear gene c-mos (n=25). This analysis was performed under the Maximum Parsimony criterion with a heuristic search. The confrontation of the hemipenial patterns with the molecular topology results in the corroboration of at least one assemblage; composed of the North American genera Lampropeltis, Arizona, Elaphe, Cemophora, Rhinocheilus and the European genus Coronella. This evidence supports the hypothesis that the New World colubrines are not monophyletic, and there is a strict relationship between the New and Old World genera. 22435: In order to elucidate the potential costs of chiggers to their lizard host, natural history studies are needed. Thus, the purpose of this study was to describe the seasonal changes both in chigger infestations on eastern fence lizards and chigger abundance within fence lizard habitats in middle Tennessee. The abundance of chiggers in habitats known to harbor fence lizards was monitored on one day in the middle of each month from April through October. Five sampling sites were chosen on the basis of their proximity to known lizard sightings and used consistently throughout the study. Larval chiggers were sampled at each site by dropping Plexiglas squares painted flat black onto the substrate. After 70 seconds the number of chiggers on each square was recorded. Lizards (males, females, and juveniles) were captured by noosing once a month from May through September. I report both infestation intensity and prevalence (the proportion of lizards infested with at least 1 chigger). Chigger abundance in the habitat was low (mean = 1.8 chiggers) in the spring (April-May), 8-fold higher throughout the summer, and declined 6-fold in the fall (Sept.-Oct.). Similarly, infestation intensities and prevalence on fence lizards (males, females, and juveniles) were low in the spring, significantly higher throughout the summer, and fell in the fall. The seasonal pattern in chigger abundance is probably driven by climatic factors, such as temperature and humidity, which influence the hatching time of trombiculid eggs, larval activity and growth, and reproductive cycles. In turn, these seasonal changes in chigger abundance appear to be a major factor influencing infestation intensities on fence lizards. Other factors are probably at play such as seasonal changes in the behavior or physiology of either parasite or host.

22436: Steroid hormones play important roles in mediating reproductive and agonistic behavior in vertebrates, including teleosts. In particular, androgens such as testosterone often facilitate the expression of reproductive and aggressive behaviors and glucocorticoids such as cortisol often counteract these effects and also facilitate submissive behaviors. Some of cortisol’s effects are direct effects on the production of androgens, but other effects of glucocorticoids are directly on target tissues. One mechanism to explain cortisol’s actions on androgen production is the activity of the enzyme 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11beta-HSD). This enzyme can and does inactivate glucocorticoids in mammals and its activity has also been shown to be higher in the testes of dominant versus subordinate male rats (Monder et al. 1994. Endocrinology). 11beta- HSD is particularly interesting in teleosts because it also catalyzes the final step in the synthesis of the important teleost androgen 11-ketotestosterone. To begin investigating the role of this enzyme in sunfish reproductive behavior, we are measuring its activity in liver and gonads of male and female longear sunfish in different reproductive conditions. These two tissues were chosen because the liver is a major site of steroid hormone metabolism whereas there are a priori reasons to expect both sex differences and substrate-affinity differences in the gonads given sex differences in circulating levels of androgens and estrogens (other important metabolites of testosterone). For this study, we incubated tissue homogenates with radioactive substrate (either testosterone or cortisol) and then quantified the amounts of the different potential steroid products. Preliminary data suggest that males and females do differ in the activity of this enzyme in these tissues. 22438: Understanding variation in species responses to both local and regional ecological characteristics has the potential to provide insights into mechanisms regulating broad-scale patterns of biodiversity. 22439: Previous studies showed that territorial male and female red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) react aggressively towards intruding Eurycea cirrigera. 22440: The increasingly common problem of non-native species introductions brings with it a considerable economic and biological cost. Knowledge of the introduction history is vital to invasive species management and prevention of future introductions. Here, we use mtDNA sequence data to reconstruct the history of a worldwide invasive species, the Brown Anole (Anolis sagrei). This lizard is native to the Caribbean and introduced to the southern U.S., Hawaii, Taiwan, and several Caribbean islands. We focus on three questions related to these introductions: 1) Where do haplotypes from introduced populations originate?, 2) What is the route of colonization for introduced populations?, and 3) How does population structure differ between native and introduced ranges? First, our analysis reveals that over 99% of individuals sampled from introduced areas have mtDNA haplotypes identical or closely related to those found in Cuba. Moreover, these introduced haplotypes originate from multiple geographically and genetically distinct areas of Cuba, strongly suggesting multiple independent colonization events. Second, despite this result, most colonization events do not appear to have occurred directly from Cuba. Instead, recent introductions to Hawaii, Grand Cayman, Taiwan, and Grenada are the result of secondary introductions from Florida, the most widespread introduction. Indeed, all haplotypes from other non-native populations sampled (except Jamaica) are identical or nearly identical to haplotypes sampled in Florida. Third, populations in the native range are strongly structured geographically, whereas the majority of genetic variation occurs within, rather than among, introduced populations. This suggests a substantial restructuring of genetic variation in non-native populations. The results of this study as a whole illustrate that introductions consisting of genetic variation from multiple source populations can produce introduced populations that are in some respects more genetically diverse than native populations. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that introduced populations can become source populations for subsequent introductions, which often retain the increased genetic variation assembled during the initial introduction.

22441: Plethodontid salamanders of the genus Desmognathus show striking patterns of divergence in life history, body size, and ecology. 22442: The study of similar species in sympatry affords comparisons of their ecological adaptations that are not possible in allopatric studies. 22443: Many studies focused on determining the mechanisms responsible for amphibian declines have been conducted at small spatial scales. 22444: Heat death in streams is often one of the most important factors affecting fish populations and often a factor overlooked by those managing fish populations. 22445: The Texas Tortoise (Gopherus berlandieri) is the smallest, most sexually dimorphic, and, arguably, least well-studied of the North American Gopherus. 22446: We have conducted a fecal analysis of hatchling diamondback terrapins in two different salt marshes of the Long Island Sound, Oyster Bay Harbour and Mount Sinai Harbour. 22447: Identification and characterization of the associated migration, colonization, and extinction processes among amphibian populations inhabiting vernal pools are central to determining the basic monitoring unit for status and trends analyses that form the basis for conservation planning. 22449: The blackmouth shiner, Notropis melanostomus, was originally discovered in Pond Creek, a tributary to the Blackwater/Yellow River system, in northwest Florida. 22451: Rattlesnakes are one of the most identifiable ophidian groups found in the New World, but few published phylogenies are available for species-level relationships within this group. 22453: The Redband Darter, Etheostoma luteovinctum, is endemic to portions of the Tennessee and Cumberland River drainages within central Tennessee's Nashville Basin. 22454: The Etheostoma spectabile species group is unusually important to the understanding of North American aquatic biogeography. 22455: Intense aggressive interactions between sympatric reptile species have the potential to significantly affect patterns of habitat use by some or all of those taxa. 22456: Sex change has evolved numerous times in marine teleost fishes and is typically accompanied by modifications in gonad morphology during some point in development. 22457: Most biologists agree that the principal causes of amphibian declines are habitat loss, habitat alteration, and habitat fragmentation. 22458: Showy male displays are a familiar result of sexual selection in conventional mating systems. In these systems, males compete for females and females play the role of chooser. Corticosterone does not mediate calling activity through inhibitory effects on androgen production as predicted by recent models, nor are potential reciprocal interactions between corticosterone and androgens masked by differences in testes mass for the two behavioral phenotypes. Rather, corticosterone may inhibit the release of arginine vasotocin from vocal control centers of the brain to mediate the expression of the satellite tactic. Lastly, I show that an increase in circulating corticosterone during vocal activity is associated with a decrease in call duration and this relationship is supported by preliminary hormone manipulation data. Satellite male toads parasitize host males producing the longest calls (presumably to increase the probability of intercepting a mate) and this relationship corresponds with significantly higher circulating corticosterone levels in non-parasitized callers versus parasitized callers. Satellite-host associations are not related to differences in circulating androgens among calling individuals. These results indicate that physiological status may have as much influence, or more, than social interaction on what reproductive tactic a male anuran adopts at any given time.

22460: Night lizards of the genus Xantusia vigilis range from southern Utah to Zacatecas, Mexico. Many populations are restricted to particular species of Yucca and Agave or exfoliating granite. 22461: Activity patterns, habitat use and population characteristics of the Western Pond Turtle (Clemmys marmorata) inhabiting rice agriculture in northern California was studied from 2001 to 2003 in Butte County using trapping and radio telemetry. 22462: South American leptodactylid frogs of the genus Phrynopus occur in cloud-forest, páramo, subpáramo, and puna habitats (1000 to 4400 m elevation) from Colombia to Bolivia. 22463: Ecological theory predicts that interspecific competition is most intense among closely related species that have similar niche requirements. 22464: We conducted a demographic analysis in a population of the knob-scaled lizard Xenosaurus newmanorum in a tropical cloud forest near Xilitla, San Luis Potosi. 22466: Historically, Gulf Coast islands have provided important nesting refugia for thousands of wading birds, including pelicans, cormorants, ibis, herons and egrets. Cottonmouth snakes (Agkistrodon piscivorus conanti) inhabit these same islands where they are entirely terrestrial and scavenge on dead or rotting fish that are dropped or regurgitated by nesting birds. Unlike many other island systems in which birds and snakes associate, cottonmouths are not direct predators on the birds but depend on them for input of fish. Scavenging of fish is limited to periods of nesting activities by birds (generally April - October) and is curtailed by drought that can shorten the nesting season, reduce the number of nesting birds, and prohibit foraging by snakes. Snakes cease to forage and retreat underground when their body water deficit increases to somewhere between a few and 12% of body mass. Thus, scarcity of water, and especially prolonged drought, can seriously impact the energetics and survival of snake populations due to combined effects on prey abundance and foraging behavior. Comparative studies of several islands within Florida's Cedar Keys suggest the relationship between nesting birds and snakes is one of mutualism. The birds provide carrion as a food subsidy for the snakes, while the snakes, in turn, appear to deter the establishment of predators on avian nests. Thus, on islands having large bird rookeries and numerous cottonmouths, there are no raccoons, no arboreal snakes, and introduced rats appear to be less abundant than in areas without snakes. Eastern diamondback rattlesnakes (Crotalus adamanteus) also occur on these same islands but in far lesser abundance where cottonmouths are numerous at bird rookeries. The success of cottonmouths in association with avian rookeries possibly precludes the establishment of rattlesnake populations, whereas the latter can be dominant on other islands.

22467: The settlement of reef-associated temperate fishes was monitored during the summer and fall of 2002 and 2003 at King Harbor, Redondo Beach, California. 22468: Two persistent phylogenetic questions about Tetraodontiformes concern: 1) relationships of boxfishes (Ostraciide) and trunkfishes (Aracanidae), collectively known as the boxfish clade, to other Tetraodontiformes; and 2) sister group relationships of Tetraodontiformes. We reviewed and fine-tuned our alignments by eye using MacClade 4.03. We analyzed the morphological and molecular character matrices alone (partitioned analyses) and combined (simultaneous analysis) using PAUP* 4.0b10. Many groups have been proposed as sister to Tetraodontiformes; based on taxa we used as outgroups to examine ingroup relationships of Tetraodontiformes, we find strong support for placement of Antigonia (Caproidae) as sister to Tetraodontiformes, with Zenopsis far outside this clade. 22469: Bergmann's rule states that, among conspecific populations, individuals are larger in cooler than in warmer environments as a consequence of selection related to heat conservation. Many of the most comprehensive assessments of Bergmann's rule to date have examined clinal patterns in body size among species assemblages. Our study is a more direct test of Bergmann's rule because we examine the pattern within a single, widely distributed species. We examined geographic variation in body and cell size in the Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata). Our analysis of 818 turtles collected from the entire range (45 degrees N to 28 degrees N), indicated that body size increased with latitude; however, the relationship was driven by a population of large turtles at the northern extreme of the species' range. When the northern population was removed from the analyses, Bergmann's rule was not supported, and the smallest turtles occurred near the central part of the species' distribution. Recent literature has suggested that latitudinal clines in body size may simply be a physiological byproduct of the effects of temperature on cell division, resulting in larger cells, and hence larger organisms, from cooler temperatures. Measurements of the diameter of skin cells did not support the hypothesis that cell size increases with latitude and decreases with temperature in the spotted turtle, nor was there a significant relationship between body size and cell size. Our study suggests that neither Bergmann's rule nor cell size variation sufficiently explain the body size cline observed in the Spotted Turtle. We hypothesize that patterns in body size are related to variation in female size at maturity and reproductive cycles.

22470: Patterns in life history are typically examined by biologists in the form of univariate correlations, which inherently do not account for the suite of variables that may contribute to phenotypes. We used path analyses to examine reproductive traits and their combined effects on egg shape in 115 species of chelonians. Eggs became more spherical as body size and clutch size increased, supporting the idea of a pelvic girdle constraint on egg shape in small-bodied species. Furthermore, our examination of the role of egg shape in Optimal Egg Size (OES) Theory tradeoffs at multiple taxonomic levels indicated that an optimal egg size is maintained through variation in egg shape. Our univariate analyses of reproductive variables in chelonians indicated that although the tradeoff between clutch size and egg size predicted by OES Theory was detected, in contrast to the theory, both clutch size and egg size increased with body size.

22471: The occurrence of hybridization between pickerels (Esox americanus americanus, E. americanus vermiculatus and E. niger) in the wild, and as a result of experimental manipulation is well known. To gain additional insight into the nature and extent of hybridization in the pickerels, we have examined DNA sequences from mitochondrial and nuclear genes in individuals from populations in which hybridization is expected to occur. The two subspecies of E. americanus occur in sympatry in the southern ends of their respective ranges in Mississippi, Alabama, Florida and Georgia. In the region of geographic overlap, individuals that show unique characteristics that prevent their assignation to either subspecies with confidence have been interpreted as intergrades between the two forms. Mitochondrial and nuclear DNA sequences confirm the hybrid nature of individuals with intermediate phenotypes and equivocal subspecies designation. The molecular evidence also revealed interesting characteristics of the hybridization between E. americanus and E. niger. Although hybridization between these two species has been documented, the frequency and geographic extent of this phenomenon remains poorly understood. The DNA sequences suggests that past hybridization events have had important consequences for the genomic compostion of widespread populations of E. niger. Results of phylogenetic analysis show the mitochondrial haplotypes from several populations of E. niger to be nested within a clade of mitochondrial haplotypes from E. americanus. In contrast, the nuclear haplotypes are congruent with the reciprocal monophyly of the two species. 22472: The eels (Order Anguilliformes) account for approximately 740 species in 141 genera presently assigned to 15 families. The anguilloids are further divided into the superfamilies Anguilloidea and Muraenoidea. This arrangement is partly based on character analyses that aimed at unveiling synapomorphic traits to delineate clades, however few character state matrices or formal cladistic analysis of anguilliform characters have been presented to date. In this context, we assembled a dataset consisting of DNA sequences from mitochondrial and nuclear genes from a broad sample of anguilliform taxa to test hypotheses of anguilliform relationships. Preliminary analyses of the molecular evidence support a hypothesis that is incongruent with many aspects of the current classification scheme. The consensus of the most parsimonious trees does not support the monophyly of Anguilloidei, Congroidei, Anguilloidea, Muraenoidea or the family Muraenesocidae. Molecular evidence supports the placement of saccopharyngiforms within the anguilliforms and, within the limitations of our current taxonomic sample, it is consistent with the monophyly of the Synaphobranchidae, Derichthyidae (with the inclusion of Thalassenchelys), and Nemichthyidae. 22474: We studied the effect of curly tail lizards, Leiocephalus carinatus, on populations of the brown anole, Anolis sagrei, on small islands near Abaco, Bahamas. Over the course of six months, survival of adult lizards ranged from 6-88%. 22475: The flyingfishes exhibit one of the most spectacular evolutionary innovations in fishes: the ability to escape predators by making long gliding leaps from the water. 22476: In the Green Anole (Anolis carolinensis), yolk testosterone (T) concentration is greater in male- producing than in female-producing eggs at oviposition, but the source and potential effects were not clear from previous studies. 22482: We present the results of a phylogeographic analysis of the scincid lizard Lamprolepis smaragdina. This species has an unusual distribution in that it is absent from the Sunda Shelf of Southeast Asia but present throughout several remote island archipelagos including the Philippines, Sulawesi, the Moluccas, New Guinea, and the Solomon Islands, as well as remote island groups in the western Pacific such as Palau, the Caroline Islands, and the Mariana Islands. Many species with such wide-ranging distributions are thought to have reached these remote island groups through human-mediated dispersal. However, L. smaragdina exhibits sufficient phenotypic variation which leaves an open question as to whether it is a recent invader of these areas or an older clade with substantial cryptic or unrecognized species diversity. We collected approximately 1400 base pairs of mitochondrial sequence data representing the CO1 and ND2 protein-coding genes and flanking transfer RNAs and analyzed these data using Bayesian phylogenetic methods. Our analyses indicate that Lamprolepis smaragdina exhibits deep phylogenetic structure and almost certainly represents multiple species. However, the data suggest that species boundaries may be complex. For example, we have found two well- supported clades with representatives in more than one major biogeographic province (such as the Philippines and the Moluccas). We have also found good evidence of at least two species on Sulawesi. We will discuss these and other implications for the biogeography of Southeast Asia and the western Pacific in the context of our Lamprolepis data.

22483: Exotic species have been implicated in the decline of various amphibian populations in the western U.S. Using field survey data and information provided by USGS, we constructed a knowledge-engineered probability model for the presence/absence of red- legged frogs in pond ecosystems, based on a suite of measurable abiotic and biotic factors. We used the field data to construct prior probability distributions for the presence of bullfrog, red-leg frog, predatory fish and dragonfly larva, pond depth, riparian vegetation and water temperature into a Bayesian belief network. Unlike a standard habitat suitability index model, the network model allows interactions among factors, providing a more accurate posterior probability distribution for the presence or absence of red-legged frogs. The model also allows us to determine the significance of introduced amphibian competitors (bullfrogs), native predatory macroinvertebrate (dragonfly larvae) and introduced predatory fish (Centrarchids), relative to the abiotic factors. These community interactions are also the subject of a mesocosm experiment to test the effects of different density combinations of bullfrog tadpoles and bluegill on red-legged frog tadpoles using survival rate, metamorphosis rate, and growth rate as response variables. Our models not only provide insight to the roles of exotic species on red-legged frogs, but also provide a framework for the assessment of multiple stressors on amphibian populations.

22484: I performed stomach content analysis on three piscivorous fish species from the fore reef of Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii to evaluate whether small, cryptic fishes provide a trophic link between small, benthic arthropods (harpacticoid copepods, amphipods, isopods, tanaids and chironomids) and larger, commercially- and recreationally-important fishes. I used sagittal otoliths as taxonomic indicators and to estimate the size of fishes consumed. Overall, 82.4% of fish prey were identified to species. Dietary importance of small, cryptic fishes varied among piscivorous species. Nine small, cryptic fish species formed a large part of the diet of, Parupeneus cyclostomus (Mullidae), representing 83.2% of total prey items and 92.2% of fish consumed. The goby, Eviota epiphanes, was the most important prey type, representing 64.9% of total prey consumed and occurring in 56.3% of stomachs. The Triplefin Blenny, Enneapterygius atriceps was the second most important prey type, representing 9.2% of total prey consumed and occurring in 50.0% of stomachs. Five small, cryptic fish species formed a smaller portion of the diet of Paracirrhites forsteri (Cirrhitidae), representing 36.5% of total prey and 54.3% of fish consumed. Eviota epiphanes was again the most important prey item, representing 28.8% of total prey consumed and occurring in 27.6% of stomachs. The introduced Cephalopholis argus (Serranidae), ate only two small, cryptic fish species, which represented only 8.3% of total prey items, even though fish formed 83.3% of the diet. Despite their abundance and rapid turnover, small, benthic arthropods do not form a significant portion of the diets of larger fishes. 22485: Reproduction in populations of wild desert tortoises, Gopherus agassizii, has been difficult to characterize in the past due to cryptic nest sites and high predation rates. Data loggers were placed in each egg nest and also in several pseudonests located at shallower depths down the burrow in order to establish a temperature profile for each burrow. 22487: Seasonal drought in intermittent streams may adversely affect assemblage diversity and fish populations. We explored this hypothesis using data collected from upper tributaries of the Alum Fork of the Saline River drainage (central Arkansas) from July to October, 2003. These tributaries are hydrologically dynamic with pools that shrink and become isolated during summer. Principle components analysis indicated that most habitat variation during summer was related to changes in pool size, which were usually more dramatic upstream. Despite significant reductions in pool size over time, we found that pool drying had little effect on species richness, but significantly influenced community dynamics. We calculated extinction rate (ER), immigration rate (IR), and population growth rate (λ) and classified sites into three main groups of communities: sources (high I, low E, λ >> 1.0), sinks (low I, high E, λ < 1.0), and transitional meta-communities (moderate I, low E, λ > 1.0). Summer drying of pools resulted in an increase in the number of sinks which led to higher community nestedness at the end of summer. Our data generally support a hybrid source-sink and meta-population approach toward understanding extinction and recolonization processes in intermittent streams.

22488: We explored the population genetics among subpopulations of Lepomis megalotis (Longear Sunfish) from the Ouachita Highlands. Subpopulations are permanently fragmented into distinct regions by a large reservoir that likely has posed increased mortality risks to stream fishes for 65 yr. 22491: Western pond turtles (WPT) face numerous challenges in several areas throughout California where human disturbances continue to impact vulnerable populations. While habitat disturbance has detrimental effects on many reptile and amphibian populations throughout California, few studies have addressed the effects of disturbance on WPT populations. One such population in Big Chico Creek, part of Upper Bidwell Park, the second largest municipal park in the country, is a recreational hot-spot frequented by swimmers, hikers, bicyclists, equestrians, and fisherman. Further upstream, an undisturbed ecological preserve, is home to a large and healthy population of WPTs that lacks appropriate management. To examine how these populations of WPTs were using their aquatic habitat in both disturbed and undisturbed environments, I used a fixed quadrat sampling method to measure habitat characteristics. Results show that although available habitat was similar in both disturbed and undisturbed areas, the use of habitat differed between the two populations. Additionally, as a result of human impacts size class distributions and sex ratios were heavily skewed.

22492: Red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) assess predation risk by sampling substrate chemicals. In laboratory studies, when red-backed salamanders encounter chemical cues from garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis) that have recently fed on P. cinereus, the salamanders prefer a distilled water substrate over one with the predator cue. Field studies suggest that this cue does not persist indefinitely. Variables that could potentially influence cue life include evaporation, diffusion, physical deterioration, degradation by microorganisms, or chemical reactions with soil constituents. We examined the role of microorganisms in limiting cue life by aging the cue under sterile and non-sterile conditions. Similar experiments were conducted in which the cue was aged in nearby spring water or in a soil rinse. When given a choice of treatment or control substrates for an hour in laboratory tests, salamanders continued to avoid snake cues aged in distilled water or a soil rinse, regardless of sterility. Salamanders did not appear to avoid the sterile cue that had been aged in spring water, but since microorganisms were absent from this treatment, a factor other than microbial degradation must have been responsible for the loss of cue effectiveness.
22493: Given the rapid loss of amphibian populations, it is crucial that we be able to identify, monitor, and predict factors that may pose threats to native populations. One such threat is establishment and invasion by the African clawed frog, Xenopus laevis. Herein, we develop and validate ecological niche models to predict the potential invasive distribution of this species in North America. Results indicate that a large area, including most of the central and eastern United States, is suitable for the species. Xenopus laevis is potentially a very successful invader, and has been shown to decimate local fauna; as such, it poses a primary threat to native amphibian populations. Because of the enormous popularity in research laboratories and the pet trade of this species, we suggest that further legislation regulating possession of this species, particularly in the central and eastern United States, be pursued.

22494: Current techniques for censusing reptile populations involve coarse identification of suitable habitat and subsequent surveys via transect sampling or pit fall arrays. I developed wildlife- habitat predictive models for Phrynosoma coronatum, Sceloporus orcutti, S. graciosus vandenburgianus, Cnemidophorus hyperythrus and C. tigris stejnegeri to identify locations that are similar to those where modeled species were observed. 22495: Gambusia geiseri is among those poeciliids long believed to provision embyros only through yolk deposition prior to fertilization. 22497: The Least Brook lamprey, Lampetra aepyptera, is a non-parasitic form widely distributed in the eastern US. It exhibits a 3-5 year ammocoete stage, depending on the population. Recent molecular evidence suggests that it shares a common ancestor with a European species, L. fluviatilis. Sequences were obtained from at least 3 individuals in 8 populations and compared to published sequences of other species in the genus. Thirteen different haplotypes were detected that differed by an average of 13 substitutions. The transition to transversion ratio was 3.5:1. The populations of Least Brook lamprey formed a monophyletic group whose sister taxon was L. fluviatilis. Several well-supported clades were identified within this monophyletic group, Upper Ohio River, Alabama, Maryland, Missouri, Terrapin Creek (neotenic), and Western Tennessee. However, the relationships among these clades were not well-supported. Specimens from other populations as well as control region sequences are being surveyed in order to further resolve the relationships among the clades.

22498: The spectacular reproductive behavior of beach-spawning grunion is justifiably well known, but their early life history is equally remarkable. Incubation of grunion eggs takes place fully out of water, with the embryos buried in damp sand. Hatching competence occurs at about 10 days after fertilization but hatching itself is delayed until the embryos are mechanically triggered to emerge by agitation in seawater. This interaction of life history and environment permits survival during the terrestrial incubation period and a rapid switch to aquatic life upon hatching. Since hatching can be triggered at any time after hatching competence has been reached, we are able to perform detailed analyses of the metabolic and behavioral events leading up to the moment of larval emergence. The anamniotic eggs of fish typically require two steps to hatch, an initial softening of the chorion by enzyme action, followed by embryonic exertion to free itself from the confines of its casing. We examined the process of hatching by biochemical assays, by interfering with different steps, and by high-speed videography through a microscope. We found that hatching takes place almost immediately after the presentation of the hatching trigger, within approximately two minutes. Hatching can be temporarily prevented by anaesthetizing the embryos with MS-222, and is inhibited in water of decreased salinity. A hatching enzyme is present, structurally related to the astacin family of metalloproteases. Prior to hatching, grunion embryos make several characteristic movements that are associated with deformation of the chorion, accompanied by leakage of perivitelline fluid. The chorion ruptures, rapidly followed by escape of the free swimming larva. We describe these actions in the first published detailed examination of the process of hatching in a lower vertebrate. 22499: Repeatability of individual differences in performance plays a central role in linking functional and evolutionary investigations of animal performance. Long-term measures of repeatability are particularly important when locomotor performance is used to predict lifetime fitness, because the performance of individuals may vary over time due to physiological or behavioral changes. For metamorphosed individuals of a semi-aquatic plethodontid salamander (Pseudotriton ruber), I examined (1) both short- and long-term repeatability of burst speed under the same environmental conditions, and (2) short-term repeatability of burst speed under different environmental conditions (i.e., aquatic versus terrestrial, low versus high temperature). The repeatability of both aquatic and terrestrial locomotor performance declined over time. Terrestrial burst speed exhibited significant short- (<3 months) and long-term (>1 yr) repeatability, whereas the repeatability of aquatic burst speed was significant only over the short term. For both swimming and running, there was a positive correlation between burst speeds at low (8 C) and high (18 C) temperature, but the correlation was significant only during running. A positive correlation between aquatic and terrestrial speeds was not significant at either low or high temperature. Differences in short- and long-term repeatability of locomotor performance show that multiple measurements over long time intervals may be needed to quantify accurately the lifetime performance profiles of plethodontid salamanders. Variation in the repeatability of burst speed under different conditions indicates that researchers should not assume that inter-individual variation in performance is consistent among different environments for a given species.
